#8362. ‘It’s Trailer Park Chemistry.’ A Hybrid Bighorn Sheep Is on the Lam and That Could Be Bad News for Wild Herds

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:47 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The two-paragraph Sept. 18 news release from Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks raised more questions than it may have intended.

The department “is seeking help from the public to locate a hybridized female rocky mountain bighorn sheep that went missing from a private alternative livestock facility near Vaughn in early September,” the release from FWP’s Region 4 office in Great Falls stated. “The bighorn ewe is described as weighing about 120 pounds and is primarily white in color with a red ear tag.”

The news release stressed wildlife officials’ concern that the ewe could come into contact with wild bighorn sheep in the vicinity. Domestic sheep are often vectors for pathogens that can fatally infect wild sheep.

What the news release didn’t disclose is that the “alternative livestock facility” in question is owned by Arthur “Jack” Schubarth, who was convicted in 2024 of violating the federal Lacey Act in his pursuit to create giant hybrid bighorn rams. Schubarth pleaded guilty to helping smuggle genetic material from Marco Polo argali sheep from Kyrgyzstan into the United States in order to clone the ram and create a “super sheep” with huge spiraling horns and resistance to the pathogens that infect North American wild sheep. His quest was enabled by Montana hunting outfitter John Lewton, who lopped off the testicles of his clients’ trophy wild bighorns, kept the gonads on ice, and later sold them to Schubarth.

The idea, Schubarth later told court officials, was to use the genetic material to incubate hybrid sheep with horns larger than any North American rams.

Lewton was sentenced last week in federal court in Billings and received a $20,000 fine and a year of probation for his part in the genetic alchemy. As a condition of his federal-court sentence, Lewton is prohibited from outfitting or guiding hunters for a full year.

The notion that a “Frankenram” could be produced with a combination of cloned embryos and artificial insemination isn’t an abstraction. In 2017, Schubarth actually produced what he called the Montana Mountain King, a pure cloned Marco Polo ram birthed to a surrogate bighorn ewe. Schubarth subsequently bred offspring of the Montana Mountain King to captive bighorn ewes on his farm west of Great Falls. It’s one of these ewes that has now gone missing, according to Fish, Wildlife & Parks.

Schubarth’s genetic hermetics has both baffled and impressed wildlife investigators, who told Outdoor Life that the sort of reproductive science that Schubarth practiced is normally limited to hospitals, universities, and other science centers with state-of-the-art facilities.

“The best way to describe his operation is trailer-park chemistry,” said a source familiar with the case who spoke on background. “He’s pulled off a pretty high-level genetics program with hardware-store gear and limited resources.”

Schubarth received probation for his guilty plea to the Lacey Act violations. In his petition to the federal court for leniency, Schubarth’s attorney, Jason Holden, noted his client’s contribution to the science of wildlife propagation.

“Jack is an 81-year-old non-violent man,” Holden wrote in 2024. “His crime, the cloning of a Marco Polo Sheep from Kyrgyzstan, has ruined his life, reputation and family. Jack did something no one else could, or has ever done. On a ranch, in a barn in Montana, he created Montana Mountain King. MMK is an extraordinary animal, born of science, and from a man who, if he could rewrite history, would have left the challenge of cloning a Marco Polo to only the imagination of Michael Crichton.”

Read Next: Montana Man Charged for Illegally Cloning and Breeding Marco Polo Sheep from Central Asia

The department’s all-points-bulletin asking the public to report a lone and roaming ewe may not produce any sightings. That’s because there’s a possibility that the ewe isn’t actually on the lam. She may have been sold to an out-of-state game farm, said sources who spoke to Outdoor Life on the condition that they wouldn’t be identified based on the speculative nature of their hunches.

Schubarth, who is on probation from the 2024 federal wildlife-trafficking charges, has been charged by FWP with failure to report the escape of an animal permitted in his commercial wildlife operation, according to charging documents at the Cascade County District Court in Montana.

The “game farm” permit requires that if anything escapes the permitted facility, owners must report within 48 hours to both FWP and the Montana Department of Livestock.

“According to our records, the ewe in question reportedly escaped on Sept. 2, and our game wardens heard about it the next week,” says Dave Hagengruber, FWP’s public information officer in the Great Falls regional office. “Wardens went out to talk with Schubarth in mid-September, and he basically said, ‘Oh yeah, I meant to tell you.’”

Schubarth told wardens the ewe likely escaped either over a fence damaged by a wind storm or through a gate accidentally left open at the end of his property, beyond lines of kennels of dogs that produce puppies sold in Schubarth’s pet store in Great Falls.

Assuming the ewe did leave Schubarth’s facility, it could pose a risk to the region’s wild sheep.

“Cascade is 30 miles from his farm, and there’s a sizeable band of [wild] bighorns there,” says Hagengruber. “The Birdtail Hills are 20 to 25 miles to the west, and there are bighorns in those hills. The Rocky Mountain Front, home to Montana’s most treasured bighorn sheep herd, is 60 or 70 miles west. Fortunately, this is not a ram, so it’s less likely to roam widely, but the threat of disease transmission is a significant concern. That’s why we want to hear of any sightings. It’s Jack’s property and his responsibility to locate and return to his facility, but we can’t have this hybrid sheep potentially contacting wild bands.”

Schubarth insists he did not sell the ewe, and suspects the fugitive sheep was killed by predators within a few miles of his facility in the Sun River Valley.

“I haven’t heard anything about her, and to my knowledge Fish and Game hasn’t heard anything for five weeks now,” Schubarth said in an interview. “With all the people out looking, we haven’t seen it and no one’s called me. I’m assuming, with her lack of experience with predators, that a coyote got her.”

“She’s mainly bighorn and probably three or four domestic crosses from the original cross that was 50 percent bighorn,” Schubarth said. “I added some more bighorn from that original [parentage]. So they’re probably 62.5 percent bighorn. They don’t have any experience of being wild. I’m pretty sure she would have watched coyotes walk right up to her” without trying to evade them.

Schubarth further confirmed that he still has “around 45 head of sheep, is all” remaining on his 200-acre game farm. “All my sheep are sold right now and just waiting to leave. I’ve kept them back because I just want the pleasure of birthing out the lambs. It’s something I like to do, and at 83 years old, I like to see new life.”

As for the descendants of the Montana Mountain King, Schubarth said that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service required him to destroy progeny of the cloned ram back in 2024. The federal court also required Schubarth to dispose of all hybrid bighorn sheep by Dec. 31, 2025, and to stop “from engaging in breeding activity of big game stock while on supervision,” according to sentencing documents.

“We had 190 head of the hybrid Marco/bighorn here at the ranch and none of them got pneumonia in the three years I held them while waiting for a forever home for them. All were slaughtered,” he says. “I did sell some, 15 in all. There are some down in Texas, and every so often I see on Facebook somebody advertising a Marco Polo, but there’s no way they are more than about a quarter Marco” based on genetic dilution, he said.

As for the Montana Mountain King himself, Schubarth says the ram ended up at a zoological park in upstate New York. Indeed, last summer the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York, announced the acquisition of “Tilek,” the cloned argali at the center of Schubarth’s case. The ram had been held at an Oregon wildlife rehabilitation center for over three years before being moved to the Syracuse zoo.

Schubarth says “Tilek” would be about nine years old, but observed that he has not yet expressed the most distinctive trait of the Marco Polo subspecies of argali: its spiraling horns.

“He’s basically still 54 to 57 inches,” says Schubarth. “He ought to have 75 inches of horn on each side. But this year they put him in a larger grass pen so maybe he’ll grow more. For safety’s sake, they should have castrated him so no more genetics could get out there. Maybe they did, for all I know. I’ll never see him again. I don’t ever leave my ranch.”

Schubarth said that statements from prosecutors that he was motivated to create a hybrid ram with giant horns in order to upsell to commercial shooting operations are wrong. He was more interested in cross-breeding to create a bighorn race that might be resistant to what’s often called “M. ovi,” a respiratory disease that often results in catastrophic pneumonia-caused die-offs in wild sheep.

“My thinking was that here’s this wild sheep that has evolved with domestic sheep for thousands of years,” says Schubarth of the Marco Polo, native to the high alpine plateaus of central Asia. “The feds and Fish and Game made it out that I was selling to the hunt community and only motivated to create bigger horns. In actuality, I was after the immune system, and the reality is that even after several generations, these Marco hybrids still seem to be immune to pneumonia. I think that’s the real story.”

If he regrets anything about the misadventures of the Montana Mountain King, it’s that he trusted the lab that created the clone from genetic tissue smuggled from Kyrgyzstan.

“I’ve been happy all my life except for this last foolishness about the Marco Polo,” Schubarth says. “I wouldn’t have done it had the cloning company not told me it was legal. They lied after they took $32,000 from me. That was the cost of stockpiling the tissue and making the embryos for me.”

The rest of the genetic work was a cinch, he says. The surrogate bighorn ewes, most of which Schubarth bought from zoos in Canada and Colorado, were selected for their ability to carry the hybrid lamb.

“Laparoscopic work is easy,” he says, and artificial insemination is an established livestock practice. The trick is creating a genetically manipulated zygote.

“You take the egg and suck out the product and you put the material from the Marco Polo into the egg and implant it in a ewe. A little electricity, and poof, the thing starts to grow.”

Schubarth says he will be entirely out of the game-breeding business by 2027.

“Fish and Game has accomplished what they always wanted: to drive me out of business,” he says.

Meanwhile, he says the captive-shooting industry is thriving. He cites high-fence operations in Kansas and Texas that would pay top dollar for his hybrid bighorns while also insisting that he sold to fellow breeders, not trophy hunters.

“The feds made it out that I was the center of this industry based on shooting animals in pens,” he says, before acknowledging that most of his animals probably met that fate. “Without the interest of the hunting community, these animals would be worthless and only sold for meat. So yes, the industry revolves around the harvesting of these animals by collectors.”

Fish, Wildlife & Parks is less interested in the commercial than in the pathological outcome of the case. The state has struggled to establish bighorn sheep populations in prime habitat in the Missouri River Breaks and in the mountains of southwest Montana. Bands that thrive for years are often wiped out in a single season by pneumonia epizootics that often originate in domestic sheep.

State game wardens are authorized to shoot on sight wild bighorns that contact domestic sheep. The fear is that a traveling ram could become infected by a domestic sheep, and then take that pathogen back to the wild herd.

“We have spent many years and sportsmen’s dollars to restore and transplant wild sheep into available habitat in Montana,” says FWP’s Hagengruber. “We’ve had recent restorations in the Belts and the Breaks, and disease is always a big concern, and so is the ability of this hybrid ewe to breed with either domestic or wild sheep. So we take the possibility that there may be a hybrid domestic/wild sheep running around central Montana very seriously.”

Anyone who sees a lone sheep with a red ear tag in central Montana is urged to call FWP’s Region 4 office at 406-454-5840.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8360. How to Field Dress a Deer Like a Pro: The Ultimate Step-By-Step Guide

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:10 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Learning (or remembering) how to field dress a deer can feel overwhelming, but if you have a sharp knife and a reasonably strong stomach, you’ll be able to figure it out. If you manage to do so without nicking the guts or yourself, that’s ideal.

Removing the guts is the bare minimum required for dropping a deer at a processor, and an essential skill every deer hunter should learn. A field-dressed deer is also a lighter deer, which makes dragging and loading it less cumbersome. And the sooner you gut a deer after shooting it, the better the venison will be. So, here’s a guide on how to field dress a deer in a few easy steps.

All you really need to gut a deer is a sharp knife and, if it’s getting dark, a good headlamp. Other deer hunters carry the kitchen sink with them and won’t field dress a deer without some or all of the following items:

Many experienced deer hunters can field dress a deer in minutes, while it can take new or casual deer hunters a half hour or more. The best way to gut a deer is to work slowly, use a sharp knife, and have adequate lighting.

Keep these gutting rules in mind before you get started:

Start by rolling the deer onto its back. It should be belly-up and evenly balanced on both shoulder blades. Adjust the rump and hips to ensure they’re as even as possible. If you’re working on a slope, rotate the deer so its rump points downhill and its head is uphill.

Ask a buddy to hold a leg. If you’re solo and the deer keeps slipping sideways or downhill, try wedging a log or stick under its rump or using paracord to tie a hind leg to a branch. Personally, I find paracord to be overkill, but will sometimes use my knee, shoulder, or armpit to anchor a hind leg or keep it out of the way as I work.

This step and the next can be done now or after opening the abdominal cavity. Grab a handful of the mammary gland, or testicles with your non-dominant hand and lift away from the deer’s body. Keeping your blade mostly parallel to the deer’s body, slice away at the base of the stretched hide until you’ve freed the reproductive organs, and toss aside. The goal is to avoid cutting into the organs and instead cutting under them.

This step can be done later or not at all, but I prefer to do this now (particularly when working alone) since it relaxes the tension between the hind legs and prevents your deer from rolling on you. It also creates more space to work while removing internal organs. I butcher my own deer and this does not sacrifice any of the meat on the hindquarters when done correctly.

Cut the muscle between the two back legs to expose the center of the pelvic bone. Find what looks like dead center on the meat between the two back legs and cut down (usually a few inches) from the top of the pelvis to the anus. Stay as close to the center as possible to avoid gouging the roasts on either leg. Don’t saw the muscle. Slice it instead, letting the downward pressure of your blade do the cutting.

Insert your knife tip into the side (not the center) of the anus. Keeping your blade pressed against the bone that encircles the rectum, cut around the rectum rather than through it. The goal is to cut the connective tissue so you can pull the tube of intestines out rather than dice it up.

This abdominal cut is often the most difficult for hunters, and the key here is not to puncture the deer’s stomach or bladder because you don’t want to get any bile or urine on the meat.

Prevent stabbing the guts by turning your knife blade up (toward the sky) and tilting it so the blade is more parallel to the deer’s belly rather than perpendicular. Working close to the base of the belly, grab a handful of hide and pull it up to create some space between the layer of hide and the organs beneath. Insert the tip of your knife and make an incision until you see (or more likely, feel with the knife tip) empty space below it. Keep the incision shallow and make the slit long enough to work a finger or two of your off-hand in the space. Take care to not insert the blade too far into the abdominal cavity.

Now that you’ve made an opening incision, apply even upward pressure with your knife blade to “unzip” the abdomen, or make a lengthwise cut along the deer from pelvis to breastbone. This is similar to using a pair of scissors to slice a piece of wrapping paper in a single, fluid motion. Don’t saw with your knife.

The organs you’re ultimately trying to remove lie in two groups: the guts (liver, stomach, intestines, bladder, kidneys, fat if present, etc.) and the vitals (heart and lungs). These two groups are separated by the diaphragm: a thin wall of purple muscle between the abdominal cavity and the rib cage.

Note: If you plan to shoulder mount your deer, do not split the ribs. You should only make your cut to the base of the lower ribcage (above) and stop there, since your taxidermist will need all that hide from the ribs to the tip of the nose (this is called the cape).

If you are planning on a skull mount or you aren’t mounting your deer at all, you can split the ribs if you want. Your blade will encounter some resistance once you hit the rib cage. If you center your knife, you can slice through cartilage in the breastplate before hitting bone. Some hunters use a hatchet or saw to split the rib cage open, but a stout fixed-blade knife will also work. Splitting the rib cage makes it easier to see (and therefore remove) the heart and lungs, but isn’t necessary if you are having trouble cutting through it. This step is especially useful if you suspect a broadhead is lodged in the rib cage.

Personally, I just carry a slim field-dressing knife when I hunt and skip this step altogether during rifle season. I don’t mind reaching into the rib cage to remove the lungs, heart, and windpipe by feel.

To access the heart and lungs in the rib cage (and ultimately free everything) you need to cut the diaphragm. Use the tip of your knife to puncture this thin layer of muscle, then circle the entire rib cage, keeping your knife close to the ribs. Once the diaphragm has been cut away, blood and jellied bits of lung usually slosh into the abdominal cavity. This is perfectly normal (and a sign of a good shot).

Work from the top of deer down toward the pelvis. If you split open the rib cage this part will be easier; if not, you’ll have to do it more by feel.

At the top of the chest cavity, you’ll see or feel a large ribbed tube. That’s the windpipe. Cut it crossways (perpendicular to the spine), then use a finger or two to grab ahold of it from the inside and begin pulling it up and away. This will begin to loosen the heart and lungs.

Grab hold of the heart and/or lungs with your off-hand and pull while continuing to cut connective tissue along the spine. Keep going all the way down to the pelvis and keep working until the stomach and guts come loose, too. Because all the organs are attached to the deer along the spine, it can be helpful to tilt the deer on its side for this part so the organs roll out of your way and reveal their connection point.

As everything loosens, just roll the guts and intestines out of the deer and onto the ground. Note: If you haven’t yet separated the rectum from the anus, the guts will still connect to the carcass by a single tube — that’s the lower large intestines, or colon. To free the guts and toss aside, slice the colon crossways just above the pelvis and tie it off (if it’s full) so pellets don’t spill inside your deer.

Read Next: How to Skin a Deer, Step by Step

To field dress big game with a hatchet, use it as you would a big belt knife, opening the paunch with a small incision at the base of the sternum. Then, tip the blade at right angles to the animal, with the handle up and your fingers spreading the skin close to the blade as you run it to the rectum. Do not try to cut the skin down into the animal; hair will collect on and dull the blade. Dump the entrails.

To quarter the carcass, hang it or set it belly-up on the ground. Loosen hams with careful strokes tight against the pelvis and through the ball joints. Don’t chop; use the blade like a knife, your fist around the hatchet head (inset). Remove the shoulders the same way, leaving the skin on unless you must remove it to let a big animal, like an elk or moose, cool in warm weather. The hatchet (or, better yet, a slim double-bit ax) excels at splitting the backbone. Hang the animal head down, rear legs spread, to facilitate this task. —Wayne Van Zwoll

It’s always best to gut your deer as soon as possible, but the window you have depends on the weather and the shot you made. If the weather is hot or even mild, the sooner you field dress your deer, the better. Within an hour of the shot is ideal in these conditions. If it’s cold, a deer can last longer before it needs to be gutted — hours or even overnight if you have to back out while blood trailing. It’s always easier to dress a deer when it’s warm and pliable.

The best knives for field dressing are usually a fixed-blade knife with a sharp blade. A smaller, handier blade makes certain tasks easier, like removing the colon and avoiding puncturing the guts. A larger, stouter blade is easier for heavy-duty tasks like splitting the ribs.

Field-dressing a deer isn’t difficult once you get the hang of it, and it’s usually easier with a buddy to help hold a leg or a light. Use a sharp knife, make slow, deliberate cuts at connective tissue. Do your best to avoid puncturing the stomach or bladder, but don’t panic if you do. More important is to avoid cutting yourself. The process may be messy or unpleasant, but ultimately you’ll end up with a cooling carcass ready for the skinning shed or processor.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8359. Why 5 Days of Heat Training May Be Enough

In a perfect world, we’d spend the month (or more) leading up to toasty races like the Javelina Jundred training to handle the heat. Actually, in a perfect world, we would heat train all year round to reap the potential physiological rewards, such as increased plasma volume, and maybe even improved Vo2 max and lactate threshold.

But we’re not all pros with flexible schedules and not everyone lives in the Arizona desert, where the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit.

The last thing any of us want is to succumb to hot conditions, much less end up in the med tent, because we were too busy for heat training. But many heat training protocols call for weeks and even months of heat sessions to induce positive physiological adaptations; time we don’t often have to spare while juggling work, sleep, family obligations, and the ever-important logging of miles.

So when I found out that endurance gravel cyclist Metheven Bond claimed he managed to acclimate to the heat in only 5 days, I was curious: Can runners implement a similar protocol?

Off his 5-day protocol, Bond rode for 43 hours and 6 minutes with no sleep through the sweltering desert of Eastern Andalusia to finish sixth overall in The Badlands. If you’re unfamiliar with the gravel cycling race, Badlands runs some 507 miles across the Gorafe and Tabernas deserts in Spain,where temperatures regularly exceed 104 F.

To find out exactly what he did and how it may apply to runners, I spoke with Bond himself, as well as Aline Barre, a competitive ultra-cyclist and triathlete with a master’s degree in Sports Performance Analysis, and Daniel Snape, Ph.D., a performance physiologist, accredited sport and exercise scientist, and researcher in endurance and environmental physiology.

Earlier this year, Bond, who races for Ribble Outliers gravel cycling team, competed in some hot races in Spain and Switzerland. Temperatures reached nearly 97 degrees.

“I fell apart even though I thought I did everything right,” he told Trail Runner. “I froze all of my bottles and was drinking over a liter an hour for hydration, but my power still dropped off a cliff, my heart rate was through the roof, and I couldn’t think properly. I knew it was from the heat.”

Racing in hot conditions can compromise endurance capacity, and, as Bond discovered the hard way, it’s not always enough to rely on mid-race cooling. “I needed to find ways to adapt so the heat bothers me less, so I looked into heat acclimation.”

The goal of heat acclimation is to cause adaptations that allow the body to more effectively function in high temps. That process involves exposing the body to hot conditions that cause core body temperature to rise. Done long and consistently enough adaptations can include a lowered heart rate and body temperature, a higher sweat rate, improved performance, and better heat resilience.

“Before Badlands, I looked at the weather forecast and knew the heat was going to be bad. I’m in the North of England where it’s colder and somehow needed to get ready to be thrown into the heat,” Bond said. He visited the lab of Precision Fuel and Hydration, a sponsor of Ribble Outliers, for a focused heat training block. There, the Precision team implemented a protocol before Badlands consisting of five one-hour heat training sessions of cycling in a heat chamber set to 102 degrees over five consecutive days.

The team monitored Bond’s performance markers—such as heat transfer and skin temperature—throughout the block via sensors like the Core 2 Thermal Sensor, which mounts to any heart rate strap and transmits data in real-time to an app or wearable.

As the sessions progressed, Bond was able to push harder without a corresponding increase in cardiovascular effort. The result: Higher power output, lower average heart rate, and improved resistance to the fatigue of heat stress.

Aline Barre is a cyclist, triathlete, and endurance performance lead at Core. Like Bond, Barre had an equally unpleasant experience racing in the heat.

“My first endurance race was Ironman Frankfurt. For training, I didn’t do any running in the heat,” Barre said. “Race day was super hot and I was cooked. I was drinking a lot, but I felt horrible during the run. I was so afraid of the heat that I went to Finland for my second Ironman.”

Barre concluded the heat was holding her back—until she focused on acclimation. “Heat training is even more important for ultrarunners than endurance cyclists. In most cases, it’s easier to cycle in the heat than to run in the heat,” she said. “That’s because you move forward at a faster pace when riding a bike than running, creating substantially more airflow to help cool your skin through sweat evaporation.”

Combine this with the fact that running creates higher metabolic heat than cycling and it’s no wonder that medical teams see more cases of heat stroke at endurance running events than at cycling races. Additionally, some studies suggest that female athletes may require a slightly longer heat exposure period (10-14 days) or stronger heat stimulus relative to male athletes (seven days) to fully develop certain adaptations, particularly those related to sweating

“Most athletes see the majority of gains after 4-5 heat sessions and the full adaptation after doing 10 to 12 sessions within two to six weeks,” Barre said.

But for Bond, five days was enough. Performance physiologist and researcher Daniel Snape explains why.

“When you heat train, the main response you get is an increase in your blood plasma volume. For Bond to increase his plasma volume across those five days is a very normal and achievable response,” Snape said. Snape is part of a team of experts at the Health and Performance Hub at Leeds Beckett University. He works with professional ultrarunners like 2025 UTMB winners Tom Evans and Ruth Croft to develop specific heat acclimation strategies.

“Also you’re becoming more familiar with the heat, so your body doesn’t have that: ‘Oh no, I’ve got to increase my heart rate to cope with this stressor’ fight or flight response. That’s why five days straight was enough time for Bond to adapt and be able to hold a higher power output at a lower heart rate.”

While five days may be enough for a professional male endurance athlete who has a stellar baseline and access to a heat chamber, core body temperature sensor, and a team of experts, it might not be for many ultrarunners.

“Even I had to continue with three sessions per week of heat acclimation at home to maintain the adaptation, riding wrapped up in layers. I kept this up until a week before Badlands, when it was time to taper,” Bond said. He also points out that while significant adaptations can occur in five days, a few weeks is preferable for the mental preparation.

“The more times you train in the heat, the more confidence you have when you face it on race day,” he said. “You think: ‘Okay, it’s uncomfortable, but not as uncomfortable because I’ve been exposed to it. I’m used to this’.”

If you’re short on time and you want to have some semblance of conditioning going into Javelina or another toasty ultra, Core has a simple but mighty indoor heat training plan to build heat into your workouts with five sessions over 2 weeks. (See below.) It includes a long run where you start cool, then dress in warm layers for the last 75 minutes, as well as an easy 50-minute run where you run cool, but add a 30-minute passive heat session after.

The long run  is best done inside on a treadmill, but a smart trainer, stationary bike, or even a rowing machine will work as well. For your layers, you’ll need clothing that is non-permeable and traps heat against your body,  such as a heat suit, thermal top, down jacket, rain jacket, fleecy sweat suit, and/or wool hat. As a last resort, Bond recommends using a trash bag with holes cut out for your head and arms.

The passive heat session consists of time in a sauna, steam room, hot tub, or even the bathtub. If you’re preparing for a hot desert race, a sauna is the way to go if you can access one. Research shows that repeated post-exercise sauna sessions can enhance key components of heat adaptation, such as blood plasma volume and thermoregulatory efficiency. To prepare for a trail run in the tropics, a steam room or steamy bath are the best options.

Alternatively, you can do a micro heat training block that includes five days of only passive heat sessions immediately after your normal training runs, when your heart rate and core temperature are still elevated. According to Dr. Snape, even this can be effective at improving performance come race day.

The benefits of heat training extend beyond simply ramping up for a 100-miler under the desert sun, however.

“With the sauna for example, we know that if you do a hill workout, then go into the sauna, it has some muscle hypertrophy benefits, helping with recovery,” Snape said. “We also know that saunas improve your immune function. And if you do a sauna session late at night, it can actually improve sleep quality.”

Before starting a heat training plan, you should already be used to training for a minimum of four days per week and at least four hours of total weekly volume. You should also be able to complete a 60-to 75-minute run workout.

“You can do heat training right up until taper week. But don’t start heat training too close to your race. If you start two weeks before your race, the chance is quite high that you’ll expose your body to unnecessary fatigue because it’s not used to the heat,” Barre said. “We recommend starting four to five weeks out. During heat sessions, monitor your skin temperature, sweat rate, and heart rate so you don’t overdo it or get a heat illness, which can be life-threatening if you’re not careful. And hydrate before, during, and after heat sessions.”

It’s important to note that even if you use a Core sensor as part of your heat acclimation protocol, you can’t wear it into saunas or your bathtub at home, so there’s no way of knowing your internal body temperature during those passive sessions. As such, active and passive heat training should only be done when someone else is with you or in a nearby room.

“Any heat acclimation protocol will induce a training stress. Respect it as an additional thing to recover from,” Snape said. “That means you will have to take some training off the table elsewhere when undergoing a heat training block. That could mean cutting nine hours of running down to eight hours.”

Heat acclimation doesn’t have to be a part-time job. If you have time for 7-14 heat sessions during or after the run workouts on your training plan, you should experience full adaptations. But if you only have time for a 5-day heat adaptation block, it’s still more beneficial than not training for the heat at all, helping you develop a base adaptation that can make it mentally and physically easier to stay on pace when the heat is on.

#8358. ‘Squirrels as Big as House Cats.’ We Competed in the Greatest Squirrel Dog Contest in the Country

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

“Neighbor down the road had a squirrel dog,” said Larry White as he led a cast of dogs and hunters to the woods. “Got its legs cut off by a mowing machine. Had to hunt that dog from a wheelbarrow.

“One day a friend asked to borrow the dog, so the owner explained that you had to push the wheelbarrow in whatever direction the dog pointed his nose. If he barked, the track was hot, so you pushed faster. When he looked up and barked, he had the squirrel treed and you got a shot. The friend came back late that night with no squirrels. His clothes were torn to shreds and his skin was scratched up and looked like a road map. ‘What in the world happened to you?’ the hound’s owner asked.

“‘What’s it look like?’ the friend snapped. ‘Your fool squirrel dog hit a deer and we ran that thing all day long!'”

Larry White was judging a cast in the 1981 World Champion Squirrel Hunt. His tale got a laugh, but it also emphasized the importance of handler/dog teamwork in any form of hunting.

A good squirrel dog works for the hunter by locating squirrels through scent on the ground and on trees as well as by seeing and following bushytails moving through the treetops. The dog’s manner of barking signals its degree of progress to the hunter. A good hunter works for the dog by staying keenly and constantly aware of what the barking means and by following almost within sight so he can get to the tree quickly and shoot the squirrel before it escapes.

Good competition squirrel dogs are more decisive, accurate and consistent than average squirrel dogs. They do the job with less wasted time and motion.

Squirrel-treeing talent always has been wherever you found it, but these days some unusual dogs are showing up in the woods. Chuck Trehern’s purebred Doberman pinscher learned to bark up a tree by watching the family coonhounds. Ronnie Liles’ 6-year-old Australian shepherd, Smokey, was never taught: he just started treeing squirrels. T.C. Jones won the 1980 Championship with a registered liver and white English pointer! Trophies similar to bowling trophies are awarded. The statuettes portray a dog barking treed.

Most squirrel dogs are not pedigreed, however. Two Illinois dogs were described as terrier and feist crosses. Randy Pannell, who trains 15 to 20 squirrel dogs every year, came over from Blue Springs, Mississippi, with a redtick coonhound/mountain cur cross. Fola Hart brought a Norwegian elkhound/feist cross from Virginia. And the 1981 winner was Orville Hart’s “Whiskey,” a 4-year-old Norwegian elkhound/feist from Leesburg, Ohio.

Feists, those wiry little mongrels that are intelligent enough to learn any job on the farm, are becoming rare because most people prefer to keep purebred dogs. As a result, many squirrel hunters are making their own mongrels by crossing two different purebreds. There’s a constant search for the best dog, and that’s one reason why Dick Sheets thought up the World Champion Squirrel Hunt.

Sheets reasoned that squirrel-dog competition would not only preserve and enlarge the sport, but that the dogs would improve through breeding. Perhaps breeds of purebred squirrel dogs of consistent ability would emerge from such an effort. The Yockanookany Coon Hunters Association of Ethel, Mississippi, agreed with Sheets and sponsored the first championship in 1980.

Yockanookany is Choctaw for “crawls on belly like snake” and also applies to the way hunters must cross a spongy swamp. The 100-mile-long Yockanookany Swamp is just two miles from the club grounds.

By 1981, competition had already influenced squirrel-dog breeding. L.E. Goutierez came over from Louisiana with two pups out of the 1980 second-place winner. The pups’ dam was Spot, his own small Chihuahua/feist cross.

Goutierez arrived a day early, pitched his tent and drove his dogs down the old Natchez Trace to the nearby woods where they could become accustomed to hunting new territory. The original Natchez Trace, which was once an extensive trading trail between the Indian tribes, runs right past the Yockanookany club grounds. The entire area is well forested with both hill-country and creek-bottom squirrel habitat.

Little Spot ran through the woods with her nose slightly down, searching for scent on the ground, on logs and on fallen limbs. Every tree got a sniff as she trotted past. But the squirrels weren’t moving. When Spot finally barked, L.E. didn’t become excited. “She scatter-barked,” he said. “It’s a cold track.”

Scatter barking is barking here and there instead of barking enthusiastically in one place such as on a hot trail or at a tree.

By the end of the championship hunt, Goutierez had learned one more thing about breeding squirrel dogs. “Have to get more size in my dogs,” he said. “My dogs can’t compete with the longer-legged, wider-running dogs.”

Four dogs were cast together in the first running of the championship in 1980 and many handlers thought that that was three too many. By nature, squirrel dogs do best alone. They’re highly intelligent, very independent and more than a little jealous of their relationships with their human partners. In 1981, a compromise was struck: only two dogs to a cast—male and female, if possible—and in weight categories of under and over 35 pounds.

The only reported fight occurred when the Doberman’s handler decided to be gentlemanly and let his competitor’s dog smell the dead squirrel, too. Getting to smell the squirrel is an encouraging reward of sorts and the Dobe was not ready to share that with another dog.

An impartial judge accompanies each cast, but it is up to the handler to “call” his own dog—that is, notify the judge when satisfied his dog has treed. As in coonhound competition, 100 points are earned by the first dog at the tree, 75 by the second. Unlike coonhound scoring, no points are awarded for striking (finding) a trail. This is because sometimes the trail is short, sometimes there is none and too many squirrel dogs are silent trailers. Also unlike coonhound scoring, tree points are not subtracted if no squirrel is found in the tree because squirrels all too readily travel from tree to tree.

If the squirrel is not found, the tree points are circled and do not count on the final score. Judges are allowed considerable latitude, however. If the squirrel is seen several trees away from the one the dog is treeing on and the judge is satisfied that the squirrel could have gotten there through the treetops, he can give the dog credit for that squirrel.

Six or eight squirrels an hour is not impossible in well-populated timber when the bushytails are really active. Ronnie Liles’ Australian shepherd treed 700 for him and his friends during the past two years. “The trick,” said Liles, “is to catch ’em stirrin’. You might not see a squirrel today. But you can come back through the same place tomorrow and see 10.”

Ronnie believes that the old hunters’ barometer, “If the cows are lying down, so are the deer,” also applies to squirrels. And as he says, the dogs are helpless if they can’t see, smell or possibly hear the bushytails. The squirrel that hasn’t been on the ground and is lounging on a limb or in a vine tangle probably won’t be discovered by a dog unless falling air currents allow the dog to “wind” it. This would happen mostly during the cool of late afternoon rather than during early morning when the warming sunlight causes air to rise.

Liles prefers hunting little cat squirrels (grays) in the big, swampy, bottom timbers. Shaking a vine spooks grays out of hiding faster and easier than it does fox squirrels. Other hunters choose the hills where more fox squirrels live because they don’t like the way grays often chase off through the treetops when a dog barks.

Randy Pannell minimizes that problem by staying fairly close to his dog and then getting to the tree fast. In competition, however, that’s not always possible. The second dog has five minutes in which to join the first dog at the tree. During that time, handlers and the judge stay clear.

Both Pannell and Fola Hart demonstrated the wisdom of walking apart from other hunters. At 79, Fola appeared to be walking far behind because of age. But he was the first to hear his dog bark treed while other members of the cast were busy talking.

The perceptive rapport between hunter and squirrel dog is nothing less than amazing. During a Friday afternoon cast, Orville Hart was reluctant to say that Whiskey had treed. “Them two dogs are looking at us,” he observed. “If they believed they had the squirrel, they’d be looking up the tree!”

When a squirrel was shot in Ronnie Liles’ cast, Smokey grabbed it and ran off with the second dog in hot pursuit. As Smokey raced past his master’s leg, Ronnie grinned. “That dog expects me to catch the other dog as it goes by. Then Smokey will bring me the squirrel. He won’t let the other dog have it. But if another dog gets to the squirrel first, Smokey won’t bother it.” Retrieving is an added nicety, but it isn’t rewarded with extra points during the Yockanookany competition.

Some dogs won’t bark if their masters happen to be present when the squirrel is treed, strongly suggesting that they have enough reasoning power to recognize that, in such a case, the boss doesn’t have to be called.

Read Next: The Ultimate Guide to Buying and Training a Squirrel Dog

One Mississippi hunter recalled a boyhood dog that would always dance around the opposite side of the tree, yanking and shaking every vine or sapling it could find. Invariably, this commotion chased the squirrel around to the gunner’s side. Since such a dog is quite rare, hunters often go in pairs, taking turns circling the tree and shaking the bushes after the dog has treed.

What’s it take to train a dog that shows interest in squirrels? Mostly, lots of time in the squirrel woods. But trainer Randy Pannell speeds things up with a slingshot and steel pellets. “Just hit the tree near the squirrel, and it will bail out or take off,” Pannell said. “The dog gets a sight chase through the treetops or maybe a short ground chase. This works best with gray squirrels, especially the young ones. And there’s no problem with game laws while training dogs because you’re not killing or hunting the squirrels.”

Never study treetops when the dog is in sight and isn’t treeing. A perceptive dog believes you see the squirrel and will start treeing. And never bring the dog running by shooting at something other than a squirrel. Fooling a squirrel dog ruins it fast.

The Yockanookany fox squirrels are flat out the most colorful in America. Some are rusty orange, as expected, but others are decorated with white noses, feet and tail tips and, occasionally, black scalps. Others are solid black. Two taken during the 1981 Championship were black with white tips. Southern grays are smaller than Northern grays, but the fox squirrels are bigger. Some, according to reliable reports, grow half again as big as their Northern counterparts and range—according to very unreliable exaggerations—up to the size of house cats, groundhogs and raccoons.

Yankee squirrel hunters are treated so many different ways during the Yockanookany event that they have to like some. They travel from as far away as Michigan to enter the event. “We welcome Yankees; it’s only the Damn Yanks we don’t like,” said one young Southern belle with a wink.

#8356. 6.5 Creedmoor Vs. .300 Win Mag: Here’s the Truth About Cartridge Selection

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:09 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

One of the most common arguments we hear in favor of choosing larger cartridges for hunting big game is that a magnum cartridge will offer margin for error. When considering cartridges like 6.5 Creedmoor vs. .300 Win. Mag., the .300 has more energy, drives a bigger bullet faster, and, we assume, will do more damage than the 6.5. That means that if we don’t hit exactly where we are aiming, we are more likely to still kill the animal cleanly by choosing the magnum. At face value, the logic is sound. But how does it hold up when we start examining what the bullets actually do downrange? You might be surprised.

There are two schools of thought that commonly divide hunters when it comes to choosing cartridges. One opts for milder cartridges that have lower recoil and are generally easier and more pleasant to shoot well. The other wants the extra power to cover their bases. Everyone, of course, falls somewhere on a spectrum, and the categories aren’t mutually exclusive.

I’ve written a lot about why I think smaller cartridges are often the right choice for big game, and it generally boils down to two observations. First, with thoughtful bullet selection, I haven’t noticed a dramatic difference between the wound characteristics of smaller and larger cartridges — and the smaller rounds have produced consistently satisfactory results. Second, milder cartridges are more pleasant to shoot and, despite having no real limitations on the cartridges I have access to, that’s what I reach for consistently. I have the rifles and ammo to torch a hundred rounds of .300 PRC in a range session practicing positional shooting but, realistically, I’m going to pick a 6.5 Creedmoor, 6 Creed, or 22 ARC to do that. Practice with smaller cartridges can also benefit how you’ll shoot magnums, but there’s a lot of value in hunting with the cartridge that you train with.

You’ll commonly hear hunters argue that you should choose the largest cartridge that you can handle without flinching — especially for larger game. Lots of hunters consider this basic conventional wisdom, and it’s rooted in the belief that a larger cartridge, bullet, or more kinetic energy will result in a larger wound and will kill the animal more quickly. This makes up for some degree of shooting error, or will allow more forgiveness on less-than-ideal shot angles. Essentially, choosing a more powerful cartridge is viewed as cheap insurance.

There are many ways that bigger cartridges like the .300 Win. Mag. outperform smaller ones like the 6.5 Creedmoor. When choosing something for yourself, you need to know what the real benefits are, and decide whether they actually apply to you and your hunting. What does that look like in terms of margin for error? That’s exactly what we took a look at in the video above.

I took a 6.5 Creedmoor and .300 Win. Mag. to the range and fired the same line of factory ammo — Federal Fusion Tipped — from each into identical blocks of Clear Ballistics gel. This gel isn’t a one-to-one representation of flesh, but it is a homogeneous, consistent medium in which we can get a side-by-side comparison of two bullets. The blocks were placed at 200 yards with a Garmin chronograph positioned about 15 yards in front of the target to record impact velocity. The Fusion Tipped bullets were 140 grains and 180 grains for the 6.5 CM and .300 Win. Mag., respectively. The rifles were the same except for different barrel lengths — 18 inches for the 6.5 CM and 22 inches for the .300. Impact velocities were recorded as 2,233 fps and 2,526 fps, with the advantage going to the .300.

As expected, the .300 Win. Mag. load delivered higher velocity and more energy at the target than the 6.5 Creedmoor. The block was knocked off the table and was clearly hit harder with the 180-grain slug than the 140. However, the actual wound cavities were not much different. The expanded diameters of the recovered bullets were within .015 inch when measuring both the extreme diameter of the jacket (which would typically be smashed down flat in an animal) and the diameter of mushroomed bullet bodies. The .30-caliber bullet left a slightly wider overall wound cavity across its traverse, disrupting slightly more tissue, but the wound channels aren’t perfectly cylindrical either. The overall diameter of the wound channels and penetration were nearly identical.

To more closely estimate the difference in wound size, I measured the width and height of each wound channel every half inch from entry to the end of the expanded cavity — both were about 14 inches. Because I’m no longer spun up on my calculus, I plugged the data into Claude AI, and it calculated the estimated volume and generated simulated models. The wound channel cross sections are star shaped, not complete empty space, so this is only an estimate of the volume of gel affected by the permanent wound channel.

This demonstration shouldn’t be taken to mean that the 6.5 CM and .300 Win. Mag. are completely equal. They each have their advantages and disadvantages. The results, however, do track pretty well with other gel testing I’ve done, and what I’ve observed on animals. Those are that, with the same bullet construction, results don’t vary too much across most common hunting cartridges. In fact, things like penetration and wound cavity size can be more greatly influenced by bullet selection than simply picking a bigger or smaller cartridge.

Some hunters place a lot of weight in having a cartridge that “hits harder.” While we can see some of the effects in the movement of the gel blocks during this demonstration, and that delta in impact force could possibly offer increased effect to the central nervous system, it’s not a reliable predictor of how fast an animal will die, or how much room for error you have. What we can rely on is the damage the bullet does.

One of the real advantages of a magnum cartridge, with a thoughtfully chosen bullet, is that it can deliver effective velocities over longer distances. A disadvantage of a 6.5 Creedmoor, in common shorter barrel configurations, is that it will produce lower muzzle velocities and result in a shorter effective velocity window. Ensuring that your impact speeds are high enough to make the bullet work properly is critical.

Our field shooting exercise did demonstrate that you might be able to shoot a magnum just as well as the 6.5. If you can, then you are better poised to take advantage of a magnum’s real benefits. Over time, most people will find that they shoot milder cartridges more consistently. It is most important to choose a cartridge that you can shoot well and will practice with.

Read Next: I Shot the First Elk With the New 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak Ammo. It’s an Undeniable Elk Hunting Cartridge

Along with better equipment and more refined shooting technique, we are constantly learning more about terminal ballistics. Many of our long-held beliefs are simply a product of lore and oversimplified logic. If you’re a successful hunter and your favorite cartridge works well for you, we’re not asking you to change. But if you’re feeling the pressure to choose a cartridge that you don’t think you’ll shoot as well, because you feel that it’s powerful enough to make up the difference, you’re barking up the wrong tree. The smaller cartridges will work just as well on the good shots, and the big ones will do just as poorly on the bad shots.

The OL editors pick the best deer hunting rifles on the market.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8354. The Overlooked Muscle You Need to Strengthen For Better Knee Health This Ski Season

SKI Test Director Jon Jay test a pair of all-mountain skis in spring crud conditions. (Photo: Keri Bascetta)

Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury. But many traditional strength training programs focus on the bigger muscles in your lower half, including the quads, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus (your largest butt muscle).

That means the smaller guys often get neglected. And one small guy in particular–the gluteus medius, which forms part of your side butt–is worth paying attention to if you actually want to reduce your risk of knee pain and injury this winter.

Because ACL tears are among the most common ski injuries, Dr. Gregory Lichtman, an orthopedic surgeon in northern California and a physician for the U.S. women’s ski team, puts heavy emphasis on strengthening the glute medius. In his view, it’s one of the most important muscles for staying safe and skiing well.

Unfortunately, even high-level athletes can have a weak glute medius, according to Lichtman. That’s because unlike the quads, hamstrings, calves, and glute max–which can naturally get strong from activities like road running and hill climbing–the glute medius typically needs to be intentionally strengthened.

Read on to learn why this small muscle is so important, Lichtman’s favorite way to strengthen it, and other essential fitness tips for injury prevention.

The glute medius is a small muscle on your outer hip that fires up when you bring your leg out to the side, a motion known as hip abduction. It also helps control the knee by preventing it from caving inward (a position known as valgus) as you perform various movements. And it assists you in balancing on one leg, which is important when loading your downhill ski, Lichtman says.

In skiing, if you get into the back seat (meaning, you shift your body weight backwards, instead of staying centered over your skis) and the knee goes into valgus, the tibia can internally rotate, “and that’s where the ACL tears occur,” Lichtman says. Even if you don’t get a full-blown ACL tear, going into valgus when you ski can contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome, a fancy term for pain at the front of the kneecap, Lichtman says.

By strengthening the glute medius, you can make it more resistant to valgus in the first place, which decreases your chances of both ACL tears and general knee pain.

There are also performance benefits: “A strong gluteus medius also really allows you to stand on your downhill ski a little bit more aggressively and really make a more aggressive turn,” Lichtman says. That’s because when you place most of your weight on your downhill ski (the one that’s closest to the bottom of the hill), your G-forces will want to throw you down the mountain. But having a strong glute medius–in addition to strong quads and core muscles–helps form a strong pillar on your outer hip, which ”really allows you to withstand those G forces the best,” Lichtman says.

One of the classic ways to target the glute medius is to strap on ankle weights, lie on your side, and lift and lower your top leg. Lichtman says. This exercise can absolutely strengthen your glute medius, but it’s not Lichtman’s go-to. That’s because it primarily just isolates that muscle and doesn’t mimic how we move in sports.

A better bet, Lichtman says, is to focus on exercises that simultaneously activate the gluteus medius and other muscle groups because that better resembles how we use this muscle during athletics. His favorite exercise that ticks that box? The monster walk. Not only does this move really fire up the gluteus medius, but it also works the core, hamstrings, quads, and glute max, he says.

Incorporate this exercise into your workouts three days a week, with at least one day off in between each session so that you give the muscle the downtime it needs to recover and build back stronger. To stave off boredom–and also work different parts of your hips and quads–incorporate different variations of the monster walk throughout the week. For example, instead of stepping straight out to the side, step forwards and backwards, or diagonally forward and diagonally backwards. As long as you have good form and keep your legs spread apart so that you feel tension from the band the whole time, “all directions can be effective,” Lichtman says.

Lichtman suggests doing monster walks during both pre-season and throughout ski season. “One of the big pitfalls is that we will all get ready for ski season, and then taper off our dry land training,” he explains. “If you’re one of the fortunate few who can ski five or six days a week, you’re probably getting enough exercise, and you probably don’t want to stress your body out any more than that. But for those of us who are skiing two to three days a week, finding some time to do some cross-training and continue to work on our core and our hip abductor strength is really important because those are the less commonly used muscles during skiing.”

Once this exercise becomes easy, level up the challenge by using a stronger resistance band.

A strong glute medius can keep you safe on the slopes. But it’s not the only fitness-related aspect of injury prevention.

Having a strong core and quads, along with good overall endurance, is also key. That’s because one of the essential components of an ACL tear pattern in skiing is getting kicked into the back seat. And while the gluteus medius helps guard against knee valgus in this position, it doesn’t prevent you from getting into the back seat in the first place, Lichtman explains. What does help? Having strong core and quad muscles, plus overall endurance. This trifecta, Lichtman says, is “fundamental” to staying out of the back seat.

On the endurance front, the goal is to be as fresh after lunch as you are after breakfast, Lichtman says. “Fatigue is definitely a risk factor for ACL tears,” he says, explaining that fatigued skiers more frequently get into the back seat and sustain injuries than those who aren’t zapped. So make sure your dryland training doesn’t just focus on lifting weights: “A balance of endurance and strength training is integral for a skier preparing for ski season,” Lichtman says.

#8353. Missouri Fourth Grader Has Already Taken Two Giant Whitetail Bucks This Season

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:01 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Noah Baker isn’t your typical young hunter. The Pike County, Missouri youngster is a hunting prodigy most sportsmen would be proud to call their son.

“He shot his first deer at age six,” his dad, Jared Baker, tells Outdoor Life. “He lives to hunt and fish. And we’d have to think about just how many deer he’s taken since that first one when he was still in first grade.”

October 25 was the last day of the Missouri early two-day youth gun deer season. Noah and Jared chose a hunting spot over a cut corn field late that afternoon near their home in Frankfort.

“The wind wasn’t great, and we just set up in a hillside haystack that overlooked a cut corn patch that was well below us,” says Jared, a 37-year-old heavy equipment operator. “We set a tripod rifle stand in the haystack, put Noah’s 7mm suppressed Remington rifle on it, and watched and waited.”

They got on the haystack about 4 p.m. on a hot afternoon. They hadn’t waited very long before a few small bucks and does started filtering into the corn to feed about 60 yards from where they were positioned.

“We were waiting for a big buck we knew was around that I named ‘Dwayne The Rock Johnson’, because he was so big and strong,” Noah says. “The deer’s head was huge, and I wanted him.”

The father-son team had two big target bucks they’d watched and planned to take this year. They’d also found shed antlers from the deer. Noah had shot the smaller of the two bucks — a 155-inch 10-pointer — with his crossbow on Oct. 2.

Now they were after the second buck – “Dwayne The Rock Johnson,” and it just so happened that the deer showed at 6:20 p.m.

“It happened fast,” Jared says. “We saw him at 80 yards, and he went into a grass patch to look at a doe.”

“I saw him first, dad was looking farther away when I spotted him,” says Noah. “Dwayne started to walk away, turning toward some smaller bucks. But dad used his grunt call, and the buck turned and looked at us.”

Noah had crosshairs settled on the deer’s chest and fired at the buck standing 80 yards away. The 140-grain Berger bullet put the buck down quickly.

“Noah and I just started fist pumping in the air,” said Jared.

Read Next: Here’s Why This Giant Missouri Buck Was Still in Velvet in Late September

They called some friends for help getting the giant 17-point buck out of the field. They didn’t weigh it, but a taxidermist who has the buck rough green-scored the antlers at 187 inches.

Noah’s other 155-inch 10-pointer also is with the same taxidermist for mounting.

“I’m going to hang both of them in my bedroom,” Noah says. “One on each side of my TV screen so I can watch them whenever I’m in there.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8352. Should You Hunt a Buck’s Bedding Area, Or Is It Too Risky?

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:42 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

A heavy-racked buck beds down for the day. Wind sweeping from behind, and eyes scanning down below, danger has little chance of finding him before he detects it. After all, that’s why the buck picked this spot in the first place.

If you scan articles on the best rut hunting spots, you won’t find many that highlight buck bedding areas as key locations to target. But often times in deer hunting, going against the grain can produce great results.

However, you can only hunt buck bedding areas well if you have a firm understanding of how bucks bed, where they bed, and how they learn to survive based on their bedding area choices.

If you are tired of hunting the same old rut stands with minimal success, consider a change. Hunting a buck bedding area during the rut could be your ticket to hanging an old bruiser on the wall. Here’s what you should know.

Let’s start by agreeing on terms. Of course, bedding areas are places where deer rest and sleep. However, it’s important to know there are different types of bedding areas. Deer have daytime and nighttime bedding areas. For this article, we’ll focus on the daytime beds.

On the surface, it can be difficult to determine the difference between buck and doe bedding areas. There are distinctions, though.

Bucks tend to prioritize security over convenience. Does usually take the opposite approach. Bucks rely on themselves to detect danger (because they typically bed alone). However, does usually bed, feed, and travel within family units. When bedding together, does bed down facing different directions. This makes it easier to detect danger from all areas around them. Bucks can’t do this so they are much choosier in their bed locations.

Furthermore, bucks might or might not bed within the same patches of cover as does. When they do, bucks tend to take the best quality bedding. For example, in hill country, that might be the upper third of a ridge line. In swamps, that might be the highest dry ground available. In big woods, it could mean interiors of timber or in spots with the thickest cover and highest stem counts.

Bucks also bed in areas that offer plenty of horizontal cover. They might bed up against a boulder, log, or other object that hides their profile. Oftentimes, from a hunter’s perspective, all you might see is their head, antlers, and maybe the neck. Other times, you’ll see nothing at all (until it’s too late).

Regardless of the habitat type or geographical layout, bucks almost always bed with certain consistencies. For example, they tend to bed with the wind at their back. This allows them to smell anything upwind (behind them) and see anything downwind (in front).

This is one reason leeward ridges are so attractive to deer. The prevailing wind brings scent from over the top of the ridge. Early in the day, thermals bring scent up from below. Oftentimes, this allows deer to smell danger from multiple directions.

Without question, savvy bucks learn how to detect danger within their environment. With time, they learn typical directions that danger comes from. With that knowledge, they bed in areas that offer visibility to see hunters or predators coming from these directions. Therefore, don’t be surprised to see bucks bedding right on the edge of thick cover within some of the areas noted above. This gives them plenty of cover to hide and allows them to see danger approaching from the open areas nearby.

It’s logical to think that once bucks become confident in certain bedding areas, they’ll go back and use the same beds over and over. In some ways, and in many places, they do. It’s especially common for bucks that live in more desolate landscapes or areas with poorer habitat quality to reuse the same beds with higher frequency.

According to the MSU Deer Lab, in areas with higher timber-to-open ratios and bigger woods settings, bucks are less loyal to specific beds. They will still bed within the same relative geographic locations. However, the absolute locations of their beds tend to vary.

Read Next: How to Hunt Cover During the Rut, with Dr. Craig Harper

It’s been said many times, but older bucks operate completely differently than younger bucks and does. They take on vastly different habits and tendencies.

A common thread through most mature deer includes the desire for seclusion. Older bucks don’t want a bunch of other deer bedded close to them. Additionally, it’s important to recognize that higher populations of does, and higher deer densities in general, can cause bucks to bed on the fringes. That’s especially true outside of the rut.

Because of everything noted above, it’s challenging to hunt close to buck bedding. It becomes even harder when the deer is 4.5 years old or older. These deer have learned to survive in part due to their bedding area choices. Therefore, it takes strategic planning and very deliberate approaches to thread the needle and get a big buck on the ground.

While it isn’t as popular as other rut-centric stand locations, it’s certainly an option. By continuing to focus on buck bedding areas (similar to early season and pre-rut plans), hunters can find a big ol’ buck.

By digging through deer research and personal experience, it’s clear that bucks express unique habits and tendencies that culminate into perceived personalities. One example is a really old buck that barely participates in the rut. That’s the exception, of course, but it would call for a unique approach. You would have to hunt such a deer as if the rut isn’t even on. You’d focus on travel routes along bed-to-feed patterns.

Some mature bucks that participate in the rut still return to their preferred bedding areas. If they don’t find an estrus doe under cover of darkness, by dawn, they cautiously slink back to one of the advantageous beds they know. When hunting this type of deer, set up between his bed and nearby food sources. Or between his bed and nearby doe bedding.

Hunting this deer is similar to hunting the fringes of buck bedding outside of the rut. Use good entry and exit strategies, and keep wind directions in mind during the approach, hunt, and departure. Don’t be aggressive with calling, rattling, or decoying since reclusive bucks rarely respond well to those aggressive tactics.

Hunting buck bedding requires a lot of planning and consideration. Hunting buck bedding during the rut requires even more. In many cases, this isn’t the right play.

Oftentimes, it’s less-dominant, uber-mature deer (5 ½-plus), or specific bucks that tend to be more reclusive across their entire lifespan, that require this hunting tactic.

Once you’ve determined you’re hunting a specific buck like this, you must hunt him carefully. Use the hunting strategies you’d typically use to hunt a whitetail bedding area with the immediacy of the rut in the front of your mind.
