#8351. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

#8350. How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 3: November 3

Last fall, a tall 8-point Michigan buck showed me just how good—and lasting—the action can be during the first few days of November. The buck hit my mock scrape twice during daylight, which tipped me off that it was time for a strategic hunt where a small woodlot met standing corn. Between my hunt that evening and another the next morning, I had nearly a dozen encounters with the buck as he zig-zagged his way through the broken acres of timber and ag fields, feverishly seeking a receptive doe. The flurry of activity finally ended when he stepped into one of my shooting lanes at 11:10 am.

Bucks are transitioning into full-blown seeking mode right now, and I’m betting that this coming Tuesday will be one of the best days of the year to be on stand. Of course, it is a big election day across the country, so hopefully you voted early or sent in that absentee ballot, because this is a day you’d probably rather be hunting over a scrape line than standing in line waiting to cast a ballot. Here’s what to expect and how to proceed for your best shot at tagging out on Tuesday.

Related: The Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut

Rut hormones are starting to peak in bucks across much of whitetail range, and more and more does are showing signs that they are ready or nearly ready to breed. It should all add up to great hunting. Bucks, young and old alike, are in seeking mode now, often visible in daylight hours and moving more with each passing day.

This is the height of what I’d call the late pre-rut, with bucks largely still hitting scrapes, but possibly your last chance to catch up to a homebody buck before he abandons those scrapes and gets wildly unpredictable in the all-out chasing phase of the rut. Now, more than ever, bucks are susceptible to a wide range of calling and decoying tactics, as their default safety mode is being overridden by their urge to reproduce. This makes setting up “close enough” a viable strategy for bowhunters with a grunt call in pocket and a set of rattling antlers in hand. So, on this Best Day of the Rut, elect to pack a lunch, sit long, and be ready to shoot on a moment’s notice, because bucks are sure to be on the move.

Things change fast in the whitetail world, and staying on top of current sign can make or break your pre-rut hunting. Hopefully you’ve been scouting as much as hunting since our last Best Day. A big mistake many hunters make is thinking more time on stand will mean more opportunities, while ignoring the scouting that actually leads to high-quality sits. At this time of year, a scrape that was smoking hot last week may be stone cold when you show up, so use a weather event or midday break in your schedule to speed-scout for the latest sign and use that info to direct your hunting decisions. This could be checking a low-intrusion camera or cruising those scrape lines to confirm recent activity. Just try to minimize your impact and keep it as low key as possible.

For your morning hunt, think like a buck and focus on the does. Look for a transition area near known doe bedding where you can catch them returning in the morning hours. Bucks will be close behind. Focus on zones with numerous attraction factors or lines of travel to increases your chances. These factors could include a scrape line, convergence of well-used trails, a fruit tree, or multiple edges of cover necking down to one location. These things will steer deer traffic right past a carefully placed stand and multiply your chances of encountering a doe-seeking buck.

With my 2025 Michigan 8-point, the only standing corn in the area, just 30 yards from my stand, was prime doe bedding. This kept the tall 8 in the area and constantly moving, attempting to see if a doe was just behind the next stalk. The block of woods created four edges where it met a neighboring chunk of timber, encouraging deer to naturally move past my stand as they followed these edges. The last factor was a mock scrape the buck had taken over, which I set in August with just this time frame in mind.

Find a similar transition zone near does and stick it out. Even if a buck happens to sneak by you, there’s a good chance he’ll be back soon to re-check the area. Be sure to avoid areas where the deer will travel as you enter. For this killer morning ambush to work, you’ll need get settled early—like and hour early—to make sure you beat the deer back to their bedding transition. And don’t be in a hurry to leave either. Remember, I shot that tall 8-point at 11:10 am last year.

Related: 50 Expert Tips for Hunting the Whitetail Rut

You can’t go wrong with an evening sit at a food-plot, ag field, or other prime feeding area that you know does are hitting consistently. They will essentially be your real-life decoys. Nearby bucks will have a hard time resisting coming into the open to check on any mature doe they see, even if they aren’t quite in estrus, giving you an opportunity if you’re ready. And speaking of being ready, it’s a good idea between and just before hunts to practice getting drawn quickly, fast target acquisition, judging distance at a glance, and stopping a buck with a mouth grunt or bleat.

As for the evening hunt itself, this is prime time to employ a 3D decoy and deep-sounding grunt tube. I say 3D because, in my experience, 2D decoys at close range can spook deer that can’t see them from certain angles. A realistic 3D decoy can change this, signaling to a passing buck that something has this strange buck’s interest which requires his investigation. Bottom line, if a buck is seeking does in daylight, he’s probably sufficiently amped up to be vulnerable to these ploys.

What about scent? Using a fresh estrus scent now (where legal) could add the realism you need and make decent setup irresistible. Use a drag rope but add this trick: Don’t drag but dab your scent-filled rag on the ground like deer footsteps, exactly what a buck would be tracking. And speaking of scent, yours should be accounted for; use rubber boots to minimize any scent you leave and do your best to allow your scent on stand to blow just off from where bucks are likely to enter. This gives them the ability to scent-check the plot while also feeling safe enough to enter it.

For the diehard public-land hunters out there, this Tuesday could thin out the rut crowd a bit and allow for some natural deer movement patterns, especially in the morning while most people are at work. From my experience, catching up to a buck on public land is still a tough task, especially in pressured areas. Being highly mobile is the fix. If you’re stuck in permanent stands, you may be left out of the action happening just a few yards away in thick cover.

Public-land bucks checking and pushing does tend to stay in denser cover for safety. The solution is to pack that mobile stand or saddle and sticks and adjust to the activity you’re seeing on the fly. If there are no trees big enough for that where the action is, consider a ground sit in exactly the right spot. Use natural cover so you don’t tip deer off to obvious changes to their bedroom or by setting up a blind. Instead, execute a quick, low-impact ambush on a rut-crazed buck on November 3rd.

Adam Lewis is a contributing writer for Field & Stream. A full-time science teacher, Lewis is a Michigan-based outdoor writer and videographer who also hosts the Deer IQ podcast and blog. His how-to articles have appeared in a variety of outdoor publications, typically focusing on finding unique angles and practical strategies for public- and private-land whitetail deer hunters. Highlights Education Lewis earned his BS in Science Education from Olivet Nazarene University, Songwriting School of Hard Knocks, Nashville, TN. Experience Born in the hunting-rich state of Michigan, Lewis grew up around deer camp with his father and uncles and picked up a bow to start chasing whitetail as soon as legally possible, on his 12th birthday. After college, Lewis set his sights on a new pursuit—singing and songwriting, which led him to the neon-lit corner bars of Nashville’s famous strip. He returned to his home state in 2010 to focus on hunting and writing and soon began penning outdoor articles for local and then national magazines. Along with teaching, Lewis currently, writes, produces video, and hosts his podcast and blog, all aimed at educating hunters for improved success in the field. Notable Work

#8349. “I Wanted to Throw Up.” I Missed 7 Bucks In a Row Before Finally Learning a Hard Lesson

Published Oct 31, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The coffee cups were almost dry again, and so were the hunting stories. Milt’s electric clock showed 6 a.m.—time to go. Moments later, the six of us were swallowed up in the gloom of a dense fog. Four inches of fluffy new snow muffled our footsteps as we began the trek to our deer stands.

There was a nervous excitement in the air that morning. We knew we were going to see deer. Rarely had we been so confident on an opening day. Almost 200 acres of willow swamp and fields belonged to us that morning and the preseason scouting we’d done plus the new snow added up to nothing but good news. The anticipation was almost crackling in the air around us.

I reached my stand first. I brushed off the loose snow and stood listening for a moment. The absolute stillness meant that my ears would be about as helpful as my eyes for the first few hours—longer if the fog remained. An inch of frost covered every limb of the big willow I occupied. I backed into a collar-high branch and a handful of the frozen dew fell, shaking any remaining sleep from me.

To my left was a standing field of short corn. To my right, the edge of a brushy swale wound its way down to the big willow swamp 200 yards away. In front of me, a fallen willow limb blocked my view. I settled comfortably against the trunk of the big tree and surveyed the fields. Sometimes the fog would allow me 80 yards of view, at other times less than 40.

When at last, according to my watch, it was 8 a.m., I knew that the sun had to be up. The light through the fog, however, had changed little. From the cornfield to my left came sounds of movement—short crunching noises. My ears strained to identify them. A cock pheasant crowed not far away and I relaxed a bit. A few moments later I watched a bluejay working over a cob. Birds were making the sounds, I told myself.

For nearly 30 minutes I continued to hear the sounds: a few crunches followed by silence. Then I saw the outline of a deer’s back moving slowly through the rows. Head down, the deer came closer, quartering across the field. At last it raised its head. For the first time I could see its crown of antlers. Not again, I said to myself, a bit of dread mixing with my excitement.

Seven times before, I’d managed to get shots at trophy bucks and seven times I’d missed—sometimes with a bow, sometimes with a shotgun. I’d got my chance nearly every season I’d hunted, and I’d gone home empty-handed every time. My hunting companions marveled at my incredible knack for being in the right place at the right time and at my equally incredible bad shooting. Despite hours of practice, something always seemed to go awry at the moment of truth. Not again, I groaned inwardly.

When it seemed that the buck was coming no closer, I raised my shotgun. The iron sights of my new slug barrel came to rest on the target—still more than 60 yards away. I fired.

The blast shook frost from the willow branches. For a moment, the buck disappeared. When I could see again, he was on the move.

Again I fired and again and again—as the buck crossed from left to right. As the big deer quartered toward me, he was hidden behind the frosty fallen branches of the willow. Suddenly he reappeared before me and I shot once more. The buck stopped just 40 yards away, his wide, dark rack swiveling like a radar antenna.

My gun was empty. I had to reload. Frantically I fumbled deep in my pocket for the shells. They were still in the box. This one time I hadn’t opened a second box just in case. Almost hysterically I tore the cardboard and threw a slug into the chamber. I took aim at the buck’s neck and fired. I thought I saw the deer cringe before he loped away down the swale toward the big swamp. Then I lost sight of him in the fog and frosty willows.

I can’t adequately describe my feelings. Despair is as close as any named emotion comes. I was beside myself. I couldn’t believe I’d missed again. The deer was right there, at the range I’d sighted-in my new barrel for, and still I’d missed. I scrambled down off the stand and began to search for the deer’s trail in hopes of finding blood, hair, anything that might mean the buck was hit. I reloaded the shotgun then and, to my disgust, found two shells in the magazine. In the excitement, I’d evidently put more slugs in the gun than I knew. I could have shot again—more despair.

In the snow, I followed the buck’s tracks across the swale, along the edge of the cornfield on the other side, way past the point at which I’d lost sight of him. For more than 200 yards I moved slowly beside the tracks. Then I was close to the swamp and my friend Steve’s stand. He’d heard the shots, but hadn’t glimpsed any deer passing by. “Maybe it was hidden in the fog,” he said.

I walked the trail many times that morning, tracing and retracing the deer’s movements in the snow. A sad realization was weighing more heavily with every step. Grudgingly, I had to admit that I must have missed number eight.

The next day the hunt ended and I went home, but the memory of the hunt stayed with me. When I tried to sleep, that morning’s events played back like a worn instant replay. Again and again I saw the buck cross and again and again I watched my shots as if I were looking for my mistake. I tried to spot and correct my error, but even in my dreams the buck escaped.

Five days later, a friend and I took to those same willows in search of pheasants. He’d heard my tale and seemed to understand. As we approached where I’d last seen the buck, I took a breath to call my friend. I wanted to tell him where the deer had been when my shots had missed. But before I could form the words, Tim stopped dead in his tracks.

“Oh no,” he said with a groan. “Oh no! There’s a huge buck lying over here.”

My first thought was that he was joking. But he wouldn’t have been, couldn’t have been. I was trembling as I waded the deep grass toward him. A sick sort of feeling began to knot my stomach. The sight of a shining antler almost put me to my knees.

There in the thin yellow grass lay my buck.

He lay there as he must have lain after the final shot that Saturday morning. He was crouched like a sleeping dog, facing the trail that I’d mistaken for his. My last shot had gone very low, into the left hindquarter and up into the body cavity. The wound hadn’t bled. That was why I’d found no blood in the snow.

I stood there in the silence thinking quickly, eyes burning. Tim shared the silence. He understood. I must have passed within a dozen yards of the buck time after time. Why hadn’t I seen him? How could a buck grow invisible in knee-high grass? Maybe he’d been deeper in the swale and had crawled out later when death approached. But why hadn’t we seen him on the second day? The trail to two of our other stands ran close by.

If only I’d gone into the swale on a hunch. If only I’d had a hunch. If only there hadn’t been such thick fog on that day, surely Steve would have seen the deer from his lofty perch. If only the wound had bled so I’d have stayed on the right trail. If only I’d shot truer. If only, if only…

But such musings were no help. I was beside myself with self-loathing. I wanted to throw up. I wanted to cry. Everything I was striving for as a hunter lay in ruin like the buck.

Tim and I returned that afternoon to take the cape and antlers. They were all that we could salvage. Silence returned as I guided the knife, wishing away the green that had begun to color the ruined venison. Forcing myself to speak, I asked Tim to age the deer. He was wildlife manager for the area’s Department of Natural Resources. He estimated 3½ years, give or take a season. That, at least, was a comfort.

I took the antlers as much out of respect for the animal as for myself. I knew the head would be a most worthy reminder.

“Well,” the taxidermist said, “at least you got the horns. You can always buy meat.” He didn’t understand.

Now the head hangs in a place of honor in my home. Beautiful as it is, I get no joy out of looking at it. It remains, however, a lasting monument to that day. I still think of the rotting venison and the slow death the buck may have had. I learned something then, something of deer hunting and of myself.

Read Next: What It Feels Like to Miss the Biggest Buck of Your Life at 45 Yards — With a Rifle

Many evenings, after the head was first hung, I would sit looking at it and recall that day. I had decided that my gun was to blame for the poor shooting, that the barrel wasn’t tightened down properly on the stock. I knew, too, that the deer had been lost because of poor tracking skills, fog, bad luck, all of the classic reasons. But I was only half right at best.

Finally I came to understand that the tale was told in those first moments when the buck raised his crown and I began to doubt myself. I forgot my skills then, thinking only of the glory or the humiliation that I faced. The strain of the moment, my self doubt and consequent loss of concentration cost me that buck. I was not a competent enough marksman to rise to the occasion, under pressure. Only more practice could be the cure.

I haven’t faced a buck since then, although I killed a doe cleanly the following season just 100 yards from the spot where I’d seen that buck. Somehow the pressure had faded then, but does don’t carry antlers. I wonder about that day to come when I’ll face a buck once more. And I wonder if the lesson that began on a frosty morning not long ago will serve me then.

This story was originally published in the November 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8348. Whatever You Think of Him, Mark Dowdle Is Built for the Backyard Ultra

At lap 87 of the Last Soul Backyard Ultra in Bornheim, Germany, this August, Mark Dowdle transformed (or regressed, he’s not entirely sure) into the football and lacrosse player he was in college.

To be fair, Ayyoub “Ello” El Osrouti pretty much started it. A backyard ultra, as you probably know by now, is a last-person-standing race not much different from “The Long Walk”—the movie about 100 boys who walk until there’s one left—except the runners in backyard races aren’t shot after they drop.

Now at 4 a.m. on August 18—three days and 15 hours into the race—it was just down to El Osrouti and Dowdle, who were engaged in a Hamilton-like duel to determine the winner. Ello busted out of the gate. The German had been trying to run faster laps to break Dowdle, but this was, by comparison, a sprint. Dowdle, deviating from his tactic of running his own race, decided to stay right with him.

Dowdle completed the lap in 38 minutes—his fastest of the race by over 5 minutes. El Osrouti got up and finished four minutes later, also his fastest lap.

But about half way through the lap, El Osrouti stopped and sat down. Dowdle stopped, too, and just stared at him in silence. It was both competitive and a little chilling, like Dowdle thought the Last Soul race was a literal invitation to collect his competitors’ souls along the way.

Dowdle’s behavior left many of his hundreds of thousands of followers on Instagram, Youtube, and TikTok a little stunned. The 29-year-old Minnesotan has become a wildly popular Internet figure through dishing out zen advice and positivity. Rich Roll, the addict turned endurance athlete who serves up mindfulness every week on his podcast, called Dowdle a “changemaker” when he had Dowdle on the show. There was a good reason for it: Basically every time Dowdle took a breath, he said something enlightening or inspiring about hard work, endurance, or self-improvement.

With two backyard ultra wins in 2026 alone, there’s little doubt that Dowdle is one of this year’s ultrarunning breakout stars, partly because of his success in the backyard format and partly because of his social media savvy. But he didn’t get that way by reading scripted platitudes on TikTok; Dowdle isn’t faking that zen.

When I told him about the Taco Bell 50K and how it attracted those who wouldn’t normally even consider running an ultra, he said, “people want to be challenged. Sometimes they just don’t know it yet.” Even when he was a football and lacrosse player at the University of St. Thomas in Saint Paul, Minnesota, drinking way too much and trying to please others at the expense of himself, he would think about the meaning of life and why people do the things they do. He attributes his personal growth to running, but also to journaling.

“These are the kinds of things I think about all the time,” Dowdle said. “I was constantly thinking about this connection between words and action and who I wanted to be.”

Dowdle works as a motivational speaker now. But deep down, he’s got an edge.

It’s that edge that makes him stand out (and ruffle feathers) in a sport known for its kumbaya positivity, especially the camaraderie-focused backyard ultra community. Dowdle likes being a little weird and competitive and even scary: He once made a YouTube video called “Ultrarunning Has A Mark Dowdle Problem.” He compares himself to Dennis Rodman, the wildly divisive and brilliant NBA player.

“I’m sure that some of these other guys who are competitive will want to put that competition right back on me,” Dowdle said. “I welcome that.”

His friend and rival Harvey Lewis seems like a golden retriever to Dowdle’s heeler. Dowdle sort of agrees with that comparison and sort of doesn’t. He points out that he and Lewis aren’t that different. (Lewis agrees with him, for what it’s worth.)

“I think Harvey Lewis is competitive in a way that’s much tricker to identify,” Dowdle said. “But I don’t hide it. There are times I don’t care. I’ll show everything on my sleeve.”

Lewis believes that Dowdle’s zen, more than his competitiveness, is what’s carried him to so much recent success. On October 17, 2026, they came together as teammates: Lewis, 50, and Dowdle lined up as part of a U.S. team of 15 against the world’s best at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship. Team USA competed on the Big’s Backyard Ultra course in Beltbuckle, Tennessee, the original backyard ultra devised by Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell. Dowdle went on to run 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best—to lead Team USA to victory over Australia. Lewis ran 83 laps.

The Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is held every two years, alternating with the individual world championship. The 2026 race began at 6 a.m. Mountain Time on Saturday, October 17, with 69 national teams competing simultaneously around the world.

The format is simple: Each team of 15 runners runs a 4.167-mile loop every hour, on the hour. The country with cumulatively the most loops completed across all 15 runners wins the team title. Team USA races on the original backyard ultra course in Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Mark Dowdle led Team USA to the win with a cumulative 1,120 laps (yards) to defeat Australia by 51 yards. He was the last American standing with 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best. Belgium’s Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts broke the individual backyard ultra world record by each running 124 yards (512 miles) before deciding to call it quits due to boredom, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports.

Since its inauguration in 2020, Belgium and the U.S. have each won two team titles.

Lewis said Dowdle’s “why” is perhaps the strongest he’s ever seen. It “cements his discipline and his unwavering desire to not give up.”

“Mark has a great energy force,” Lewis said. “He has a level of enthusiasm that’s immeasurable.”

But what, exactly, is an energy force? Is it zen or competitiveness? Dowdle likes to ask it another way: Why can’t it be both?

Take a wild guess who inspired Dowdle as a collegiate football and lacrosse player to turn his life around and start running. It wasn’t Joe Rogan, but if that was your first guess, you’re on the right track.

Feeling sorry for himself on the bus ride home after losing two of three lacrosse games his senior year, he listened to David Goggins on Joe Rogan’s podcast. Goggins talked about how running carved him into the person he was today. The way he bragged about pissing blood, shitting himself, and eating only saltine crackers during his long runs spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle already knew he needed to change.

He went for a run when they got back to campus—even though it was 2 a.m.

If Goggins lit the fire, James Lawrence, the Iron Cowboy, stoked it. Lawrence had completed the 50/50/50 challenge, or 50 Ironman-length triathlons in 50 days across 50 states. The way he leaned on his family during that journey spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle, to this day, gives all the credit to his wife, Lucy, for centering him and scolding him whenever he acts, for lack of a better description, too much like a bro.

Dowdle tried for many years to make it as a running guru—some might say influencer—and ultrarunner. He found some limited success. Runner’s World interviewed him in 2023 for his calendar challenge, when he ran the number of miles corresponding to the day of the month, for a full month. (For example, 26 miles on the 26th.) By the beginning of 2026, he had 40,000 Instagram followers and a modest apparel sponsorship that netted him $200 a month. And then he entered the BPN Go One More backyard ultra this April.

Dowdle had already won the Arrowhead 135-miler in January, finishing in 35:48:00—a four-hour improvement over his 2025 fourth-place finish. But he chalked that up to his ability to withstand the Minnesota winter conditions that dropped to minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

The BPN Go One More was another story; he hadn’t even made it to 100 miles in a backyard ultra before. He could sense other peoples’ doubts—they didn’t drive him, but they did irritate him a little. He mumbled at one point that they “had no fucking idea.”

Dowdle ended up running 306 miles in 73 hours of rainy and muddy conditions, and the way he did it captivated people: He looked fresh and happy most of the time, like he was playing tag on the playground. In a few days, his Instagram following jumped to 108,000, and brand deals were knocking at his door. He also began booking keynote speaking events, sometimes for conferences that he helped set up the year before for one of his odd jobs to get by while he pursued running.

He proved that BPN was no fluke two months later, finishing second to Lewis at the Mid-State Mile, a last-person standing event in Franklin, Tennessee.

But Last Soul sent him into a new stratosphere. After their fateful showdown on lap 87, Dowdle and El Osrouti dueled for another six hours. And despite the German banking a cumulative five hours of extra rest over the course of the race, after that 93rd lap he gave out. Dowdle ran the final lap solo to win the race with 94 loops, or 391.7 miles. The race attracted 10 million viewers to the livestream and more than 100,000 at any one time, attention that Lewis called “freakishly different” than any other ultra in history, even Western States or Rachel Entrekin’s historic overall win at the Cocodona 250.

After Last Soul, Dowdle’s Instagram following jumped from 108,000 to over 400,000.

“It’s been everything I’ve been trying to build for several years now,” Dowdle said. “But nothing really has changed. It’s sort of weird because I’ve been saying the same thing now that I have over the past seven years. But people are willing to listen more when I go 94 hours in a backyard.”

Dowdle, a Christian who has described his goal in races to experience suffering in a way that brings him closer to Jesus Christ and to others, says he’s handled his newfound success because of his wife. Everyone, he said, should get a Lucy. On the way home from the BPN race, Lucy saw his phone blowing up and reminded him that many of those people were loving him because of what he just did, but that she and his friends loved him for who he was.

Dowdle’s breakthrough would not be possible without the backyard ultra format, and not just because he’s one of the best in the world at it. The race, as Lewis alluded to, is insanely popular: What started as another one of Laz’s harebrained ideas with the Big’s Backyard Ultra in 2011 has ballooned to over 1,000 independent backyard ultras across the globe.

Lewis was perhaps the event’s first breakout star. He was known, he said, after winning Badwater in 2014, but the attention was far different after he won Big’s Backyard in 2023, his second victory, and set a backyard world record by running more than 450 miles. The format changed the high school teacher’s life.

“I was doing other cool stuff but never got noticed,” Lewis said. “But after the backyard, I was invited to all these running events, at no cost, places I’d never get to go to as a teacher. Australia, Botswana, all over the place. In Botswana, people knew who I was, and I was like, ‘really’? It just created so many more doors opening.”

Backyard ultras favor a unique skillset. Neither Lewis or Dowdle have the legspeed to compete for a top spot at a “fast” ultra like Western States. But, Lewis counters, a top contender at Western States may struggle at a backyard ultra.

“I’ve seen collegiate-type runners, and they get totally destroyed,” Lewis said. “It’s a different type of grit that’s required for running five straight days.”

Lewis and Dowdle possess that special mindset that doesn’t have much to do with a training plan. Lewis is writing a book on mindset, in fact, that will be released next fall. For Dowdle, the ultimate challenge (and intrigue) comes in the unknown.

“You have no opportunity to say ‘in 10 miles this race will be over,’” Dowdle said. “You just have to wrestle with the discomfort.”

Dowdle does that, he said, by using skills he learned from his parents. His relentless, even disturbing, will comes from his mother, and he got an addict’s penchant from his father. His dad, he said, has been sober for nearly 30 years by using his addictive personality for good, investing his energy in Alcoholics Anonymous and helping others overcome their itches.

But Dowdle also excels by finding out who he was as a person: “Running helped me figure out the person I was running away from and also running toward the person I wanted to be.”

There is a dual narrative in his head, one that every ultrarunner facing the highs and lows of a long race knows. The first tells him he’s not worthy. The other feels only elation. Neither, he said, is true.

“I know that the narrative playing in my head at that moment is not the full truth,” Dowdle said. “And the narrative that tells me I’m not good enough. As long as my feet are still moving forward, I can combat that thinking and know that’s not the full truth.”

Proving that imposter syndrome wrong is his part of his “why,” the magic power that he and Lewis seem to possess that helps them run much farther than just about anyone else. But that’s not his only motivation.

Dowdle was, at one point, a football coach. But when he examined his life, he didn’t think football was the right avenue for what he truly wanted to do. He wanted to connect with young men and try to help them crawl out of the same situation he was in years ago, before he began running and journaling. So he traveled across the country and hosted beer miles. He still does this, though he drinks non-alcoholic varieties now, or he simply challenges athletes to beat his beer mile time. (It’s 5:51.57.)

When the race is over, he sits down with athletes and talks with them about their lives. He tells them he was like them once, a little lost and full of doubt and pain, with only alcohol seeming to help. There are other ways, he tells them. Running could be one. A personal journey, like that of the Iron Cowboy, could be another.

“I watched the Iron Cowboy documentary, and it made me realize that I do have control, and that I can do hard things and I’m capable of more,” Dowdle said. “That’s the gift he gave me in that moment. Now I’ve been on a mission to try to give that gift to other people.”

#8346. The 15 Best Spots to Hunt During the Peak of the Whitetail Rut

Published Oct 31, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The big-racked, muscled-up brute crashes through cover. Operating like a pedigreed cutting horse, he carves out two rival bucks and sends them packing for distant hills. Quickly, he returns to the small patch of cover where the wide-eyed estrus doe waits. The pair will likely stay in that obscure piece of real estate for the next 24 to 48 hours. That’s well away from most other deer — and hunters, who are focusing on better-looking ground with better traditional habitat hundreds of yards away. But it doesn’t have to be that way.

While traditional rut stands work just fine during the peak rut, other unorthodox spots can, too. Hunters should be aware of both sides of that coin. The rut-hunting playbook isn’t as small as some might believe. That’s why I’ve ranked the best 15 spots for peak-rut deer hunting.

Funnels and pinch-points are among the most orthodox stand locations during the rut. These are simply natural terrain features that encourage deer to travel through confined spaces. Of course, these are crucial for bowhunters, but they serve as excellent stand locations for gun hunters, too.

Because they’re so effective, however, funnels and pinch-points draw attention from a lot of hunters. On public land and shared private properties, such spots can become pressured and overhunted. In these scenarios, study a parcel’s pressure levels to determine if these spots are worth your time.

Does usually use the same, or the same few, bedding areas throughout the year. Over time, bucks learn where these locations are. During the rut, they’ll visit these in search of estrus does. Hunters should know where these are located, too.

Hunting doe bedding can be tricky, though. As with hunting any bedding area, you must get in early — long before daylight. Settle in on the downwind side of bedding areas and intercept bucks cruising these edges as they scent check for does. If multiple bedding areas are connected by cover, set up along these routes as bucks travel from one to the next.

Topography plays a major role in deer movement. Specific features can influence how, when, where, and why deer traverse certain routes. One such feature is an upper-third bench. This is a bench that, as it sounds like, spans the higher part of a ridge — but not the top of the ridge itself. Because morning thermals rise, this is a common area to catch bucks cruising the first few hours of the day. They can smell potential does down below. Furthermore, bucks often prefer the leeward side of the ridge because they can smell from both directions.

Similarly, lower-third benches are important, too. These are more effective hunting locations later in the day. In the evening, and sometimes even earlier in the afternoon, thermals fall. As the evening air pulls downward, scent collects and pools in the lowest points of the landscape. That’s why bucks travel along lower-level benches to detect potential does that are traveling, or have recently traveled, along the ridge above.

Now, back to those leeward ridges I mentioned above. These are simply the downwind sides of ridges, and they’re excellent locations to intercept deer travel patterns. These serve as great bedding areas as well as travel routes for deer, which mean they’re especially great stand locations during peak rut. Whether deer are bedding there, or merely using these as travel routes, hunters can intercept them.

Another hill-country feature to hunt is the famous saddle, or a low spot between two ridges. It might be where the same continuous ridge dips down and rises back up. Or it might be where two ridges running in different directions taper and meet. Either way, a saddle allows deer to pass through from one side or the other without having to climb up and over. It’s a smart spot to lie in wait for when they do.

Throughout the whitetail range, early successional habitat is vital to deer. Overgrown fields can provide that necessary edge cover. Oftentimes, these fill up with briars, brambles, grasses, and even forbs. Such growth might not look like much to us, but it provides good bedding cover and food sources. During the rut, bucks might even push estrus does into such areas to get them away from rival bucks.

Deer drink water year-round, but bucks get especially thirsty during the rut. All the cruising and chasing develops a need to rehydrate, and they frequent watering holes. Isolated water holes are especially attractive. Deer have limited options for finding water, particularly in dry conditions, and that increases the odds of shooting deer over one. You can hunt natural water sources or create your own, although creating these in huntable locations can require some serious strategy.

Deer spend most of their lives within cover, and that’s the best place to find a big deer. But during the rut, don’t overlook the power of a quality field-based food source. Standing soybeans, freshly cut corn, or any other crop with waist grain on the ground can be great. So can food plots, especially those planted with timely species. Hunting deer over food sources that are directly adjacent to quality bedding cover can produce sightings of a lot of deer, including mature bucks that are checking does or replenishing their energy.

Buck bedding areas are incredibly productive spots throughout the early season, pre-rut, and late season. Don’t overlook these areas during the rut. Often really old bucks will continue bedding in the same areas they have been using all fall, and only search for does at night. If they don’t find a hot doe, they retreat to the bedding areas they feel safest in.

So, continue to monitor the edges of these areas with trail cameras, and move in to hunt as necessary if you think a buck is still bedding there. Keep in mind that bucks and does often bed within the same block, but bucks tend to bed at higher elevations or in areas that are more advantageous.

I know, scrapes, go cold during the peak, rut, right? Sure, scraping activity drops off. But they don’t completely shut down. Bucks continue to check scrapes, and so do does. Does, and bucks that are between does, continue checking scrapes. So it doesn’t hurt to consider their prcense as a secondary or tertiary element when weighing strand locations, especially if scrapes are nearby an area you already plan to hunt.

Bucks don’t like competition. Because of this, older deer that know what they’re doing tend to push does into random areas the remainder of the deer herd rarely uses. Often this includes random brushy areas. Maybe it’s a fencerow, thick sinkhole, patch of grass, or other obscure — but maybe visually obvious — location.

Similarly, other small pockets of cover can be good, too. Even a half-acre, or even quarter-acre of cover can hold a breeding pair of deer. If it looks like a spot at least two deer could hide from other deer, and hunters, they might just be there. It might feel weird or unproductive to hunt these spots, but if you have good reason to, it just might pay off. Perhaps you saw a buck run into such a spot, maybe you didn’t. But during gun seasons, you should at least glass these areas or consider doing a deer drive through  these small pockets.

Drainage ditches are always overlooked. After all, who wants to hunt a hole in the ground? But drainage ditches with the right characteristics can hold deer. At the very least, deer might travel across or through it. Ditch crossings can be good all season long, but during the rut, it’s not uncommon for bucks to push does into brushy areas within ditches.

This is another area you wouldn’t expect a deer, but one worth considering. Brush piles with enough cover can hold a couple deer, and breeding pairs often shack up in such spots. Finding ways to hunt these can be difficult, but don’t overlook potential activity in such areas.

#8345. Matt Robertson Just Won $1.25 Million In the Champions Tournament. It’s The Largest First Place Payout in Professional Bass Fishing History

Published Oct 31, 2026 6:48 PM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

With a final day tally of 20 pounds, 2 ounces, and a total 3 day weight of 56 pounds and an ounce, Matt Robertson won a first-place payout of $1.25 million in the Champions bass fishing tournament on Old Hickory Lake in Tennessee. This is the largest first-place payout in the sport’s history and it represents an interesting turn in pro bass fishing.

Before we dive into the rest of the results, here’s what you need to know about the tournament and how it all came together.

It’s been just over 8 years since the professional bass fishing world effectively split the best anglers in the world into two separate organizations, the Bassmaster Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. In that time, new names have risen to the top of the leaderboards, and the old guard has won their fair share of events as well.

But the question that seemed to circulate year after year was who really is the best angler in the world?

Since the two organizations don’t cross-compete well, the answer remained shrouded in speculation and uncertainty. Sure, Jacob Wheeler might be the best at catching the most fish under the MLF BPT format, but could he still sack up 5 giants for 4 consecutive days in an Elite Series format? Would the young gun, Trey McKinney, give Wheeler or Kevin VanDam a run for their money in an MLF-style event?

The bass fishing world figured we’d never know, that is, until February of this year when World Bass Enterprises introduced The Champions Tournament. CEO Brian Bird announced the tournament, and an eye-popping $3.25 million purse to go along with it. Bass fishing fans from around the world started to pay attention.

To qualify for The Champions Tournament, Bassmaster Elite Series anglers and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers fished their respective 2026 tours throughout the year. After each event, they were awarded Angler of the Year points. The Champions Tournament lineup consisted of the top 25 in AOY points from the Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. The additional spots were filled based off of a “win and you’re in” ruling that applies to anglers who won one of the major events, but didn’t make the points cut.

Two additional anglers were selected through a random draw that WBE put on for those who pre-ordered the Pay-per-view streaming service.  Due to naming rights, the anglers were split into teams. Elite anglers were assigned ‘Team Stars’ and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers were assigned ‘Team Stripes’. The two randomly drawn anglers are Eric Giessing (Stars) and Kyle Carr (Stripes).

At the end of the event, a trophy was awarded to the top performing team, also “settling” the debate of which organization has the better anglers. For the 2026 Champions Tournament, Team Stars (Elite Series) has won bragging rights for the year.

“There has always been friendly competition and banter between the anglers on each tour, but no way to actually settle the score on the water,” MLF Bass Pro Tour 2025 Angler of the Year Jacob Wheeler said in a statement. “The opportunity to crown a true world champion across the entire sport is something our anglers have wanted for a very long time.”

The Champions Tournament was held on Old Hickory Lake, launching out of Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The launch and respective FanFest was full of attractions like a petting zoo, kids fishing area, inflatable archery, cornhole tournament, boat demos, and more. They even had the legendary Bill Dance fire off a cannon during the shotgun launch on the first day of competition.

Unsurprisingly, forward-facing sonar was addressed for this event, and seemingly played into a 50/50 outcome. For the first two days of competition, anglers were able to select which day they’d fish with live sonar, and which day they’d go without it. Then for the top 15 anglers fishing the final day, they got to use live sonar for 3 hours of competition.

To add to the pomp and circumstance, as if $1.25 million wasn’t enough, the weights also reset for the top 15 anglers heading into the final day. Making it truly anyone’s ballgame coming into Saturday. Old Hickory Lake put on quite a show for the first two days of competition, with largemouth, spotted bass, and smallmouth all making their way to the scales. The smallmouth dominant bags carried the most weight due to the minimum keeper size being 18-inches, while largemouth and spotted bass only needed to be 14-inches to make the cut.

The final day featured the following anglers fighting for the first place prize.

Matt Robertson, Ron Nelson, Bob Downey, Fisher Anaya, Pake South, Jason Christie, Trey Mckinney, Takahiro Omori, Kyle Welcher, Cole Sands, Chris Johnston, Cody Meyer, Bryan Thrift, Michael Neal, and Wesley Strader.

And while they all certainly wanted the top prize, the second place through seventh place payouts weren’t anything to scoff at either. Here is a look at the top 7 anglers, their final day weights, and their payouts after the final weigh-in. 15th place made a cool $20,000 and the payouts increased in $5,000 increments up to 7th.

1st Place: Matt Robertson (20-02) — $1.25 Million

3rd Place: Wesley Strader (11-02) — $300,000

4th Place: Trey Mckinney (11-0) — $200,000

5th Place: Michael Neal (10-10) — $100,000

While we put the largest professional bass fishing payout ever in the rearview mirror, it’s worth considering what The Champions Tournament means for bass fishing fans everywhere. Personally, there’s a bit of a shock factor involved. The payouts for the Bassmaster Classic and MLF Redcrest combined don’t even sniff the purse that was just awarded during this three-day event. That’s truly awe inspiring.

But what it really has shown me is that the two major organizations need to do some soul searching. If World Bass Enterprises can come out of nowhere and pull this off, perhaps it’s time to look at how they were able to do it successfully. Would fans pay a yearly subscription to watch a Pay-per-view Elite or BPT event? If so, could that increase the purses for those events and help the professionals in our sport actually make a living? I don’t see why not.

I know change is difficult for outdoorsmen and women, it’s in our nature to hold on to traditions and the status quo, but this weekend has shown me that there is a way to actually grow the sport of competitive bass fishing in a meaningful way. Now we’ll see if either organization actually has the guts to give it a try and truly make their anglers’ lives better.

As a final thought, I was blown away by the live coverage and the fanbase that showed up in-person and online, especially with the seasonality of this event. The bass fishing world was hungry for The Champions Tournament, and World Bass Enterprises pulled it off in epic fashion. I’m already looking forward to the 2027 lineup.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8343. Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to a Top Deer Expert

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:14 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Jeff Sturgis has the unique experience of living through dozens of deer seasons all at once. As the founder of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, he works with clients around the country to improve their deer hunting and private land habitat.

But before ever stepping foot on a property, Sturgis does in-depth interviews with these hunters to understand what they’d like to improve and what problems they’ve been having. Through this process, trends start to emerge.

Sturgis calls these problems “huntisms.” But they could also be described as misconceptions, misunderstandings, or straight up bad information. Whatever you want to call them, there are certain things that hunters get wrong when it comes to hunting mature bucks and managing habitat for those mature bucks.

So in this episode of the Outdoor Life Podcast, Sturgis will reference his decades of experience working on private land habitat as well as his time spent hunting on public ground to outline the most common and detrimental deer hunting mistakes. Heed his advice for a better season next year.

This common mentality of having to pound the woods and hunt all the time has saved a lot of big deer over the decades, Sturgis says.

“In some cases I can see this being partially true,” Sturgis says. “Maybe if you’re hunting public land, you’ve got ten spots and you’ve got the time to hunt freely.”

But if you’re hunting small parcels where you can’t afford to spook deer, then it’s usually smarter to stay home when hunting conditions are poor in order to not burn out your stands.

“There’s something to be said for minimizing your hunting, taking care of other priorities in life and expecting a higher rate of potential success because you’ve not over-pressured your stand locations.”

“It’s not just your stand locations [that you don’t want to burn out, it’s also your family, your career, your friends — it extends to an entire way to look at things. When I go out in the woods I want there to be a reasonable expectation that I’m going to shoot a deer for this reason.”

Sturgis says that if you have a “rutcation” planned where you know you’re going to hunt for a solid seven to nine days in a row, then it’s critical to reduce your impact. Instead of charging into a core area regardless of conditions, hunt spots where your scent cone won’t spook deer (because it’s blowing over a lake or off a cliff). And when conditions aren’t ideal, hunt transition areas where you could catch a big buck walking by, but you won’t spook deer near bedding areas or primary food sources.

Sturgis works with many clients who have the financial resources to grow and maintain sprawling food plots on their properties. Many of these clients believe that growing the maximum amount of food on the property will translate to holding the most amount of mature bucks in the fall.

But that’s not how it plays out most of the time. Growing too much summertime food — like big clover or bean plots — will increase the number of does and fawns on the property. During the summer and early fall, mature bucks don’t like to live on crowded food sources and bedding areas, Sturgis says.

“When you add summer food to good cover, you get a lot of does and fawns,” Sturgis says. “And those does and fawns that are here today are here to stay.”

These deer take up space and resources. Mature bucks will live on the fringes of these high-density deer areas but not establish a core zone there.

“Yeah, some bucks will come through during the rut. But bucks, the older they get, they don’t want that commotion and stress of a bunch of does and fawns. That’s why they live somewhere else.”

Sturgis says it’s better to focus on a comprehensive management strategy with proper deer cover, screening cover, sanctuaries, water holes, fall food, and yes, maybe some summer food plots, than it is to simply plant clover plots throughout the entire property.

“If you want to raise the population, add summer food. If you want to lower the population, get rid of summer food,” Sturgis says. “When I go to a client and see 20 acres of beans on their 200-acre property and we drive around and see over 100 does and fawns and only a couple bucks, they have a severe problem. I’d rather have those does and fawns be somewhere else in the summertime and shift over to the property starting in September and October.”

Don’t read this as an attack on food plots. Sturgis has written countless articles on the benefits of food plots, he’s got an online food plot class, he’s authored a book on the subject, and Whitetail Habitat Solutions sells food plot seed. So yes, food plots can be a critical element in consistently harvesting mature bucks.

But that doesn’t mean you should always hunt over them.

“This year I shot four bucks in four states with my bow … and not one of them was shot on a food plot,” Sturgis says. “Then I go to clients and they’re spending 90 percent of their hunts on food plots — and I’m not saying I never hunt on food plots — but the point is that the vast majority of my bucks are shot not in food plots.”

Sturgis tries to convince his clients to hunt away from food plots. Focusing instead on waterholes or funnels in the woods that might lead to food. This helps hunters spook fewer deer and see target bucks during daylight hours.

“Food plots have the greatest level of potential reward and the greatest level of risk,” Sturgis says. “If you spook out those food plots, you’ve just destroyed your property.”

Even though Sturgis has access to prime whitetail properties in the Midwest, he also hunts public land in Pennsylvania every year. In 22 seasons of hunting the same public area, Sturgis has shot 18 bucks.

It’s pretty common for him to bump into other hunters on these hunts, but he doesn’t sweat it. He just moves somewhere else. The key is being flexible and using tactics that match the conditions. For example, if it’s snowy and windy, Sturgis might still hunt through an area. If the woods are blanketed in crunchy leaves, he’ll opt to sit for the day.

One way that Sturgis makes sure that he avoids other hunters is by walking in at twilight (not in the dark).

“You don’t have to be to your spot before light,” Sturgis says. “When I’m walking into a spot like that, I don’t know what tree I’m going to be sitting under or in… So we’re walking into an area in daylight and still hunting [our way in].”

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season

It’s also important to remember that other hunters will bump deer long distances, not just a few hundred yards.

“Public land deer will get pushed a long way,” Sturgis says. “Especially in open woods. Where we hunt we can get 200-yard shots in the woods in some places. So when people push deer out there, they’re moving three quarters of a mile. So don’t think about just one little thicket. Think about how deer are moving in the big picture [across the landscape].”

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8342. The Best Weather Radios, Tested and Reviewed

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

A good weather radio is a must-own these days, especially considering today’s unpredictable climate. Unexpected natural disasters can strike quickly and cut off vital lines of communication. Hurricanes, tornados, blizzards, floods, and earthquakes are just some of the natural disasters everyone should prepare for. Fortunately, a weather radio can convey vital pieces of information when the internet and cell phone networks fail.

The great news is that today’s weather radios are extremely affordable, so there’s really no excuse to not have at least one in your home in your home survival kit in case disaster strikes. We took the time to test out six of the most popular options available to see if they live up to the hype—and which are the best weather radios you can buy.

Most weather radios have a battery around 2000 mAh. Givoust stepped things up drastically with an 8000 mAh offering that gives this radio superior battery life to all the others on this list. I ran it for days without losing power once it was fully charged. And if you’re utilizing the hand crank and solar panel, you won’t need to worry about it running down very often. The antenna on this radio is very nice. I was easily able to listen to NOAA forecasts and AM/FM broadcasts while in my basement, away from the windows. This is the one to pick if you are concerned about getting a signal in a shelter or a canyon with steep walls. The sound is clear and crisp.

While the radio features are great, the lights of this radio are even better. The powerful flashlight feature on the front is blindingly bright. It has several different settings for lighting up a dark room. There’s also a nice little flip-up reading light that nicely illuminates the area around the radio. This is one I want to keep close for power outages. The SOS alarm is also extremely loud. It would be great to signal for help in a pinch.

The only complaint I have about the radio is that the compass on the strap isn’t anything special. It’s a standard, cheap compass that’s sold in the sporting goods section of every outdoor store. Everything else about this radio is top notch and very well designed. They used quality components for just about every aspect of this build. This radio charged my cell phone quickly while making almost no dent in its own battery.

I ran this radio for well over 12 hours straight without making much of a dent in the 4000 mAh battery. This is a great option for anyone who’s anticipating the possibility of multi-day power outages. I really liked the exceptionally bright LED flashlight and reading light on this radio, both of which are extremely bright and perfect for blackouts. Given the larger size of the battery, there’s less of a worry about running it down using these lights.

This radio features a dedicated SOS button that emits a loud siren. I like the fact Drained Snail made this a dedicated button instead of just incorporating the signal into the flashlight button. I didn’t have to worry about tripping the sound by accident either since the button needs to be held down a few seconds to activate it.

One standout feature I like better than the other radios is that fact that you can listen to it and charge a cell phone simultaneously. Most of the other radios on this list only you to do one of those things at a time.

This radio has a shorter antenna than I’d like, which slightly affects the sound quality. Expect a little bit of static in enclosed rooms. The crank handle also feels just a little too long when compared to other radios. This was my least favorite to crank.

When deep in the backcountry, an emergency weather radio can keep you informed of the weather where cell signal is non-existent. I like the Midland ER210 for this scenario because it has a very small profile. It’s only about 7 inches long by 3 inches high and just over 2 inches wide. The hand crank folds down almost completely flush with the body of radio. There aren’t a lot of points where it will snag up on parts of a backpacking backpack. The weight also feels decent considering there’s a 2600 mAh power bank included inside. A small solar panel helps keep it going while far from civilization.

The sound quality of this radio is rather surprising as it outperformed every other radio on the list. The AM and FM stations come in quite clear and crisp with none of that “tinny” sound that often accompanies smaller speakers. Plus, the flashlight is surprisingly bright. The third setting is an automatic SOS beacon for emergencies.

The antenna is a little short. It didn’t work well in my basement. However, outside it gets great reception. You shouldn’t have trouble getting updates from higher points. For $50, this radio offers a ton of features in a small package.

This nifty little radio came with my Decked/Uncharted emergency supply kit, but you can also buy it separately. I’ve found the hand crank charger on this radio works perfectly. Just crank it for a few minutes and you’re good to go. I’ve left this radio running in the background through a full eight-hour workday with no issues losing power. It has a shorter antenna than the others on this list. While it picked up FM signals just fine in my basement, I had to go upstairs to get the NOAA forecasts. That shouldn’t be an issue for anyone who lives in an area where basements aren’t the norm, though.

I had some issues with the phone charging features of this radio. They just flat out didn’t work on my model. But I don’t really see that as a downside because the basic light and radio features work so well. You don’t ever have to worry about batteries with this unit, and the size is compact enough for the smallest RVs and cars. I think this would be a good option if you’re looking to stock several homes and vehicles with an emergency weather device. It’s also a good option for an emergency kit because it takes up so little space.

The battery on this radio is one of the smaller ones I tested. However, it has a rather unique feature in that there’s space to insert three AAA batteries. Add in the solar panel and crank, and there is no excuse to not get this radio running in an emergency. While this radio got a regular FM signal in my basement, it wouldn’t pick up the weather forecasts unless I was above ground level. This is probably a radio better suited for areas where people don’t use a basement for shelter.

I like the buttons on this radio a little more than the tuning knobs on some other radios. It just helps to be more a little more precise in locking onto a signal from a station that’s in between frequencies. I also found it to be rather efficient on battery life. It ran for a solid 10 hours before it finally ran out of juice.

I thoroughly tested each of these weather radios because I’m a firm believer it’s best not to wait until disaster strikes before seeing if a piece of equipment really works. After making sure each radio had a full charge or fresh batteries, I ran all the radios continuously for at least 12 hours or until they died. I wanted to see what kind of runtime users can expect. For the testing of signal, I ran all the radios outdoors, indoors, and in my basement.

My goal with the basement test was to simulate taking shelter from a tornado or other severe weather. If the best weather radios can get signal in a basement, they should get a signal anywhere. I then evaluated the sound quality of each. I also considered the following factors:

With considering the best weather radios, the key feature to look for is one capable of receiving forecasts and alerts from the NOAA Weather Radio network. This information is gathered by the National Weather Service (NWS), which then broadcasts it using eight different stations. It’s important to note these broadcasts cannot be heard by a regular radio.

The forecasts are read by an artificial voice and are distributed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. They’re a little strange to listen to, but they’ll give you all the weather information you could ever need. And they’re usually more accurate than a cellphone app. I live about 30 miles from the shores of Lake Michigan, so my local broadcasts also include information on lake conditions, including surf warnings for dangerous waves and rip currents. If you’re looking for a radio specifically for emergencies, an NOAA radio is the way to go.

This acronym refers to specific area message encoding, which allows you to get county or township-specific weather alerts for a specific area of your choosing. It’s a nice feature to have, especially if you live in an area prone to tornadoes or other severe storms. Radios with this function will give off a high-pitched alert like the emergency broadcast system to alert you something is going on with the weather.

Depending on the radio, you may need to input a location code to the radio to start receiving SAME broadcasts. The method of doing this will vary based on the make and model of radio. However, the National Weather Service provides a handy listing of all the codes and counties on their website. Sometimes codes will be out of service, so it’s handy to check if you’ve already been using a code for years that suddenly stops working.

Compared to other electronic devices, weather radios usually offer an incredible amount of value and versatility because most are built to be multi-function devices that serve as more than just a way to get emergency information. All the models I tested have USB ports for charging cell phones and other compatible devices from an internal 2000 mah power bank. Some have power banks that are larger than that.

Many models now offer an integrated flashlight feature with bright LED bulbs that will brighten a dark room. I’ve seen some flashlights on these radios that rival dedicated lights of the same price.

Another common feature is a lithium-ion battery with multiple ways of charging it. Let’s face it, most of us probably do not check the batteries in our emergency supplies as often as we should. It’s a nice little peace of mind when you can quickly charge a weather radio with a hand crank.

Crank radios usually deliver about six minutes of run time for the radio feature for every minute you turn the crank. Alternatively, you’ll get around the same amount of runtime from built-in flashlights depending on the different flashlight settings. Higher brightness will obviously drain it faster.Many models now also feature a small built-in solar panel to keep running when all other power sources fail.

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), their seven VHF public service band frequencies include 162.550 MHz, 162.525 MHz, 162.500 MHz, 162.476 MHz, 162.450 MHz, and 162.425 MHz. Most weather radios have a dedicated knob for cycling through these bands.

In my experience, crank radios are worth the cost. After all, it’s easy to forget to change out the batteries and have a radio that is completely dead in storage. But a crank radio allows you to quickly charge it back up and get relevant information in a hurry. It’s great when you cannot find the appropriate batteries, too.

Make sure the radio’s antenna is fully extended. You might have to move it around to find the best position for a clear signal. It also helps if you can place the radio near an open window with a clear view of the sky. If that fails, try getting to a higher spot.
