#8331. The FN Mauser Is the Best Deer Rifle that History Forgot

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Hunting rifles come and go and sometimes even good ones don’t stay around. The decades following World War II saw a boom in hunters and a voracious appetite for new rifles and cartridges. This was the heyday of the Pre-64 Model 70 and the Winchester Magnums, but we no longer hear much about the many Mauser sporting rifles made by FN and imported from Belgium.

I recently got my mitts on one of these rifles, which belonged to my great grandfather, chambered in .270 Win. While this gun undoubtedly rode around in the rifle rack of Grandpa Curtis’s truck when I was a youngster, I’m looking at it anew. According to my dad and uncle, Grandpa’s brother was a gunsmith and built the rifle for him. This was after he’d raised a family in a log cabin in Colorado during the Depression and developed a taste for July mule deer. He used this rifle to shoot a lot of deer and elk.

A family heirloom like this gives me a perspective on what a quality hunting rifle looked like in the 1950s, and an idea of how well it’s held up over time. It’s also fun to compare it to the rifles we have today.

It’s common to hear or read about the many sporterized military rifles that post-war hunters adopted. These would typically be either 1903 Springfields or remnant military Mauser rifles. But these FN Mausers weren’t sporterized — they were manufactured for a couple decades as sporting-specific guns. Many, including this rifle, were imported by Firearms International Corp. and marked as such on the receivers.

They were brought in and sold by various companies and in numerous formats. An ad in the November, 1951 Issue of Outdoor Life displays the JC Higgins Model 50 — which was simply an FN Mauser and sold at Sears, Roebuck. They had the chrome vanadium steel barrel and even came with a 2.5-power scope, for $135. Another ad, from the September, 1952 issue, for the Parker-Whelen Gun Catalog, lists .30/06 and .270 FN Mausers for $137.50 without a receiver-mounted rear sight. That would cost you another ten bucks. This could be a clue to the specific origin of this .270, as the front of the barrel has markings that appear to be where a front sight was once mounted, but there is no evidence of a barrel-mounted rear sight like you’ll see on Pre-64 Model 70 rifles and others like the Remington Model 721.

Ultimately, lots of these guns were imported in various forms and were sold by companies like Weatherby, Harrington & Richardson, and Colt. Complete FN rifles, according to what little I could find, had a specific pearl edge to the checkering on the grips, but it’s likely that not all of them did. Barrelled actions were also imported and built into custom hunting rifles.

This particular rifle appears to be either one that showed up as a barrelled action — possibly with a front sight. The barrel and receiver both bear the appropriate stampings for a matched pair that left the factory in Belgium. But the 22-inch barrel appears to have been cut down and re-crowned — as these were generally 24-inch barrels. It’s stamped with the year “1951” and bears matching 2837 serial numbers.

The stock has a handsome grain and good ergonomics. It lacks any checkering, but the fore-end has a nice belly and is capped with an ivory-colored plastic cap. The grip is capped with a similar plastic cap and its vertical orientation provides a wonderful balance of trigger reach and allows a crisp perpendicular squeeze. The raised comb is, in part, made from a separate block of wood. It’s pinned atop the buttstock and shaped to match, but the seams are still visible.

The floorplate isn’t hinged on this rifle. Rather, it’s detachable and retained by a spring-loaded button at the rear and retaining lip at the front. The fitting of the stock is very precise and, despite being bedded from the tang to the cap on the fore-end, very little bedding material is visible alongside the metal. Pillars around the action screws also help create an incompressible bridge between the bottom metal and action. The precise fit of metal and wood are things we’ll only see today on custom rifles and the highest-end production guns. Factory stocks — both wood and synthetic — are either CNC-milled or molded with baked-in tolerances rather than hand fit. The workmanship on my 1954 Model 70 is good, but not to the same level.

The barrel is a pretty standard sporter taper, finishing at .635 inches. I assume it has been cut down from 24 inches to 22. It’s a heavier barrel than you’ll see on classics like the M70 featherweight and contributes to the rifle’s roughly 9.5-pound overall weight.

The action and barrel share all matching and appropriate proof marks, and remain in good shape, with the bolt sliding like glass down the slick raceways. The bottom of the bolt handle is flattened and knurled for a better grip, and is generally smoother to operate than my previously mentioned M70. The safety switch is textured on both sides. It appears to be pitting because of its irregularity, but no other parts show similar signs of corrosion.

The receiver is topped with a one-piece Redfield mount and Bear Cub 2 ¾-power scope that uses a post-style reticle. In the early days of magnified optics, this gave a sight picture similar to that of a front post iron sight — to which most shooters would be accustomed. It was fitted with a Canjar trigger — a premium aftermarket upgrade, that breaks at 3 pounds, 7 ounces as set.

To test the rifle for accuracy, I fired four five-shot groups with several different types of contemporary .270 ammo. Where we would normally aggregate these five-shot groups into a single 20-shot group for each type of ammo, It was apparent that the system was limited, in part, by the optic, so I’m just sticking with the group size averages.

I believe the rifle is certainly capable of better accuracy than this but, considering the vintage scope, it proved itself perfectly capable of hitting a deer or elk cleanly out to 200 to 300 yards. Frankly, it’s not uncommon for us to test modern rifles with high-magnification scopes that average worse. A low-power optic itself doesn’t prevent a rifle from shooting accurately either, but this style of reticle requires the correct-sized target and a lot of concentration to maintain a consistent hold. The post covers about four inches of a 100-yard target. When the barrel warmed, mirage definitely affected sight picture too. I tried both a six-o’clock hold and a navy hold (dead center), and saw some vertical stringing with both methods.

Read Next: 10 Classic Hunting Rifles Every Hunter Should Own

For as much as we hear about classic rifles like the Savage 99 and Winchester Model 70, I’m surprised that Mausers like this haven’t carried a similar reputation. So many rifles, including the Winchester, were derived from the Mauser action itself. The rifles even commanded a higher price than Model 70s at the time. While precision manufacturing, materials, and coatings have gotten better, a rifle like this one could still hold its own today.

The OL editors pick the best deer hunting rifles on the market.

#8330. A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

Published Nov 3, 2026 2:09 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Robert Denninger was in a tree saddle the afternoon of October 23 when he spotted a deer in a creek bed about 75 yards away. He’d accessed the Oklahoma public hunting area by kayak, paddling up a creek to a remote spot that he’d pinpointed the previous day.

“I decided to slide down quietly with my bow and get a better look at the deer in the creek,” Denninger tells Outdoor Life. “When I got close to the creek I spotted two big mature bucks fighting and they were locked up tight by their antlers.”

He knew he was witnessing an epic outdoor event and he shot video of the fight on his phone.

“The bucks were plowing into each other and into the creek bank,” says Denninger, a 42-year-old retiree from Dallas. “Mud was flying everywhere. My mind was racing – would attempting to harvest these bucks be a hunter’s gift or a violation of fair chase?”

It was clear the bucks were not able to separate their antlers. Denninger struggled with what to do and pondered if it would be ethical and legal to shoot the larger of the two bucks, which was a 12-pointer with a typical rack. He recalled a friend telling him a story of once finding a pair of locked-antler bucks dead in a pond. They had been killed and half eaten by coyotes.

Before deciding what to do, Denninger called a game warden.

“I spoke with a local [Oklahoma] Game Warden who assured me he didn’t have any on-call vet who could have come out to sedate the animals and attempt a safe unlocking,” Denninger says.

“The thought of letting ‘nature run its course’ and coming back in the following days to spook a pack of coyotes off two rotten carcasses or trying my best to put an ethical kill on these animals were what I believed my choices were,” he explains. “I decided to shoot the 12-pointer.”

His first arrow was deflected by brush. But his second arrow found the deer’s heart, and it quickly died.

“I watched to see if the eight point could free himself, but he only struggled more, barely able to move the weight of the harvested 12-pointer,” the bowhunter says.

Denninger had no way of freeing the deer, so he decided to shoot the second buck with his bow. Even when both deer were dead, it was impossible to unlock their antlers.

That’s when he called a couple younger buddies, who eventually arrived with a wheeled wagon.

“We tried to unlock their racks many times, and were unable to,” Denninger says. “We field dressed them. But it was a rugged haul to get the two bucks out, taking well over three hours to get them to a truck and out of the woods. It was almost midnight [by the time we were done].”

He called his Texas friend and taxidermist Dustin Moon and told him about the locked-antler bucks and his hunting tale.

“Dustin and his wife Stephanie of New Story Taxidermy drove five hours (on their sixth wedding anniversary) to where I was so they could see the bucks and help my deer processor get their antlers unlocked.”

Eventually they succeeded and the deer were separated. They will be mounted, though Denninger doesn’t know if he’ll have them in a locked-horn mount or separate mounts.

The 12-pointer is believed to be 7.5 years old and has a rough green score of 152 inches. It’s the biggest buck Denninger has taken during his dedicated bowhunting career. The 8-pointer is thought to be 5.5 years old and scores 132 inches. Both bucks have typical racks.

“I think what I did was the most ethical thing I could have done with my two Oklahoma buck tags, especially considering the alternative of having them suffer and die in their struggle, or have coyotes kill them.”

#8329. Swarovski NL Pure Binocular Review: The Best Glass Money Can Buy

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Let me tell you a story about how good the Swarovski NL Pure binocular is. On a combined elk and deer hunt in Montana, a fellow writer, two guides, and I were glassing a bedded whitetail buck from long way off, trying to figure out if he was worth a stalk. I was looking through the NL Pure, and the other guys were peering into various other high-end binos, none costing less than a grand and some costing much more than that.

Studying the deer, I said, “He’s got decent mass but isn’t super tall or wide. He might go 130 inches.” The other guys asked how I’d surmised all this from so far away. I handed him the NL Pure, and one after another, they said, “Oh!” and “Ah!” and “Holy sh*t!” Finally, they all agreed that the buck was somewhere between 125 and 130, and we tromped off to go look for another.

That’s what next-level resolution does for you. It doesn’t come cheaply, of course, but it makes a real difference in the field. And so, with that in mind, let’s take a close look at the Swarovski NL Pure, how it performed in my testing, and why I think it is the best hunting binocular you can buy today.

Related: The Best Binoculars of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

The NL Pure is not new. Not by a long shot. The first models in the series hit shelves way back in 2020, one of the few good things to happen in a no-good, rotten year. All the more impressive then that now, six years later, the NL Pure is still as good a binocular as you can find.

Not long after those first NL Pure offerings debuted, I awarded the 10×42 model our “Best Binocular at Any Price” award in F&S’s annual binocular test—and it has not relinquished that distinction since. Every year, I test the latest and the greatest glass, and I keep a 10×42 NL Pure handy to compare to the newest contenders. And for now, at least, it is still at the top of the heap.

I have written before that the gap between good and great binoculars is closing. That’s great news for hunters. But a handful of models still stand totally apart, and the NL Pure is the finest example of that. My 10×42 test model notched perfect scores in the resolution and image quality tests. With lots of binoculars, you have to look and look and strain your eyes to detect small differences in resolution. Not with these. The NL Pure’s advantage in resolving detail is immediately obvious, and the picture is as clean and bright as you could want, with virtually zero color shift, field curvature, or stray light. But it’s not enough to say that the binocular’s optical performance is the best or even perfect. It’s more like a revelation. You peer into it, and the world looks like a better place.

Meanwhile, the NL Pure’s innovative hour-glass, open-bridge design saves weight and balances perfectly in the hand, making it easy to stabilize the binocular on long glassing sessions, and an available forehead rest adds to the comfort. The focus wheel is large, precise, and silky. The diopter and eyecup adjustments are positive and exact.

Related: How to Use Your Binoculars and Spotting Scope to Hunt Elk, Mule Deer, and Antelope in the West

If you want to see exactly how I tested the NL Pure, you can go to our annual binocular test and look at the section called “How I Tested and Score Binoculars.” In a nutshell, I used a 1951 USAF Resolution Test Chart to test resolution in daylight and low-light conditions. I used a color-artifact chart to test for chromatic aberration. I also tested for edge-to-edge clarity, feeling of immersion (which we’ll get to), overall image quality, handling, ergonomics, build quality, and weather resistance.

In all of the optical categories, the NL Pure set the standard. Resolution was nothing short of astounding. But world-class glass like this offers more than just stunning detail; it immerses you in the image. An optics professor I used to test binoculars with calls this “feeling of immersion.” With the NL Pure’s huge field of view and field-flattening lenses, you get the sense that you’ve stepped into the picture and that everything there is brilliant and vivid and free of the little imperfections that otherwise distract you from the experience.

The quality of the construction is obvious the second you put this binocular in your hand, and everything from the focus wheel to the diopter functioned just as it should. All of that said, the NL Pure is not flawless. To my surprise, it pretty much bombed my weather-resistance test, which involved a half-hour submersion in a creek and then a half-hour visit to the deep freeze. After the submersion portion, the image was usable but not especially clear, and it was close to unusable coming out of the freezer. I should be clear that my test is obviously tougher than what most hunters will face in the outdoors. Still, it provides an apples-to-apples comparison, and only one binocular out of about 10 tested did worse.

That, however, is the NL Pure’s only flaw. In every other way, this binocular is spectacular. The other thing that is spectacular—as in breathtaking—is the price. The NL Pure now comes in seven configurations, from 8×32 to 14×52, and ranges in price from $2,799 to $3,849. For most of us, that’s a whole lot to spend on a binocular. But some hunters are willing to pay top dollar to own the best of the best. And the NL Pure is exactly that. Give it a little extra protection in rough weather, and it will show you things other hunters will never see.

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

Dave Hurteau took the position of assistant editor at Field & Stream in 1994, and has been with the brand ever since. His first job was to work on F&S’s 100th anniversary issue, and in 2020, he helped spearhead the 125th. In that span, he’s worked with many of the magazine’s greats, from Gene Hill and Bob Brister to Bill Heavey, and David E. Petzal. Highlights Education Hurteau graduated from the University of Rochester with degrees in English and philosophy, the latter of which helped him to rationalize the days spent hunting and fishing in western New York when he should have been in class. Experience After graduating college, Hurteau launched a regional hunting and fishing magazine from an apartment in Ithaca, New York, and soon parlayed that into the job at Field & Stream. He’s had no less than eight titles with F&S, from gear editor to contributing writer and, now, executive editor. He’s been nominated for a National Magazine Award as a writer and was part of an F&S editorial team to win two National Magazine Awards for General Excellence—the highest honor in magazine journalism. Hurteau oversees much of the brand’s hunting, gear, and general outdoors coverage. An serious hunter and angler himself, he is co-author of The Total Deer Hunter Manual and the The Total Bowhunting Manual. #8326. One Wrong Move Could Be Fatal. So Why Are These Climbers Competing at Free Soloing?

Michael Reese at the top of the First Flatiron in Boulder, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Michael Reese)

About our reporting: Climbing reporter Holly Chen interviewed three free soloists and one additional speed climber in Boulder, researched fatalities in Accidents in North American Climbing, and pulled from her own experience free soloing the Second Flatiron to answer questions about the world of competitive free soloing.

I stood waiting in front of a health food restaurant in south Boulder, Colorado. The Flatirons rose high above the building, their slabs of red sandstone jutting out of the mountainside like the spines of a prehistoric monster.

On September 3, 32-year-old climber Michael Reese broke the First Flatiron’s fastest known time (FKT) from the dirt at its base to the summit anchor, with no rope. He climbed the Direct Route (5.6,R; 1,000ft) of the East Face in 7 minutes 51 seconds, breaking what he believed would be the last minute barrier of this generation. The previous record was 8 minutes 33 seconds, set by Joe Kennedy in 2022.

Which one is Michael Reese? Everywhere I looked at the restaurant, less than a 10 minute drive from the Chautauqua trailhead, I saw La Sportiva and Scarpa running shoes, Salomon running vests, and folded ultralight running poles sticking out of ultralight backpacks. Any of these people could have just come off the climb.

The ease was the first thing I noticed about Reese. For someone who holds multiple FKTs in the Flatirons and one on Yellow Spur (5.8; 550ft) in Eldorado Canyon, I expected him to be cocky, confident, maybe a little elitist; he was anything but. Reese smiled easily, laughed easily, and spoke candidly, unperturbed by the recorder sitting between us. He was leaving for Yosemite the following day, and we exchanged stories of our experiences climbing in the Valley. When I joked about my personal best up the First Flatiron–somewhere shy of an hour, although I did not officially keep time–he congratulated me genuinely.

“You can do it,” Reese urged. “Get some racing shoes. Do some warmups … You’ll be going faster.”

As climbing has grown, it has increasingly legendized free soloing and going fast—but we’ve rarely seen these two disciplines combined and going without a rope. The Oscar-winning film Free Solo (2017) made the term so mainstream that it recently appeared in a Taylor Swift song, and speed climbing records have made headlines again and again. But these fantastical feats of risk and speed are usually in the hands of highly experienced climbers, such as Alex Honnold, the spectacular pendulum of Dean Potter, or Yosemite Search and Rescue members. Additionally, most of these races happen on cliffs that the average person can’t easily ascend, such as El Capitan.

Reese is a different kind of figure. A Boulder local, he is not sponsored, and not a professional. Reese started climbing at the University of Colorado (CU) Boulder in 2014. The first time he went up the First Flatiron, he said to himself, “If I get off this [alive], I’m never climbing again.” And the First Flatiron is far from inaccessible; with the base a 1.3-mile hike from the trailhead, for many people, the barrier to entry is only a pair of shoes.

The new FKT leaves me with an uneasy mix of admiration and doubt. A person’s risk is not entirely his own when he takes it in a busy place like Chautauqua Park, where hikers, runners, picnickers, and climbers share the same space. So is competitive free soloing on low fifth-class terrain something to celebrate or a toxic addiction to discourage? A fatal fall is always possible, and the barrier to entry is so low. In fact, anyone writing about it, including myself, is working on blurry ground where reporting and the glorification of risk are hard to tell apart. Does this recognition create a feedback loop that incentivizes more to partake in the risky sport?

To understand how competitive free soloing actually operates, I had to go back to the people who have been going fast on this rock for decades before Reese.

The history of speed records in the Flatirons runs through a small, unusual club called The Satan’s Minions Scrambling Club, which Bill Wright started in 2001. Three of its members told me they don’t “race” each other. Instead, they have “personal time trials,” to avoid the ire of the Parks & Open Space regulations, which prohibit races.

The club keeps books. Stefan Griebel, a longtime member, whom a mutual friend described to me as someone who holds “every record under the sun,” has a meticulously kept log book detailing every FKT on a Flatiron dating back to the 1980s. Today, members’ times are verified by Strava entries.

Griebel met Wright in 2003 and joined the club’s annual Flatiron scrambles, which have now run for about 22 years. Each one starts at a trailhead, free solos a Flatiron, and ends back in the parking lot. Buzz Burrell, a trail-running legend then 52, reset the trailhead-to-trailhead mark at 35 minutes and change. Griebel, who was half Burrell’s age at the time, couldn’t keep pace.

“[Buzz] just dropped every single person that day,” Griebel reminisced.

A year later, trail runner Dave Mackey took Burell’s trailhead-to-trailhead FKT down to 33:19. But being a trail runner, Griebel knew he would have the upper hand on rock. In 2010, Griebel closed the gap, and took the record to 33:05. The record changed hands to Mathias Messner in 2015 and Kyle Richardson in 2019.

In the spring of 2020, Reese returned to Boulder from a biotech master’s program at California Polytechnic State University. The COVID pandemic had canceled the triathlon nationals he’d spent months training for, and he had a season of fitness and nothing to spend it on. He decided to see how fast he could go on the Flatirons. It began as a text-message rivalry with Joe Mitchem, a friend from CU’s cross-country team, over Freeway (5.0; 600ft) on the Second Flatiron. Reese didn’t have Strava and didn’t know the records existed until the two of them realized they’d gone under the standing Freeway mark of about 6:20. That fall, he entered the club’s time trials and finished second.

Griebel remembers meeting Reese on the First Flatiron. The two soloed to the summit and trotted down together. “He can run uphill like nobody I’ve ever seen,” Griebel said.

The base-to-summit FKT, the one Reese prefers, was still Griebel’s in 2020, at 9:25. Reese told me the time stunned him. That summer, Reese broke it by seconds. Then Joe Kennedy, a California athlete, broke that in 2022 to 8:33. That sent Reese into harder training than he’d done in 2020 or 2021, and this September brought the record down to 7:51.

The club looks different today. It is still heavily male dominated; Griebel estimates eight men for every one woman participant. And membership is less casual. “We have some entrance requirements now,” Griebel said. “We don’t want to invite people into the club that aren’t okay with the risk and that are also very solid, obviously, on the rock.”

What the club shows is a culture more wary than toxic. It vets its members, keeps careful books, and wants to stay on good terms with the land managers. It also shows a feedback loop; each record pulled in the next challenger. Reese told me every broken record “ingrains it more as something to go for.” He felt inspired when he learned of Griebel’s record. Camaraderie and friendly competition keep people incentivized and returning. But this wariness only goes so far; while the Satan’s Minions can vet their members, they can’t actually stop others from trying competitive free soloing, too.

Reese said he has now climbed the First Flatiron 800 times. It taught him that the risk “is never zero,” but he believes it to be smaller than most people imagine.

Even inside the scene, no one agrees on what speed does to the odds of surviving a free solo. Griebel says that when he’s pushing hard, heart pounding and moving upward, he’s “less likely to make a mistake.” Kate Kelleghan, who holds the women’s Naked Edge (5.11b; 460ft) record with Laura Pineau, says free soloing only makes up about one percent of her climbing. “This is super high risk and low reward,” she told me. “I’ve always felt way safer and stronger on a rope.” John Alcorn, who holds the Diamond speed record, free soloing Casual Route (5.10a; 900ft), says going fast piles more risk onto something already dangerous. “You get one shot,” he told me, “and if you blow it, you’re dead.”

In his trip report, Alcorn wrote, “I accept the position that climbing without a rope is a pretty dumb thing to do, and I believe that it shouldn’t be glorified, normalized, or encouraged in any way.” When a friend’s wife called it “incredibly stupid” over dinner, he agreed.

Alcorn said the FKTs are “extremely competitive. We’re essentially all competing with each other. But all these guys are my friends.” He admitted that if someone took his Diamond time by a minute or two, “Oh, I’d be pissed.” Then he caught himself: “That’s just pure ego … one of the worst reasons to climb without a rope.”

According to Accidents in North American Climbing, there have been six fatalities in the Flatirons since 2016. All of them involved free soloists, although none of them involved speed climbers. That number puts the danger in soloing, not the speed.

Low fifth-class terrain pulls in runners, a demographic far larger than climbing. “The accessible, low-angle slabs of the Flatirons frequently lure inexperienced or ill-prepared scramblers,” wrote the ANAC editors in 2017.

Reese has noticed more crossover of hybrid athletes; people coming from a very high level running background. Alcorn saw the same shift from the trail running side: As running records multiply, people are “diversifying what counts as a goal,” and he finds it hard to say where running and scrambling stop and climbing begins. Griebel says the overlap between strong runners and people comfortable soloing is thin, and that overlap is the only reason he has ever held a record.

This summer Reese found a 20-year-old about 100 feet up at dusk, shaking, with no headlamp, his feet slipping. Reese guided him down a gully. By the time they reached the ground, it was too dark to see his own outstretched hand.

I have felt that same dread myself. In the summer of 2025, I took out-of-town friends up on a free solo of the second Flatiron. Near the top, three college-aged men were climbing without a rope, one in climbing shoes and two in running shoes. The leader, about fifteen feet above me, was shaking badly. I waved my friends to the left, afraid that if he fell, we would be in his path.

But inexperienced climbers aren’t always the ones to watch. In 2020, a man fell to his death on Freeway, even after he reportedly had climbed it “hundreds of times.”

The scrambling club’s precautions don’t reach the people who get in trouble because those people aren’t in the club. And just because one is solid on rock doesn’t mean they’ll never fall. Its members can be practiced and clear-eyed about the risk, but the rock belongs to everyone. “They don’t do it because they see somebody going fast,” said Griebel, referring to inexperienced scramblers. “They just see somebody soloing.”

The stereotype is that this is a content game. Climbers like Lincoln Knowles, who posts his free solos to a large and young following, make the impression that free soloing is about social media fame and monetization.

The record-holders I talked to disagree. Reese began timing himself in 2020 without Strava, unaware the records existed. “If there was no social media, no recognition of any kind, would you still do it?” I asked Reese. The answer was an unequivocal yes. “I’m more interested in doing the actual thing than the broadcasting of what I’ve done,” Reese said.

Alcorn never posted his Diamond record, a choice he called intentional. “I just don’t even want ego in the loop,” he said. Griebel’s Instagram account is private except to close friends. Reese’s posts reads more like a logbook than a boast.

Still, the pull of recognition isn’t zero. Reese allows that recognition probably motivates him now that it exists, but he still climbs for himself and not a like button. Alcorn admits that without a culture of records he probably wouldn’t have tried the Diamond record. Kelleghan sits in the middle. She has a following and has been paid, including for a watch ad, but says she has never climbed something just to post it.

Whatever these climbers are after, audiences both on and offline take their own lessons from the best in the sport.

On the Flatirons, free soloing and speed have become synonymous; on the Naked Edge, a short drive south, they still sit apart, for now. Some Boulder climbers are free soloing the Naked Edge already, Kelleghan said, and she knows at least one who has soloed it quickly, though not for a record. This climber, who Kelleghan refuses to name, believes the speed record will eventually belong to a free soloist. Kelleghan disagrees. A free soloist can’t push as hard, she argued, because “if you’re simul climbing, if you fall, it would be unpleasant, but you wouldn’t die.”

The people I spoke with showed that records have a way of recruiting. If someone does set a free solo speed record on the Naked Edge, will it stay an outlier, or become the standard, the way that free solo ascents became the standard on the Flatirons? Kelleghan is betting against it.

So for most people who hold these records, it isn’t a content game. But a motive doesn’t have to be public or monetized to be contagious. Each time a record falls, it tells the next climber what is possible. The risk the last person accepted becomes the new baseline.

For all the attention these records draw, free soloing mostly regulates itself. Most people look at the First Flatiron and never think of climbing it, let alone without a rope. Alcorn points to an innate fear of falling “baked into us” and doesn’t expect the number of people doing this to explode just because a few records have been broken.

Some people chase records, but does that make this a toxic culture? From what I saw, it doesn’t. The record-holders I met were generous rivals, wary of their own egos, more interested in doing the thing than in being seen doing it. But “not toxic” isn’t the same as “not influential.” We are not solitary creatures, we have family and friends who love us, so a risk taken is never entirely one’s own.

Reese was as easy at the end of our conversation as at the start. By the end of our meal, I had decided we were friends, so as we said goodbye, an uneasy feeling settled in my stomach.

Walking to my car, I looked up at the Flatirons. A friend of mine, Bailee Mulholland, still holds the female trailhead-to-trailhead speed record on the First. She belonged to the same scrambling club Reese does now. In 2023, she died free soloing a 5.4 route on Ypsilon Mountain (13,520ft) a few hours north. I remembered Mulholland’s unwavering bubbly personality; she smiled easily and laughed easily, too.

I don’t think the scene she came from is toxic. But I know what losing her did to the people who loved her. The risk may belong to the one who takes it. The grief never does.

#8324. Where Did the Midweight Ski Touring Boot Go?

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The men's Tecnica Zero G Decoy Pro, staged and ready to go for a backcountry adventure in Cooke City, Montana. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: Midweight ski touring boots, historically three buckles and 1,300 to 1,500 grams, can handle the whole range of backcountry skis, yet the class has stagnated while lightweight and crossover boots got most of the industry’s R&D. Writer Bergen Tjossem, a former ski-shop employee, argues the next big touring breakthrough should come from the midweight category.

It’s 4 a.m. and the biting cold plunges into the open garage as I stuff my partner’s idling Forester with gear. But I stall, hovering over my collection of ski touring boots. Big boots or little boots? Neither seems right for the day. I throw my thrashed 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots over my shoulder, snap on my headlamp, and lug my skis to the car. I don’t know why I still hesitate at the start of every backcountry ski day—I end up picking the workhorse boot over the specialists most of the time.

Why, then, is the industry trying to squash this midweight ski touring boot class? Even the Maestrale RS, my beloved midweight archetype, is graduating toward the next class up this season, with a fourth buckle and more heft.

Owning a quiver of boots and skis is fun; it gives you options. But if you already own a pair of alpine boots like most skiers do, one dedicated touring boot could accomplish the vast majority of your needs. Yet where backcountry skis fall on a neat bell curve of dimension and weight, the boots we can buy to pilot them are bimodally distributed: ski shapes cluster in the middle, touring boots at the extremes. The evolution of midweight ski touring boots—the ones that best serve the majority of backcountry skiers—has stagnated compared to their cousins at the ends. It’s the “missing middle” problem every ski town knows from housing.

There’s no rule or buckle count dividing touring boot classes, but allow me to split them for the sake of the rant: lightweight boots typically have two buckles and top out around 1,200 grams, like the La Sportiva Kilo. Midweight boots historically use three buckles and weigh 1,300 to 1,500 grams. Then there are crossover boots that blend touring and alpine: four buckles, around 1,500 grams, typically with a GripWalk sole compatible with tech and alpine bindings, like the Dynafit Tigard.

Ski touring dogma says the optimum backcountry quiver is two pairs of ski touring boots and two pairs of skis: one lightweight and distance-oriented, the other beefy and fun. But here’s the catch—lightweight boots struggle with big skis, especially in poor snow, because they lack progressive flex and damping. And the opposite is also true. Crossover boots are a real drag on lightweight skis. Aside from the cumbersome ROM, the added stiffness, high cuff, and heft quickly overpower lightweight skis. Yet midweights can handle the whole ski spectrum.

When I worked in ski shops in the early 2010s as ski touring took off, midweight boots were the benchmark. Dynafit’s Vulcan and the Scarpa Maestrale were the choice for skiers who wanted to climb efficiently without giving up too much on the descent. What followed that workhorse boot era was an explosion of lightweight options, as almost every company in the business invested in svelter chassis while skis got lighter and less demanding. The rise of resort uphilling and Skimo racing only fueled the growth. Lately, lightweight boots such as La Sportiva’s Kilo XTR have been beefed up to claim more of that middle segment without overtaking it completely. But lightweight two-buckle designs with sturdier components still come up short on the leverage and suspension big skis demand.

Crossovers got the next round of R&D in the name of capturing the massive resort-hybrid buyer. Scarpa’s 1,500 gram 4-Quattro XT with a legit 61 degree range of motion (ROM) revolutionized the segment in 2022. All of a sudden, boots with alpine-like skiing capability unlocked a bigger ROM, while better materials and design brought weights down to 1,500 grams per boot or less. It also introduced freaky new levels of “quiver overlap” for skiers who already own alpine boots with a walk mode.

Smooshed between the crossover and the lightweight segments is that increasingly scant boot group, the midweights. It’s not that these midweight boots don’t exist—the Scott Cosmos Pro and Fischer Transalp prove they do—but rather that they’ve gotten the shaft on R&D over the last decade. Most of the remaining midweights are just stale, longing for a refresh, a trickle-down of new tech, and a burst of innovation.

A radical solution would be to have fewer skis, and I can’t believe you’d even suggest that. I’ve got a better idea: Give me one boot that can cover the entire ski quiver: three buckles, a camming power strap, over 65 degrees of ROM, under 1,400 grams, and minimal fiddle factor. Oops, I just mostly described the Scarpa Maestrale that’s been around for sixteen years. That’s because the industry is barely competing to refine that basic formula into its state-of-the-art form.

As a skier of many setups, I can say there’s a mismatch between the boots I want and those available. Lightweights and crossovers have had their run. My hunch is that the next big touring breakthrough will be, and should be, in the missing middle. Until then, you’ll catch me clinging to my 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots like the gear troll I am.

#8322. For Rifle-Season Elk, “Bad” Weather Is the Best

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’re day dreaming about an upcoming elk hunt during rifle season, it probably looks something like this: A wall tent set in a small clearing surrounded by aspens trying to hold onto their last bits of gold. You and your buds inside, huddled around the stove, bs-ing and making plans for the morning’s hunt. And, as long as you’re conjuring up the ideal scene, you should also picture a fresh blanket of snow dusting the meadow grasses and blanketing the slopes around you.

Weather is everything when it comes to rifle-season elk hunting, and nothing promises to put bulls on their feet like a forecast that begins with a snowflake icon. So pray for the white stuff and follow this advice.

From August through May, snow can hit the high country at any time. During October and November, waking up to white on an elk hunt is almost a guarantee, and whether Mother Nature gives you a half inch or 6 inches, consider it a gift. Weather fronts move elk, and when the storm stops, you need to be out covering ground or posted up on an elevated ridge and glassing with quality optics.

Elk, especially those traveling in a herd, typically to drop in elevation if new snow measures several inches or more. They are simply moving to where food is more accessible. Older cows know where these locations are and will rally the herd—usually consisting of cows, calves, and smaller bulls—to beeline to the new spot. Unless the snow is measured in feet and not inches, larger bulls may not make such drastic movements. Still, these elk need to eat and will shift to south-facing slopes where forage is available and is easier to get at.

New snow in the high country gives you four big advantages as an elk hunter. Here’s what they are, how they help you, and what you should do to take make the most of each.

A 600-plus-pound animal with a tan hide and dark mane really stands out against a white backdrop. When the snow hits, my elk hunting companions and I will typically climb just a little above where we think the elk are and spend hours moving from vantage point to vantage point, picking the country apart with optics. The key is positioning yourself in locations where you can see lots of ground. Don’t move from an area too quickly. Be sure and pick timber pockets apart, as these are great locations to find and put a bull or three to bed.

If you’re out burning boot leather when the snow stops and come across a set of lone bull prints or lots of tracks left by a herd, you know those tracks are smoking fresh. Don’t start following them aimlessly, though. Pull out your digital mapping app and look at the terrain. Is there an open meadow or sage flat ahead where the herd can paw down to some good forage? What about a semi-open south-facing mountainside where the sun is warming the ground? Put some thought into what the elk might do, and then make a plan of attack. When following tracks, don’t get mesmerized by them. Keep your eyes up—continually look up and ahead for a flash of tan. Each time the landscape changes, whether you topped a ridge or popped out of some tight timber, stop and glass ahead.

Nothing makes for an ultra-stealthy stalk like fresh snow. If possible, try to spot elk from above and stalk downhill to them them. Carry a bottle of wind checker and puff it often to stay in tune with fickle mountain breezes. If you’re rifle hunting with a partner or two, take the time to develop a smart game plan where if one hunter bumps elk, the others are in position to take a safe shot, or are at least in place to glass and mark animals when they more.

One big thing to remember when stalking in the snow is that you become much more visible to elk. Blaze orange is a requirement in most elk-rich states during rifle season, and that blaze orange can look like the lights of the Vegas Strip when its set against a white background. If you spot elk but the cover is too sparse for stalking or you feel the stalk is a low percentage one, simply wait those elk out instead. Set up in a good ambush spot down or crosswind of the elk, and be ready to capitalize when they get up to fill their bellies.

Another solid bonus to snow is that blood and tracks will be easy to follow if you need to trail a hit animal. This means that even with a marginal hit, you are much more likely to get a lethal follow-up shot or recover your bull at the end of what would otherwise have been a difficult, if not futile, trail job. Remember, this is your dream hunt, and the perfect elk foray ends with you sitting behind your trophy.

Jace Bauserman is a full-time freelance outdoor writer who has been working with Field & Stream since 2017. Before going full-time freelance, Bauserman was the editor-in-chief of Bowhunting World and Archery Business magazines.  Highlights Education Bauserman earned his Bachelor of Arts degree with an emphasis in interdisciplinary studies from Adams State University. Bauserman has also completed several journalism and creative writing courses. Experience While Bauserman loves to chase all game species, his passion is western big-game hunting. Each fall, he hunts pronghorn, mule deer, elk, and other western species with archery tackle. In addition to being an accomplished big-game bowhunter, Bauserman is also a gear nut and does tons of product testing each year. He is a master of his craft and has developed a strong following by those who crave the latest bow-and-arrow gear know-how. Before going full-time as an outdoor writer, Bauserman was the editor-in-chief of Bowhunting World and Archery Business. Bauserman has penned many award-winning articles about bowhunting and in-the-field gear testing during his time in this position. Bauserman also has a passion for chasing whitetail deer and waterfowl, and writes numerous articles each year for F&S on these two topics. #8321. Des Linden’s Simple (and Somewhat Shocking) 100-Mile Fueling Plan

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Boston Marathon champion Des Linden will toe the line at her first 100-miler on October 31, 2026, at the Javelina Jundred near Fountain Hills, Arizona. To prepare for the distance and hot desert conditions, she worked with a team of sports scientists, including Olympic-marathoner-turned-ultrarunner-champion Magda Boulet, to dial in her metabolic needs and a fueling plan. She will primarily rely on liquid calories, with the addition of some more out-of-the-box products like “cooling” menthol gels, while understanding that mid-race adjustments will be key.

For Boston Marathon champion-turned-competitive ultrarunner Des Linden, one question keeps driving her forward: “Can I do this?”

After years of racing some of the world’s most prestigious road marathons, the two-time Olympian is shifting her focus to off-road competitions. On October 31, she’ll attempt her most ambitious athletic endeavor yet when she toes the start line of the Javelina Jundred, a 100-mile trail race through Arizona’s Sonoran Desert that also serves as a Golden Ticket race into the 2027 Western States 100.

“I feel like part of me is just missing being afraid of something; the unknown,” Linden tells Trail Runner. “What is this going to pull out of me? What is this going to ask of me? That’s all really fascinating.”

In addition to the distance—nearly 40 miles more than Linden has ever covered in one go–Javelina presents a slew of unfamiliar challenges. One of the biggest is fueling and hydration over the course of 13-plus hours in desert conditions. Linden got a small taste, literally, at the Black Canyon 50K in February. It was her first ultramarathon and she acknowledged after the race that all of those years of fueling on the roads was only so helpful.

“I went into Black Canyon 50k with a loose fueling plan—to have a Gu at each aid station and sip on an electrolyte beverage between stations,” Linden said. “I wasn’t diligent about it during the race and certainly didn’t account for the time required for trail miles versus road miles. After the race, I realized it was a very easy place to make improvements, and getting it dialed before MDS would be important.”

It’s a relatable learning curve that Linden has taken seriously in the eight months since. Together with a team of sports scientists, including Olympic-marathoner-turned ultrarunning-champion Magda Boulet, Linden has tested her metabolic needs under hot ultramarathon conditions to develop a (somewhat surprising) fueling plan for October 31.

Linden retired from professional road running in 2025 after an illustrious career that included two Olympic Games, two runner-up finishes at both the Chicago and Boston Marathons, and an iconic win at the 2018 Boston Marathon—becoming the first American woman to do so in 33 years. Rather than hanging up her running shoes, Linden is targeting some of the world’s most prestigious trail races.

“I think a lot of this part of my career is getting away from comparing myself to my former self. So this is uncharted territory for me,” Linden says.

This past April, Linden, 43, competed in only her second ultra-trail event, finishing third at Marathon des Sables (MDS), a six-day stage race in the southern Moroccan Sahara often referred to as the “Toughest Footrace on Earth.” While Linden has spent her career refining how she fuels for peak performance and recovery, her MDS experience reinforced just how critical nutrition is to sustaining her endurance and rebounding after hours on her feet. She adds that ultrarunning has pushed her to reevaluate her approach to nutrition as she continues to take on longer and more demanding challenges.

“The distance itself makes nutrition so much more important,” Linden says. “You can’t cover that distance if you’re skimping or shortcutting getting the calories in throughout the day.”

The Javelina Jundred is an open and exposed course. The race is defined by heat: the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit and the average low is roughly 58 degrees. Managing more time on her feet also creates more opportunities for things to go awry. Research has long suggested that heat stress can reduce appetite: A 2018 study in Nature found that exercise suppresses appetite by heating up a region of the brain responsible for regulating eating. Of course, this appetite suppression is counterproductive since you are expending lots of extra energy while running, and create a negative feedback loop that self-perpetuates.

Along with dehydration, racing in the heat creates a unique set of challenges. Linden has been working hard to prepare for them.

To prepare for the challenge, Linden enlisted experts from Gu Energy Labs, based in Berkeley, California, including Roxanne Vogel, Ph.D., nutrition scientist, exercise physiologist, and director of research and education, and Magda Boulet, Gu Energy Labs president and one of the world’s most accomplished ultrarunners. Boulet’s own evolution from Olympic marathoner to Western States 100, Leadville 100, and Marathon des Sables champion has made her a valuable resource for Linden’s own ultramarathon journey.

“I imagine most ultrarunners will look and be like ‘you’re not ready at all.’ But they don’t necessarily know that behind the scenes I have the ultrarunner,” Linden says.

Ahead of MDS this spring, Linden underwent laboratory testing at Gu’s Performance Lab with the goal of understanding her energy expenditure, hydration needs, and fueling tolerance during ultramarathon efforts. As part of the assessment, Vogel set out to measure Linden’s sweat rate and sodium losses under heat stress, her caloric demands at race pace, and how her body uses carbohydrate versus fat in simulated desert conditions.

The data helped Vogel develop an individualized metabolic and hydration profile for Linden. Vogel discovered that Linden isn’t a very salty sweater, and she also learned that Linden needs approximately 10 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight per day. (For a 120-pound person, that’s roughly 550 grams of carbs.)

Going into MDS, the team developed a precise nutrition strategy for Linden, which included Gu Roctane Drink Mix along with gels and chews for her on-course fueling. After each stage, Linden leaned on nut butter and Roctane Protein Recovery Drink Mix to supply the necessary carbohydrates, electrolytes, and 20 grams of whey protein. Her dinner included a savory dehydrated potato mash with added protein and sodium. Linden also integrated Gu Roctane BCAA capsules before and after the stages to support muscle repair and reduce soreness.

Vogel says those core principles will be part of Linden’s approach at Javelina, but the demands of a single day 100-mile race in the Arizona desert will require some adjustments. For Javelina, liquid calories will be the backbone of her nutrition strategy. The target is to consume approximately 16 ounces (500 milliliters) of Roctane Drink Mix per hour. Per 16-ounce serving, it offers 250 calories, 60 grams of carbs, and 320 milligrams of sodium. Linden also plans to integrate some products that remain under development, Vogel says, including Roctane MC-318, a patented menthol-based energy gel designed to help athletes feel perceptually cooler. The product is not yet commercially available, but has already been tested by athletes at races such as Badwater 135, Western States 100, and Marathon des Sables.

The Javelina course consists of five loops along rolling desert singletrack. It’s a format that allows for both Linden and her crew to accurately anticipate her arrival at aid stations, where she’ll be able to replenish supplies and, crucially, will allow for crew to frequently assess how she’s managing the nutrition and hydration plan.

The terrain will help determine when Linden takes in different forms of fuel. Uphill sections, when she’s moving more slowly, provide an opportunity to take gels or chews. On downhills, when she wants to let her legs unwind and rip down as fast as possible, she’ll focus more on liquids. Her approach also reflects a shift from road marathon racing, where fueling opportunities are often more structured and brief.

“In the marathon, [every] 5K you grab the bottle, you want eight to 10 ounces and you want to get rid of the bottle as quickly as possible. We have the luxury of carrying it and sipping on it, and also strategizing,” Linden says.

Temperature will be one of the most significant variables. Research has found that during prolonged exercise in the heat, gastrointestinal symptoms are greater.

“People think it has to be really hot for them to need to make changes to their nutrition or their electrolyte plan,” Vogel says. “The cutoff is somewhere around 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Above that, you’re certainly going to be at an increased level of needs in terms of your hydration and electrolytes, plus also potentially your carbohydrate needs. Even in somewhat moderately warm temperatures, athletes can be needing more than what they would normally take in.”

As the temperature rises throughout the day over the course of the race, Linden anticipates leaning more heavily on liquids. The drink mix can provide fluid and carbohydrates while helping her meet her electrolyte needs, and gels with water will fill any gaps.

“She’s never done a [single day] race this long. The longer you’re out there, the more likely your gut is going to have some issues,” Vogel says. “When you’re exercising, blood flow is going to your working muscles. Less of it is going to your digestive track. So that’s one thing that’s putting stress on the system that makes it harder to digest and absorb [nutrition]. Hence the whole reason for things like gels. They’re easy to digest.”

During the hottest part of the day, Vogel says the team may decrease Linden’s carbohydrate intake to account for changes in digestive tolerance. But as temperatures fall into the night, they’ll look to increase her carbs. Vogel says caffeine will require similar consideration.

“During very hot weather events, caffeine can actually be triggering to the gut in a bad way,” Vogel says. “Rather than following a fixed schedule regardless of conditions, we might actually pull back on caffeine during the heat of the day and start to strategically add it back in as it cools off later in the day.”

Another factor to consider: flavor fatigue, when sensory receptors on your tongue that detect flavor become less responsive with repeated consumption.

“Flavor fatigue is something we know and understand. In hot environments, you don’t generally want to have things that are what we call indulgent—chocolates and caramels and vanillas that are going to stay heavy on the palate. We want more things like citrus and light fruity or even sour, tart flavors that are going to clear the palate or stimulate some thirst,” Vogel says.

Ultimately, the goal is to make the strategy simple to execute, Vogel says. Linden’s success will depend not only on having a precise nutrition plan, but on adjusting on the fly when fatigue and discomfort begin to accumulate.

“I feel like it’s a race within itself. Did I try to execute as well as possible? Did I follow the plan? Did I make good decisions?” Linden says. “I want to finish, and I think there’s so many things that can go in so many different directions in that amount of time and that distance. So if I fueled enough to get myself through 100 miles, that’s a victory.”

#8320. Christopher Wren, Climber and Legendary Reporter, Had a “Wry Sense of Humor”

Christopher Wren at basecamp during the 1974 Pamir Expedition. In this photo, he is using a typewriter to draft the New York Times story that revealed the deaths of American climber Gary Ullin and eight Soviet female climbers. (Photo: Courtesy of Jed Williamson)

Christopher Sale Wren served as The New York Times bureau chief in Moscow, Cairo, Beijing, Ottawa, and Johannesburg. His creative life was deeply intertwined with a respect for nature, big expeditions and the many people he met on assignment. He passed at his home in Vermont on February 15, 2026, at age 89.

Wren began climbing as a student at Dartmouth, where he sometimes felt out of place, according to his daughter, Celia. A scholarship student whose parents were actors, he had little interest in fraternity life. In the outdoors, he found a bigger sense of kinship. He learned to climb with the college’s mountaineering club, practicing on campus at Bartlett Tower and on the nearby cliffs of Orford and Owl’s Head. According to Samuel C. Silverstein’s memorial in The American Alpine Journal, he once ended a public-speaking assignment on mountaineering by rappelling out of the classroom’s third-floor window.

In 1962, Wren joined the six-man team that made the first ascent of Denali’s Southeast Spur (Alaska grade 4, 65-degree ice). The expedition became the subject of his first major article for Look magazine, merging his climbing with his reporting into a career he chased around the world.

Twelve years later, while stationed in Moscow for the Times, he joined an American expedition to the Pamirs. On Lenin Peak (23,406ft), Wren and fellow climbers Jock Glidden and Allen Steck encountered members of a Soviet women’s team who had died in a storm. His reporting brought their tragedy to the Times front page, breaking the news of deaths Soviet authorities had kept secret.

For Jed Williamson, who was also on the Pamirs expedition, Wren’s contribution to mountaineering extended to his ability to tell its stories. “What he really brought to the mountaineering scene was his ability to write about it and put it out there,” Williamson said. “He had a really good sense of humor. He could turn a situation that one might not think was so humorous into one that was humorous.”

Even when faced with tragedy, Wren found a way to bring levity to dangerous moments. Celia remembered one story her father told about provisioning the Pamirs expedition. The American climbers wanted peanut butter, which he couldn’t find in Soviet shops. Instead, he packed tins of caviar for protein. “His teammates thought it was disgusting,” she remembers. “But he was a Renaissance man with an incredible sense of humor.”

Wren played guitar and banjo and wrote songs, two of which Johnny Cash recorded: Jesus Was a Carpenter and Gospel Road. “It was a fun thing that he did, and he was good at it,” Williamson said. “But he was never a chest pounder about that kind of thing.”

At home, Wren’s appetite for being outside became part of family life. During the family’s years in the Soviet Union, Celia remembered her father heading out on skis, pulling her and her brother behind him on a sled. He penned numerous books, from a biography of Johnny Cash to Walking to Vermont, an account of his roughly 400-mile walk home from Manhattan after retiring from The New York Times.

Williamson remembers that despite the breadth of his traveling and range of his accomplishments, Wren was down-to-earth.  “He wasn’t aloof or standoffish or anything like that,” he said. “He was happy to share.”

Late into retirement, he continued to ski and ride his mountain bike around the nearby lake. Celia remembered his ability to keep moving ahead. When recalling difficult experiences, he would often say, “Well, you know, that’s all behind us now.”

#8319. There Are Over 40 Resorts Planning To Open In November—Here’s Where Experts Say Conditions Will Be Best

Mammoth Mountain opening day 2025 (Photo: Courtesy of Mammoth Mountain)

Some folks may think skiing in November is crazy: the snow is rarely good, and the mere thrill of lifts spinning often attracts crowds larger than downhill capacity should allow.

It can be difficult to know where, if anywhere, it is worth skiing in November. While resorts are making snow around the clock, the decision to open boils down to weather.

For Colorado skiers, the weather may finally be on your side. According to Open Snow meteorologist Joel Gratz, November is set to start with a “bang.” He predicts a storm arriving Sunday will drop 6 to 12 inches on nearly all mountains, with some spots seeing up to 20. Did someone say powder day?!

Several Colorado resorts are opening their lifts before Halloween is over. Arapahoe Basin opened Oct. 28, Keystone follows on Oct. 30, and Wolf Creek on Oct. 31. Snow is thin at all three for now, but their high elevations should set them up for a stronger start to November.

Breckenridge and Copper Mountain are planning to open on Nov. 6, and if the snow comes in like Gratz is predicting, their opening days could feature more than just a white ribbon of death.

A little later into the month, Vail and Eldora are both planning Nov. 13 opening dates. It’s too early to tell if temperatures will preserve the snow from earlier storms, but as long as cold air remains, these are resorts to keep on your radar for potentially decent skiing.

Neighboring Utah resorts aren’t expected to receive as fruitful a snow bounty. They’ll see the same storm as Colorado, with the highest accumulations on Sunday, says Open Snow forecaster Evan Thayer. “Cooler air will eventually lower snow levels, with some decent accumulations possible up high.”

As of the time of publishing, Brian Head is planning on opening on Nov. 6. If Thayer’s prediction is accurate, the Southern Utah resort could see “decent accumulations” on its highest peaks. Alta, Park City, and Solitude are all planning on opening on Nov. 20. It’s too early to say how these resorts will fare, but cold temperatures will be the biggest asset.

California skiers will have to wait a bit longer. Open Snow forecaster Bryan Alleretto predicts the Tahoe region’s snowy start will likely come after Nov. 10, which could be good timing for Mammoth Mountain, set to open Nov. 20. Mammoth isn’t a Tahoe resort, but it tends to share weather patterns with those to the north.

The East Coast has had a warm fall, but that could change. There’s no official snow report yet, but Maine’s Sugarloaf plans to reopen Nov. 20, likely making it the region’s first resort to welcome skiers back. Vermont’s Sugarbush follows on Nov. 21, while nearby Killington, which often opens early, hasn’t announced a date as of press time.

#8317. I Hike With a Flip Phone. Here’s the Tiny Camera I’m Bringing Along.

Over the past few years, I’ve learned I’m much happier when I don’t have my smartphone on me—I’m not sure the human mind evolved to have 24-hour access to all of the Internet’s information on demand. In an effort to disconnect and be more present, I took a page from the Gen Z playbook and started carrying a flip phone instead. It’s been great—except for the camera.

A while ago, I started testing a potential solution in the Life Camera S168, a thumb-size digital camera built to compete with the Kodak Charmera. How did it actually perform on the trail? Check out this video to see what kind of photos and footage this $30 gadget is capable of turning out and read our full review for more.

A while ago, I swapped out my smartphone for a flip phone. I was getting tired of how distracted I was—doomscrolling, checking my emails—and I wanted to simplify things. This has really done the trick. On the trail it’s pretty much everything I need. It can send messages, make calls, if I need to get a hold of 911 in an emergency, it can do that. It has an MP3 player, so I can listen to podcasts at night, and it even has a rudimentary mapping app, although I’m not sure I’d trust it, I always bring a paper map and compass as backup.

However, it does have one big shortcoming: the camera on this thing really sucks. The pictures are grainy, blurry, and usually blown out. It’s not how I want to remember my trips. I often find myself hiking with my smartphone just so I can get better pictures and video. I’ve been looking for a solution, since that kind of defeats the purpose of ditching the smartphone, and I think I’ve found one.

This is the Life Camera S168. It’s part of a crop of new thumb-sized digital cameras that are designed to appeal to the retro crowd, they’re kind of like old digital cameras or old film cameras, you know, the disposable you used to take to summer camp with you. The most familiar one is the Kodak Charmera, you may have seen that in stores.

However, according to a lot of online reviews, the Life Camera’s photos and video quality is significantly better, and it has, from what I’ve seen, a fairly decent camera, you’re not going to confuse it with an iPhone or anything, but it may be enough for my purposes.

So, is the Life Camera a gimmick or a game changer? Well, that depends on you. If you’re like most hikers and you have your phone in your pocket most of the time, it’s definitely a gimmick. Your phone can do anything the Life Camera can do, and probably in better resolution.

If, however, you’re part of the small subset of hikers like me, who find they’re happier when their phone is off and in their pack, or if they’re just carrying a flip phone, you might give the Life Camera a try. No, the resolution isn’t anything to write home about, but it can capture your life on the trail in adequate detail, and if you don’t mind that retro vibe, it’s kind of fun. I’ll be carrying one on my next hike.

#8316. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

Bert Verbist on his way back to the camp after yet another successful loop.

Common duties by different hands. Although the race is repetitive, the things that need to be done are endless and carried out by volunteers throughout all the hours of the day and night.

The remains of a celebration for Merijn Geerts, who turned 52 during the race.

Evariest Callens gets a massage on his throbbing legs after 69 hours of running.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

In running and in life: Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts celebrate with their wives as well as crews after setting the world record.
