#8315. We Need to Move Past the “Shut Up And Die Like a Man” Mentality in the Mountains

Will Gadd (left) and his friend, the late Ken Wallator. (Photo: Will Gadd)

“Shut up and die like a man!” sounds like a line from a bad action movie, but we all heard it on the radio from the paragliding competition director. The director was yelling at a terrified pilot who thought he was falling to his death. The pilot had accidentally keyed open his radio’s shoulder mic, allowing his frantic screams to be broadcast across the competition frequency.

The unfortunate pilot begging to god to not die had collapsed his wing and plummeted in front of my eyes. Twenty-one years later, the memory of this sight and soundtrack is unforgettable, and so was the director’s barking, because there was clearly no sympathy for what the pilot thought was his final, horrific ride. Miraculously, the pilot recovered his wing and flew out to land and reflect on his life choices alone.

Most pilots didn’t think the competition director’s statement was out of line for the time. Many still don’t. I see terrible parallels between flying culture and some facets of climbing’s; in alpinism especially, some see death as an attractant, or an inevitability. Over my 40 years as an alpinist and 35 as a pilot, I’ve watched climbers experience gut-wrenching trauma—then do their best to ignore it, too scared or proud to deal with the ugly, messy truth. This avoidance sends a message to younger climbers, much like the competition director’s statement so long ago: Suck it up, move on, and die with honor if things go bad.

But living with trauma doesn’t have to be that way.

When my late friend Ken Wallator was 21, he climbed Mount Belanger in the Canadian Rockies with his girlfriend Heidi. They reached the top of the difficulties, unroped, and walked along a low-angle snow ridge to the summit of the peak. But the snow ridge was actually a massive, overhanging cornice of windblown snow, and it collapsed as they stopped to take a photo. Ken somehow managed to leap to safety but Heidi fell hundreds of meters down the face.

Ken, a brave bear of a man, downclimbed the face, found Heidi somehow still alive, and started carrying her out to a distant hut. She died before they reached it.

In the aftermath of Heidi’s death, I watched Ken receive a surprising amount of blame from grieving members of the climbing community. Didn’t he know better than to walk on a cornice? Why weren’t they roped up? Ken was already wracked with guilt from the accident. When his community piled on, their condemnation lit an internal firestorm.

Thirty years later, in 2019, Ken helped me re-roof my house. He still had the strength of a bear and I watched him haul 100-pound loads of shingles up my rickety ladder. In a rare moment of emotionality, he told me how he still hadn’t gotten over Heidi’s death, or the climbing community’s blame. We talked more about trauma, and I realized only then how that day on Mount Belanger broke my friend in a way that never healed.

As two young, hungry alpinists, Ken and I didn’t know what mental “help” looked like 30 years ago, and Ken was too much a product of his culture to take it 30 years later. Despite his immense physical and mental strength, Ken died by suicide a few weeks after our talk.

More recently, Will Stanhope’s death has brought to mind this idea of “asking for help” once more. For years Stanhope had battled desperately with alcohol. He was facing various charges at the time of his death—including assault and sexual assault—while still succeeding on difficult routes as a professional climber and mountain guide.

In our last real conversation, Stanhope talked about needing to “harden up and stop letting the carnage get to me” one minute, then sobbed about the “death camp” of hard alpine climbing the next. Like Ken and me, he had lost many friends in the mountains.

“You and I [watched] our mentors and friends die, one after another, as if everyone around us was climbing their way to oblivion,” his friend Kieran Brownie wrote in an obituary. “We couldn’t return to the mountains, we couldn’t return to each other.”

Stanhope carried a heavy weight in the final months of his life, made even heavier by grief, guilt, and irreversible mistakes. After a lifetime of hard solos and even scarier roped climbs, it seemed impossible that Stanhope would ever fall off an easy 5.11. But when he did just that last April and succumbed to a head injury, to me and other friends, Stanhope’s death felt more related to the weight he carried in his head than the climb itself. His family and friends made truly profound and sometimes wrenchingly difficult efforts to help him, but, like falling, the weights of addiction and trauma develop their own momentum.

Hard drinking, hard living, and celebrating dangerous acts—usually lauded as “bold”—are hallmarks of every mountain sport I’ve ever done, from kayaking to flying to skiing to climbing. Our literature is full of stories celebrating those who climbed hard, drank hard, and died silently.

I can’t help but wonder if our literature strives to make these deaths seem somehow valiant and necessary, like dying in the mountains is a noble sacrifice rather than the tragedy it really is. The classic mountaineering texts rarely explore the trauma that comes after seeing a friend die. They barrel ever onward to the summit.

Military veterans and first responders have a trauma-treatment framework that climbers should strive to adopt. Soldiers are not considered “weak” if they are affected by bloody combat. Paramedics are not ridiculed for taking leave after responding to a grisly car wreck. These are normal human responses, and professional groups typically have protocols for helping those involved in traumatic situations. These groups have no other choice; a traumatized team simply cannot function.

Those professional protocols weren’t there for Ken, Will, that terrified pilot, or many others, including me.

When I was 19 I tried with every tool I knew to save a fellow kayaker stuck just inches from the surface in his boat. I couldn’t reach him, and he drowned in front of me as I tried to remember how to rig a better haul system. I had nightmares for years of the paddler chasing me in the dark beside that river.

Only decades later did I seek help, after a divorce and a lot of behavior I understood even less than that terrible accident. I’m lucky I survived and sought belated help. Ken and Will and many others didn’t. Many more in our community—your friends and mine—are barely standing today, carrying crippling loads. They need help putting those loads down.

The pain of trauma does not disappear with six or 600 beers. Doing dangerous climbs or flights or other high-stimulus experiences temporarily distracts from the weight, but doesn’t solve it. There is no pack heavier than one filled with trauma you can’t put down.

One of the smartest things I’ve ever heard about trauma came after we failed to resuscitate a dying man at the base of an ice climb a few years ago. A professional responder on the scene could tell I was shaken, and looked me in the eye and said, “Post traumatic stress is normal; post traumatic stress disorder is optional—if you get help. Get help.”

I see real change today, from my wife Sarah Hueniken’s Mountain Muskox foundation to the American Alpine Club’s Grief Fund, two organizations built to support mountain-trauma survivors.

But I also still see a lot of the “Shut up and die like a man” attitude, and the celebration of “bold” yet physically unimpressive climbs that are often little more than Russian Roulette. Huge, low-angle alpine routes with immense serac and avalanche hazard are not that cool, in my book. And I see many climbers who still romanticize the wrong parts of climbing, whether that’s meaningless objective hazard or the very idea of “suffering silently.”

We need to recognize that a mountain death doesn’t end with the funeral; often that’s just the start of a very long and difficult process for everyone involved. In climbing more people die on the descent after the summit than on the climb itself.

At times I’ve felt deeply angry about our outdoor tribe’s celebration of “bold” hazards, and our denial of the after-effects of engaging in high-risk sports where participants die regularly. We often celebrate the bold free solos or dangerous alpine routes where everything clicked into place. We never celebrate the dead parent who doesn’t show up for their kids’ birthdays.

But the truth is that I laughed when the paragliding competition director said his infamous line. I promised myself that if I was in that situation in the future, I’d shut up. That became my normal. Today, I hope I’d speak up on the comment, and reach out to the guy who almost died that day. Because I’ve been him, and it sucks, and I’m trying to do better.

I’m less angry today when I think about Ken, Will, or others who have left the game, and just hope that our culture continues to evolve in the same way the first responders did, and that we ultimately celebrate survival more than dying silently. We can do better, if we want to.

Finally, if, like me, you’ve been through the trauma wringer, it often takes help to sort it out. We’re not tougher than the veterans or first responders even if our culture says we “should” be—we’re just less educated about intense trauma.

The goal is to return to full function and fly in life, not get stuck in the inevitable mental dust devils of mountain death. Peace to those hurting, it can get better with help. Substances and more dangerous living may distract us short term, but long term the combo is deadly despite the romantic words we historically place on both. I write these words for the future Wills and Kens, they are me, you, our friends.

Shutting up is not a solution, because silence is death.

#8314. Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination

Owl's Head Ski Resort at sunset. (Photo: Cantons-de-l'Est © Cantons-de-l'Est/BBT Productions)

Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border.

Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.)

Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it

Looking for spectacular scenery? Unbelievably long runs? Buttery maritime snowpack coming in off the St. Lawrence River? Northeast of Québec City, you’ll find all three in Charlevoix, where the steep slopes of Le Massif de Charlevoix hover over the water, serving up mountain-meets-river views that are totally unique, and plunging valleys and sweeping bowls attract skiers looking to test their skills amid the serene quiet of a Québécois winter. Le Massif serves up the biggest vertical drop east of the Canadian Rockies, while Mont Grand-Fonds offers a compact layout, laid-back atmosphere, and terrain for all ability levels.

Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time.

Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing.

The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow.

Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character.

Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards.

Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home.

Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure.

Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here.

Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.

#8313. I Escaped Zion’s Crushing Crowds at Red Cliffs, a Desert Dupe Just 45 Minutes Away

I just wanted one picture of my son without a sea of people in the background. We were hiking The Narrows in Zion National Park, a bucket-list adventure that has you wading for miles through knee-deep water in the belly of a canyon. It’s awesome. It’s also crowded. And getting a photo to commemorate the adventure without a bunch of strangers in it was proving to be difficult.

Crowds are simply a fact of life when it comes to visiting Zion, which has skyrocketed in popularity over the last 20 years, doubling its visitation rates from 2.5 million in 2005 to almost five million in 2025. That’s a lot of people to squeeze into Zion’s 146,597 acres, so you’re going to have company on your hike.

Fortunately, there’s an alternative nearby. Red Cliffs National Conservation Area is less than an hour west of Zion National Park with a desert landscape that’s just as stunning but only attracts a fraction of the crowds.

Red Cliffs National Conservation Area is about 45,000 acres, which is less than a third of the size of Zion. But the smaller size is a bonus here. Since you won’t have to navigate mandatory shuttles or shift your plans to avoid crowds, the compact size of the park allows you to knock out a variety of adventures in a short amount of time. And there is an amazing variety of adventures inside Red Cliffs, which is packed with sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and miles of slickrock, all of which are traversed by more than 100 miles of developed trails. The area is managed by the Bureau of Land Management, so don’t expect visitor centers or rangers on hand. This is a raw desert landscape that’s set aside for you to explore on your own.

Once you get inside the conservation area, keep your eyes out for some unique wildlife, most notably Gila monsters and a rare species of desert tortoise. I spent two days exploring Red Cliffs with my son during a recent trip to southern Utah, and it made me want to go back for more.

Here’s a first-timer’s guide to exploring Red Cliffs National Conservation Area.

If you’re only going to do one trail in Red Cliffs, this is it. And I’m using the word “trail” loosely here. Sometimes called the Red Cliffs Nature Trail, Red Reef does in fact start out as a mild walk through a picnic area, but quickly gets interesting as it delivers you into the heart of a slot canyon. The three-mile out-and-back is more of a choose-your-own-adventure as you move across the sandy desert floor into a slickrock canyon that gets increasingly narrow as you move deeper into its belly. There’s some light scrambling involved, with one fixed rope that you’ll need to use to get around a small waterfall. And be prepared to get wet; there are a few pockets of deep water in the narrowest channels that were up to my chest. You can turn around if it gets too deep, though.

The rock outcroppings just outside of the canyon are also fun to scramble and explore after you’ve navigated to the end of the canyon. It’s an ideal slot canyon experience for first-time canyoners, and you’ll probably have it all to yourself once you climb past that first waterfall.

Moab is known as ground zero for slickrock, but the town doesn’t hold a monopoly on the grippy rock surface. This 7.5-mile loop is mostly slickrock with the occasional singletrack connector. The loop has steep climbs, the occasional sandy wash, and plenty of long-range views of the surrounding sandstone cliffs. Keep an eye out for prehistoric dinosaur tracks—along Dino Cliffs Trail you’ll find 17 well-preserved tracks left by meat-eating theropods during the Jurassic period.

Snow Canyon State Park is its own pocket destination with 7,400 acres of cliffs, petrified dunes and black lava rock, located within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve. The majority of the trails are short, making the park the perfect one-day adventure. You’re going to want to hit the Petrified Sand Dunes Trail, which traverses rolling humps of hardened sandstone. It’s a 1.2-mile out-and-back, but you can spend some time exploring this wild beach of petrified sand.

Just be sure you leave yourself enough time to explore the Lava Flow Trail, a one-mile out-and-back that traverses a black lava flow that cuts through the center of the park. You’ll get views of the surrounding tan cliffs as you hike, but the real joy of this trail is ducking into the three lava tubes, a couple of which you can scramble into and spend some time poking around beneath the surface of the desert floor (bring a headlamp).

Red Cliffs even has an arch. It’s not a particularly large arch—just 10 feet wide and eight feet tall—but it’s tucked into a beautiful expanse of sandstone outcroppings hovering above the Virgin River. Combine a series of trails from the Sand Cove trailhead for a 2.2-mile out-and-back that traverses sandy singletrack, slickrock, and a steep sand dune to reach the arch. There’s also a side trail that leads down to the Virgin River if you want to take a dip. Like most trails in Red Cliffs, it’s as much fun to explore the rock formations surrounding the path as it is to hike to the destination.

Red Cliffs has portions of two federally designated Wilderness areas within its borders. The standout of the two is Red Mountain Wilderness, an 18,700-acre slice of desert that sits just north of Snow Canyon State Park. The Red Mountain Trail is a 12.8-mile out-and-back that traverses the wilderness with a trailhead that’s just off of Highway 18. No need to hike the full trail though; knock out the first 2.3 miles and you’ll climb from a sandy desert with sagebrush and pinyon pines into the sandstone outcroppings where Red Mountain Overlook delivers an amazing view of Snow Canyon and the St. George valley below.

Red Cliffs has two campgrounds, the developed Red Cliffs Campground, which has 11 sites with shade structures that will put you within walking distance of the Red Reef Trail ($15 per night, reservations available six months in advance) and the tougher-to-reach Sand Cove Campground, a primitive, backcountry group campground with room for 20 people that’s only accessible by 4WD vehicle (free, but permit required).

If you camp at Sand Cove, you’ll have immediate access to the one-mile out-and-back Anasazi Valley Trail (or Tempi’po’op Trail), which leads to well-preserved ruins of the Puebloans that once called this area home.

Beer: The town of St. George is just 15 minutes away so post-adventure beers and food are readily available. Silver Reef Brewing Co. is known for its barrel-aged beers, which might not be what you’re looking for after a day in the desert, but they have great lagers too, as well as a kitchen pumping out pizzas and wings.

Best Season: Fall through spring for mild temperatures.

Graham Averill is Outside magazine’s national parks columnist. He doesn’t mind a crowd, but understands the value of standing in the middle of the desert all alone.

#8312. Nearly Half of US Hikers Use Cannabis, And Other Strange Findings From the ‘Hiking While High’ Survey

Most hikers have experienced a natural high at some point in their outdoor adventures. Whether it’s the buzz of an athletic flow state or being straight-up stupefied by an amazing view, we’ve all been there. Endorphins fire, oxytocin floods the brain, and you’re overwhelmed with energy, good vibes, and a general sense of peace.

It’s also not news to anyone that some hikers use drugs in nature. People smoke weed on the trail, eat edibles, drink beer, and even take psychedelics. Every year it seems like we publish at least one story with a headline like, “Hikers Rescued After Mushroom Trip Goes Bad” or “Two Hikers Reported Their Friend Dead. It Turned Out They Were Just on Mushrooms.”

But how many hikers are actually hitting the trail under the influence? Those questions and several others led the team at Climbing Kilimanjaro, a Tanzanian guide company, to conduct its “Hiking While High” survey. It polled U.S. adults who hike to find out once and for all how many of them use cannabis, mushrooms, alcohol, and other substances, and importantly, in what circumstances.

The results surprised the folks at Climbing Kilimanjaro. Not just because of how many hikers admitted to using substances on the trail, but because those who do are “surprisingly disciplined about where and when,” Brian Raffio, Kilimanjaro consultant for Climbing Kilimanjaro, says.

“On one hand, we expected to get some respondents who were very into using substances while hiking, and others who were as sober as sober gets,” Raffio says. “What we ended up with was much more of a grey area.”

For the survey, Climbing Kilimanjaro polled 1,008 U.S. adults between September 1 and 3, 2026. The sample was 52 percent women and 46 percent men, all of whom counted hiking as a core interest or hobby. They also grouped respondents by experience level. Hikers self-reported as casual hikers (people who hike a few times a year), regular hikers (people who hike roughly monthly), or avid hikers (people who hike weekly or more).

Of the 1,008 U.S. hikers surveyed, 44 percent said they have hiked under the influence.

Cannabis is far and away the most popular trail substance. A notable 35 percent of respondents admitted to having used it while hiking. Of hikers who take anything, 80 percent said they are reaching for weed. Behind cannabis, alcohol was the second most popular, with 23 percent percent admitting to having drunk beer or liquor while hiking. In third were magic mushrooms, with 15 percent admitting use (and another 24 percent saying they are curious to try psychedelics in nature but never have).

However, a majority—56 percent of hikers—said they have never used any substances on the trail. And while 7 percent of hikers who enhance their hikes say they have felt judged for doing so, surprisingly more of the sober hikers (9 percent) said they have also felt judged, but for their choice to abstain.

“Hikers feeling judged for staying clear-headed rather than for using something was a bit of a head-scratcher for sure,” Raffio says. “Apparently ‘no thanks, I’m good’ raises a few eyebrows.”

What surprised the Climbing Kilimanjaro team even more wasn’t these reported use rates. Instead, it was the level of caution users claim to have when they’re hiking high. More than half (51 percent) said they seek out shorter, easier hikes, and would never try to hike under the influence at high altitude. And nine out of 10 who hiked under the influence said: “There’s at least one place they would never use a substance.”

“In the end, hikers seem to be a fairly self-policing bunch,” Raffio says. “The summit push is where folks want to stay sharp and have their senses fully alert. Whatever [substance] a hiker packs, the trail rewards you when you know the terrain, and you understand your limits.”

The final result that stuck out to Raffio was how many people use hiking to recover. Roughly half of the hikers surveyed said they hit the trail sometimes “to reset after drinking or a night out.”

According to the Outdoor Industry Association (OIA), there are roughly 63 million hikers in the U.S. That makes this sample size anything but definitive. The most obvious takeaway is that people like to enhance their hikes with substances—whether it’s cannabis, magic mushrooms, or something else.

Climbing Kilimanjaro’s results also suggest that hikers are fairly split when it comes to substance use on the trail. While the majority of the respondents had never used anything while hiking, a 56/44 split isn’t that wide of a margin.

For those who do partake, it’s clear (and unsurprising) that cannabis is hikers’ substance of choice—by a long shot.

The Hiking While High survey didn’t poll hikers on their feelings around the topic, and that was intentional. The guide company didn’t want to present opinionated data. It just wanted to open up an honest conversation around the rates of drug use on the trail.

“We asked ourselves: What if this was discussed more openly?” Raffio said. “We wanted to come from a place of curiosity, not judgement.”

#8311. Vanja Matijevec Gave Up His Own Everest Summit to Save Three People

Vanja Matijevec on the Lhotse wall during his 1981 Himalayan expedition (Photo: Aleš Kunaver, kept by the National Museum of Contemporary History of Slovenia)

Vanja Matijevec belonged to a generation of Slovenian alpinists who pushed onto some of the biggest walls in the Himalayas, but one of the defining moments of his climbing life came when he chose not to summit.

On his legendary 1979 expedition to Everest, Matijevec gave up his own planned summit attempt to help Stipe Božić, Stane Belak and Ang Phu, who had become stranded above 8,000 meters during their descent. Božić later remembered Matijevec’s selflessness as helping him survive after he lost a crampon high on the mountain.

Born in Ljubljana on October 14, 1946, Matijevec first encountered the Slovenian mountains as a child, tending cattle on pastures above Tržič. He came to alpinism later, after meeting climber Jože Hočevar through his field work, and began training as a mountain guide in 1975. In 1979, Matijevec, Lado Vidmar and Blaž Oblak made the first ascent of Lucifer (WI4+), a roughly 200-meter frozen waterfall in Gozd Martuljek. The climb, completed with equipment Matijevec later remembered as rudimentary, helped usher in the era of modern ice climbing in Slovenia.

But Matijevec’s ambitions stretched far beyond Slovenia. In 1981, Matijevec and Franček Knez climbed to the rim of Lhotse’s immense South Face, then considered one of the great unsolved problems of Himalayan alpinism. Over the course of his life, Matijevec accumulated more than 30 first ascents, including a direct new route up the West Face of Trisul in 1987. Despite his achievements, his peers remember his kindness more than anything. Fellow Slovenian alpinist Viki Grošelj, who had known Matijevec since their early climbing days, remembered him after his death as a distinctive personality and, simply, “the right man in the right place,” he told Slovenian newspaper Delo.

#8310. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8309. Go Further in Québec’s Winter Wilderness

Snowshoeing in Gaspésie. (Photo: Gaspésie © Gouv.Qc / I. Roberge)

Let this sink in: More than 92 percent of Québec is public land. Come winter, those millions of acres of woods, trails, and open glades get absolutely buried in snow, turning the province into a sprawling winter playground where opportunities for ski touring, Nordic skiing, and multiday snowshoeing abound.

All that wild landscape would be nothing without a trail system to match—which is why it’s a darn good thing that groomed trails and skintracks cover the province, courtesy of Québec’s adventure-minded culture and infrastructure. Cozy rustic huts dot the high country, Nordic centers pepper the lowlands, and there’s an extensive network of designated ski-touring areas across the region.

Behind Québec’s extensive network of winter trails and refuges lies a long tradition of winter travel and exploration.

Long before winter travel became a recreational pursuit, Indigenous peoples used snowshoes and knowledge passed down through generations to navigate the territory now known as Québec. Today, these snow-covered landscapes offer countless opportunities for exploration, from Nordic skiing and multi-day snowshoeing to backcountry adventures.

Today, Québec boasts 28 national parks and dozens of Nordic and cross-country centers. It also boasts plenty of grassroots backcountry ski areas, each complete with trail maps and designated runs. There’s no avalanche mitigation at these sites—they’re wild at heart—but the effortless parking, signage, and basic infrastructure make them a perfect stepping stone between sidecountry and true backcountry. Always remember to come equipped with the appropriate training, equipment, and avalanche awareness. And if you’d rather explore with a qualified guide, you can find businesses certified through Aventure Écotourisme Québec’s Quality-Safety certification program, which sets recognized standards for risk management, guide training and service quality.

Looking to do a little bit of everything? Try Vallée Bras-du-Nord. This all-season adventure center maintains both groomed cross-country ski trails and designated backcountry terrain. Its varied slopes and jaw-dropping views guarantee an unforgettable outing, while a collection of yurts and cabins make it a true ski-in, ski-out getaway. You won’t find a backcountry experience like it anywhere else in North America.

For a more homegrown vibe, head to Sommets du Fjord, a blues-and-blacks zone just beyond the charming village of Petite-Saguenay. The town sits right on the edge of the legendary Saguenay Fjord National Park—yet another ski touring and snowshoeing epicenter—which makes it an ideal multisport base camp.

Want to turn a great day into a great week? Treat yourself to a fully immersive multiday traverse through Québec’s snow-draped winter landscapes. Robust hut systems in national parks like Mont-Tremblant and Monts-Valins make it easy to plan linkups via Nordic ski or snowshoe, and village-to-village trips in the Laurentians like those along Les Routes Blanches offer chances to discover culture and cuisine alongside the stunning landscapes. Simply choose a trail to one or more of the parks’ remote refuges and use them as stopover points to cook, relax, and connect with your adventure buddies—and recharge by a blazing woodstove before hitting the trail again the next day.

The adventure doesn’t end when the skis or snowshoes come off. Beyond the trails, Québec’s welcoming villages, local flavors, and cozy inns offer the perfect setting to unwind and reconnect. Share a well-earned meal, raise a glass of a local wine or brew with your fellow adventurers, and relive the day’s discoveries. Because sometimes, going further isn’t just about the distance you travel, it’s about everything you experience along the way.

Your next winter adventure starts here. Whether you’re seeking powder-filled backcountry descents, multi-day Nordic ski routes or peaceful snowshoe expeditions through snow-covered forests, Québec invites you to explore further. Discover inspiring winter experiences and start planning your next expedition with Bonjour Québec.

#8308. The Best Midlayers for Men and Women (2027)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

November 2026: After testing 63 midlayers while hiking, skiing, fat-biking and climbing in wintry weather, we named the Arc’teryx Atom Hoody our Best Overall pick for its do-it-all balance of warmth, breathability, and weather protection. The most durable option is Mountain Hardwear’s Kor Alloy Jacket. The best for ultra-cold conditions is the Marmot WarmCube Active Novus Hoody.

Midlayers have an outrageously demanding job description. Unlike the super-puffy parkas and belay jackets that we wear to stay warm while hunkering down, midlayers provide insulation during activity—a role that calls for a true multi-tasker. Its duties include keeping us warm while venting excess heat, whisking away sweat, and shielding us from the elements. It’s a tall order, yet our testing team found six insulated midlayer jackets that check all the boxes.

These breathable insulators successfully regulated testers’ temperatures while they skied, hiked, biked, and ran in winter weather conditions. Testers typically sandwiched these jackets between a base layer and a waterproof shell. On climbs, or in dry weather when they ditched the shell, testers also evaluated these toppers for their ability to shed precipitation and buffer gusts.

Sizes: XS-XXXL (men’s), XXS-XXL (women’s) Weight: 12.5 oz. (men’s), 11.3 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Balanced performance + Extended sizes + Lots of pockets – Lacks abrasion resistance

The Atom has been one of our favorite midlayers since its debut in 2009, and its design has hardly changed over the years except for sustainability upgrades. With stretchy fleece side and underarm panels bridging generous helpings of synthetic insulation in the torso, hood, and arms, it strikes the ideal balance of warmth and breathability for cold weather conditions. We found the Atom’s insulated panels—packed with 60 grams of polyester loft—plenty warm down to the teens without an outer layer while skinning and bootpacking in the Tetons. One tester, who wore his hoody ice climbing in Silverton, Colorado, called the Atom’s mix of insulation and breathable fleece “perfectly balanced.”

The unconfining cut fits most bodies, small or large, and two hand pockets and one internal chest pocket secure valuables. The cinchable hood is big enough for a helmet, which came in handy when temps plummeted during one Idaho-based tester’s fat-bike ride in the Tetons. The fabric’s fluorocarbon-free DWR finish repelled drizzle during late-November training runs. But the Atom delivers too much insulation for mild conditions and shoulder seasons (at 35 degrees and above, consider the Atom SL.) And although the breathable fabric feels soft next to skin, it gets pilly after repeated encounters with pack straps and other abrasive tools.

Sizes: S-XL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 18 oz. (men’s), 15.6 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Attractive patterning + Warm – Large packed size

Proving that midlayers don’t have to be thick and bulky to provide significant warmth, this Merino-stuffed puffy goes relatively light on the filling (80-percent wool with biodegradable, bio-based polyester). But even on a 5-degree day in the Tetons, one tester comfortably wore this midlayer while yo-yo-ing backcountry slopes. That wool/synthetic blend stays warm when wet and doesn’t accumulate body odor after a season of sweat. It also scores high marks for sustainability: Ortovox sources wool from sheep living in the German Alps for a shorter supply chain, and the jacket’s shell and lining fabrics use 100-percent recycled polyamide.

Veering from the sausage-casing cut of most Ortovox apparel, this boxy jacket easily accommodates underlayers and pairs best with a loose, freeride-style shell. The matte shell fabric proved plenty abrasion-resistant when worn beneath a pack, and the fabric ably buffered gusts. Testers also liked it at the resort, when the airy fit and naturally regulating insulation (wool breathes better than synthetic fills) kept them comfortable through hard efforts and chilling lift rides. But the teeny zipper pull is tricky to operate with or without gloves, and packability isn’t great, owing to the jacket’s generous cut and less-compressible wool fill.

Sizes: S-XXL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 11 oz. (men’s), 9.5 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Abrasion-resistant + Warm for the weight – Expensive

Here’s an armor-tough jacket that actually breathes—an uncommon combination that made it our Idaho tester’s new go-to. “I’m tired of tearing and patching midlayers,” he said. But this nylon ripstop is far more abrasion- and tear-resistant than anything else I’ve used.” That outer shell uses two versions of 20-denier Pertex Quantum Air: A coated variety on the front body and sleeves to repel precip, and an uncoated stretchy one for the underarms and back. Inside, a ventilating lining made of polyester Octa fibers (called AirMesh) and 40-gram PrimaLoft Gold Active insulation (60-percent recycled) deliver breathable warmth.

The combination creates a highly versatile layer. “From resort skiing at Bogus Basin, wearing it under my shell, to skinning the backcountry at Mores Creek Summit, to climbing at Leslie Gulch and The Fins, this midlayer kept me comfortable, and it didn’t tear while bushwacking or being brushed against rocks,” reported one tester.

Four front pockets hold a satellite communicator and other essentials, and are placed out of the way for belaying and active climbing. Fit is just right—accommodating underlayers without bagging—and the lack of a hood trims unnecessary bulk. But it’s not as warm as some other jackets in test; we found it best used in temperatures above 20 degrees.

When effort and conditions change, this is the breathable, ultralight midlayer that will keep you free and regulated all day long. The PrimaLoft Active Evolve fleece manages your temperature and keeps you dry without trapping heat. The stretch knit has an athletic fit that doesn’t restrict mobility, so you can scramble, climb, and transition on the pitch with ease and comfort. It’s also compact, stowing away into a hidden neck pocket with an elastic cinch and carry tab, so you can stash it away whenever you need to drop a layer.

Sizes: S-XXXL (men’s), XS-XXL (women’s) Weight: 12 oz. (men’s), 10.4 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Sweat-wicking + Very compressible – Minimal insulation

The Dawner is basically a stretchy windbreaker with a fleece liner, making it an all-season midlayer for high-energy activities like cross-country skiing, running, summit-bagging, fat-biking, and more; this was one of our testers’ most-worn pieces thanks to its versatility.

The supple, 20-denier stretch nylon shell (with nine percent Spandex) has a DWR finish that sheds light rain (but won’t hold up in a storm), while 100-gram Octaknit insulation—one of the lightest, most breathable polyester fleeces on the market—lines the interior. It’s exactly what testers wanted while moving fast: the fuzzy interior mopped up sweat as quickly as they produced it, and the lightweight insulation complemented high-output body heat.

The jacket’s generous cut fits over thicker baselayers, yet it’s slick enough to slip under heavier shells. A cinchable helmet-compatible hood and hem made it easy to batten down the hatches during cold starts on pre-dawn backcountry missions. And because it packs down to the size of a grapefruit, it migrated into our Teton tester’s pack for summertime mountaineering adventures too. But this is no super-toaster: During light exertion or in cold temps below 15 degrees, testers wanted something warmer.

Sizes: S-XL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 13 oz. (men’s), 11 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent breathability + Stretchy and unconfining – Not for large bodies

When breathability bests warmth in the Roshambo contest between jackets, this hybrid insulator wins. The First Light 1.0 Stretch Hoody is zoned for high-output activity, with most of its insulation (thin panels of PrimaLoft Gold Active) in the chest, hood and outer arms. The back and underarms are made of a Merino wool jersey (knit with 46 percent nylon) that’s supremely stretchy and breathable. The 20-denier stretch-nylon shell fabric has a DWR finish to repel light snow.

“It works perfectly with a pack—my back is where I usually get too hot and sweaty,” said our Tahoe area tester, who wore it for a season of cross-country skiing, touring, and resort snowboarding (when he topped it with a shell). Testers felt that this jacket worked best in cool to cold temps above 20 degrees.

Packability earned praise, with the whole jacket tucking into the zippered chest pocket around the size of a liter bottle. Two zippered hand pockets and a helmet-sized hood round out the features. The hood lacks adjustability, but our ski-touring tester deemed it functional during above-treeline deployment. Downsides? Sizing tops out at XL, and the jacket fits snug, even on slim builds.

Sizes: S-XXL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 17 oz. (men’s), 15 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Highly insulating + Doesn’t feel bulky – Not weather resistant

This jacket’s triumph is the way it pairs heavyweight insulation—testers wore it in temperatures from 10 below zero to 15 degrees—with outstanding breathability and mobility.

That’s achieved by surrounding plump squares of “featherless” synthetic insulation (polyester flakes that imitate the soft, body-conforming feel of down) with uninsulated strips that promote mobility and ventilation. “It let me move around a lot in cold weather without overheating,” reports our New Hampshire tester after wearing it while backcountry skiing near Zealand Falls Hut and hiking around Franconia Notch. “The gaps in the baffling allow for so much airflow, yet that maximized airflow somehow doesn’t compromise heat retention,” she explains.

Those air channels are just as good at letting wind in, however, so our testers topped this jacket with a shell whenever conditions grew gusty or wet (the 100-percent preconsumer recycled nylon ripstop doesn’t offer much protection beyond drizzle). “This jacket is surprisingly sleek for a puffy, so it doesn’t feel bulky when I wear it under a shell,” said one tester who stayed cozy in it while skiing Sugarloaf in 10-degree temperatures.

Two zippered hand pockets and two internal drop pouches secure handwarmers or a collapsible flask (our fat-biking tester loved this storage for keeping water from freezing). The fit, however, is universally roomy: Some shoppers may want to size down.

Selecting a midlayer is all about finding the sweet spot for your activity and weather conditions. Unlike heavy down hoodies and parkas meant for sitting around camp or belaying ice climbers, midlayers need to keep you warm while also offering breathability.

The warmth-to-breathability ratio is key: In general, a great midlayer should keep you warm, but not so warm that you overheat and soak it with sweat. Protection from wind and precipitation is a bonus, but midlayers are often paired with a waterproof shell in bad weather, so finding that magic warmth-breathability balance should be your priority.

Synthetic fabric and insulation are key to almost all midlayers. Fleece-backed jackets, with their porous fibers, offer the best breathability, but can often be too thin and permeable for very cold or windy conditions. Hybrid or “body-mapped” designs that blend baffled panels with other fabrics are excellent when working up a sweat in colder conditions. Minimally vented synthetic insulated jackets provide the most warmth at the cost of breathability, although they are still a better choice than sweating it out in a down puffy.

Here’s how to decide which midlayer is right for you:

If you are planning to work up a lather, look for breathable layers that will keep you from getting clammy, which can make you hypothermic if you stop moving or encounter big winds. Fleece-backed jackets, like the Stio Dawner (which uses loosely knit Octa fibers), are king when it comes to breathability. If conditions are too windy or frigid, however, ramping up to a midlayer with some synthetic fill, like the Arc’teryx Atom, is a better choice.

Down-filled layers have the best warmth-to-weight ratio when it comes to outdoor gear, but quickly lose that advantage if you’re sweating from the inside or getting soaked from the outside. Synthetic fill (used in most midlayers reviewed here) and fleece-backed jackets keep you warm when wet. So does wool (the Ortovox Ravine Metawool 90), though it does absorb water over time and becomes a soggier, heavier insulator.

If you know it’s going to be frigid or you’ll be moving slow, by all means, go for a thicker puffy like the Marmot WarmCube Active Novus. But if you’re moving fast in typical winter temps, chances are that much insulation will be overkill. It’s not a bad idea to pack two midlayers, or at least include a fleece in your kit, to be prepared for changing temperatures and exertion levels.

If you plan to wear a wind- and waterproof shell over your midlayer, you won’t need to worry about the storm cutting right down to your base layers. If not, look for a piece that offers some wind and water resistance, like the Ortovox Ravine Metawool 90 or Arc’teryx Atom.

Q: What’s the best type of insulation for midlayers?

A: Moisture-resistant synthetic or wool insulation does the best job at maintaining warmth when exposed to sweat and light precipitation. Synthetics come in a range of fibers and constructions, including carpet-like fleeces, sheets of batting, and loose fibers that get sewn into baffles to imitate the warmth and appearance of down (but with superior moisture resistance).

Q: Should I get a midlayer with a hood or without?

A: Depends on how many other hooded jackets you’ll layer with it. A hooded midlayer provides additional warmth and weather protection, but heavy snow can soak it unless you cover it with a shell—which can add up to surplus headwear. A hoodless midlayer under a hooded shell is generally a better choice for stormy conditions.

Q: Why are there no down puffies among the midlayers in this review?

A: Down loses its insulating qualities when it gets damp (as it will when worn as a midlayer for sweaty pursuits). Looking for a technical down jacket? Read on.

Q: Why are midlayer jackets so expensive?

A: Making materials that are simultaneously warm, breathable, and protective is a technological feat that doesn’t come cheap. These multi-tasking materials cost more than ones that do just one job well.

Our testers spend a lot of time outdoors—they qualify as obsessive skiers, mountaineers, ultrarunners, climbers, hikers, and view-admirers. But they also possess the gift of gab. Our testers must be able to say much more about a piece of gear than “it’s awesome” or “it sucks.” They sweat details about, well, sweat, and how apparel responds to their sweat or contributes to its production. They note what makes a jacket feel unconfining, how much wind protection it delivers, and whether it plays nice with a backpack.

For this test, we evaluated 46 of the most breathable midlayers on the market, including full-zip and pullover styles. We asked testers to consider the fit, the breathability, the warmth they enjoyed from each midlayer, and its best application: Is the jacket best for ski-race spectating? Nordic skiing? Après at the resort? All of the above? Only the items that earned raves on performance and livability won coverage among these reviews.

Kelly Bastone moved to the Colorado Rockies in 1998 and has pursued outdoor sports ever since. A freelancer who writes about gear and other outdoor topics for publications such as Backpacker, AFAR, and The Red Bulletin, Bastone has contributed many gear reviews to Outside over the years. An avid skier (resort, Nordic and backcountry), fly-fisher, mountain biker and mushroom forager, she gets the news she needs from the weather report.

#8307. This Sound Map Will Transport You to the PCT From Anywhere

Most backpackers memorialize their trips through photographs. But when LA-based hiker Tom Kelly hit the PCT in 2023, he wanted to document a different, more sensory experience of the trail. Kelly, a nature sound field recordist, composer, and musician, toted 40 ounces of audio recording equipment during his 2,650-mile thru-hike, pausing along the trail to capture the acoustics of the journey. Kelly set up his microphones along burbling creeks and amid chirping insects; he recorded the rustling of grass in the wind, rain on a tent fly, or the chatter of passing hikers. Upon completing his thru-hike, Kelly spent two years compiling his recordings into an interactive and freely accessible sound map.

Reporter Amelia Arvesen spoke to Kelly about his project, the challenges of capturing sound in the backcountry, and what he hopes listeners can gain from the map.

Tom Kelly: It was beautifully calm, really nice day. And we all went to bed, and I woke up to the sound of a great horned owl calling across the lake. And so, the last thing I want to do is wake up and do something, you know? It’s hard enough to wake up to go to the bathroom, much less take your recording equipment, go hike, set up, and you know, do the whole recording process.

I’m a nature sound field recordist, I’m a composer, and music performer based in Los Angeles, California. What led me to recording sound on the PCT is kind of the natural history I have of recording sound in spaces that I would travel to in general. Leading up to the PCT, I’ve always had a field recorder with me because it is just very natural for me to bring it along as my way to interface with the space that I’m in. Getting to the Pacific Crest Trail, I knew that this was going to be my method of creativity while I was hiking. When I set out, I didn’t necessarily know what the project was going to be, or if there was even going to be a project to begin with. But I knew that I wanted to engage in the practice of listening and recording sound along the trail.

In the Mojave Desert, on the north side of the LA Aqueduct, I just sat down on the ground, pulled out my recorder, and started listening. And it was in that moment that I became very aware of where I was and what I was doing. And honestly, I could not be happier in that moment. Comparing the scale of these things—like this massive trail, and then here’s like this little moment—and it’s just, for me, taking in kind of just the depth of those small moments all along the trail is something that’s been really rewarding for me, and has been something I’ve worked through this project to try and convey, and offer as a gift to everyone. I hope that when someone sets out to interact with the sound map that I’ve put out there, that they’re able to get just a little piece of what I was able to experience out there. And that is just the ability to slow down and just really experience nature along the Pacific Crest Trail in this kind of embodied sort of way.

#8306. 5 DIY Climbing Projects to Get You Through the Long Winter

From garage-hammered pitons to swami-belt harnesses, climbers have been making their own equipment since the sport was in its infancy. Gear has come a long way since then. It’s also gotten a heck of a lot more expensive. While we can’t in good faith recommend you save money by making your own chocks and cams, there are still a number of things you can DIY for cheap.

Earlier this month, I went on a DIY kick and decided to hand-make a few pieces myself. Some were items I’d seen friends carry around at the crag. Other ideas came from online forums (and this magazine). With a single trip to the hardware store and a heap of old gear that’s been rotting in the trunk of my car, I was able to make five things—and saved $183 total. Here’s what I came up with, how much each item cost, and what I would do differently next time.

Usual cost: $39.95 for an Edelrid Spinner Leash on Backcountry

Dropped tools are no joke. At Colorado’s ice parks, losing one will typically earn you a swim in a very frigid creek. On multi-pitch ice, you could end up stranded. The trick is to clip your tools to your harness via a bungee system that’s elastic enough to preserve freedom of motion, but not so springy as to send your dropped tool boomeranging pick-first into your thigh

Purpose-made leashes are pricey. A DIY version is free if you have old tent poles lying around your house and only $5 if you need to purchase new shock-cord. I started by clipping the bar tack off an old piece of double-length tubular webbing. I then tied one end of the shock cord to a piece of wire, and shoved it through the tube (this took forever). Once I could access the shock cord from either end, I tied an overhand knot in the center to create a girth-hitchable loop for my harness. I then scrunched the webbing down as much as possible over the two legs of the shock cord, tied overhangs for both carabiners, and melted the edges to finish them.

(Note: For another $10, you can purchase a swivel from most hardware stores, putting the result on par with $80 swiveling leashes.)

Usual cost: $17 for a Personal Tool Tether on Gear Keeper

Some nut tools come with integrated leashes. These don’t add a ton of cost to the tool, but they are boring as all get out. Aftermarket versions from Gear Keeper, Amazon, and beyond aren’t much better. The answer: Make your own out of an old spring-coil keychain bracelet.

First, snip the bracelet in half and feed an electrical crimp onto either end. Next, fold one end of the coil around the inside edge of a nut tool, tuck the end into the nearest crimp, and squeeze the crimp shut with pliers or a crimper tool. Then do the same thing around a small accessory carabiner to complete the tether.

Usual cost: $94.95 for a Metolius Basic Stick Clip at REI

The cost of stick clips has always baffled me, especially since you can make one yourself with a tree branch, a small stick, and a bit of tape. However, I’ll concede that not everyone loves tramping around the crag looking for an appropriately sturdy stick. For those folks, try this trick.

You can buy a painter’s pole from just about any hardware store for relatively cheap. The ones at my local were $20 for 8 feet or $40 for 23. Once you’ve got that, use a couple of stainless steel hose clamps (basically big metal zip ties) to attach a small spring-loaded clamp. Voila!

Usual cost: $54.95 for a Panic Quickdraw on Kong

The internet said I could make one of these by stuffing a piece of webbing into a section of transparent vinyl tubing and tying carabiners to the ends. I tried this and found the result upsettingly floppy. Vinyl tubing is also much more expensive than heavy-duty housing wire, which you can purchase by the foot at Home Depot. Tubing has the added benefit of being foldable.

So, after my first attempt failed, I went back to an old Matt Samet recipe and shoved a section of wire into the hollow core of a length of tubular webbing. I then tied the ends with a water knot to make a continuous loop, and duct-taped a Mad Rock Trigger Wire Carabiner and a bent-gate carabiner to either end. It’s not quite as long as other purpose-made stiffy draws, but it does the trick at a fraction of the price.

Usual cost: $24.95 for a Trango Cord Trapper on Backcountry

I first saw a DIY rope tarp like this at the notoriously dusty Vail Amphitheatre. It’s incredibly lightweight and astonishingly cheap. All you have to do is cut a four-by-four section from a painter’s plastic drop sheet and affix loops to opposite corners. (Note: I used 1 mm-weight plastic, but it felt a little flimsy; 2 mm would be better and only costs $1 more. Tyvek House Wrap would also be superior, but it tends to be more expensive if you don’t happen to have a housing contractor in your life.)

I found that heavy duty plastic shipping tape (especially the kind designed for long-term storage) sticks better than just about anything else. Tape a loop to either corner, and add colored tape to distinguish the belay end from the climber’s end when the rope is stacked.

Do you have the patience of a saint and the multitasking skills of Leslie Knope? Then the Race Director costume is the perfect choice for you. Your night is going to consist of making sure there are ample snacks for all, that trick or treating/holiday party schedules stay on track, that everybody stays safe and healthy, and about a dozen other things that everyone else surely overlooks.

When you select this costume for the spookiest night of the year, the assignment is clear: only speak in the past tense for the entire night. You’re full of nostalgia and cynical disdain for anything modern. You’re basically the Uncle Rico of the evening.

Time to update your watch to the current model, recharge your heart rate strap, and cover every inch of exposed skin with wearable storage.  Because the funnest part of your Halloween is going to be teaching all your friends about the newest and techiest gear on the market.

For this costume, it is crucial that you log more photos than miles.  You are in this costume purely for the likes and kudos. If you exit Zone 1 at any point, you’re doing it wrong.

No pacer or muling needed with this costume. Thanks to your vampire diet and a steady dose of nipple chafing, you’ve got all the nutrition you need to conquer any ultra distance!

#8304. The Joy and Agony of the New York City Marathon’s Five-Borough 50th

The Monday before my second New York City Marathon, I was at Avenue Sky Lounge at the Peak, perched on the 101st floor of 30 Hudson Yards, for the after-party to the New York premiere of Everest: The Other Side. A good room for thinking about big climbs.

Rich Roll, the ultra-endurance athlete and podcaster, was there. We got to talking about Sunday. He admitted he was nervous. A year and a half earlier, after spinal fusion surgery, his surgeon had told him to forget about running. If a man who has built a life on going long was nervous, I figured I was allowed to be, too.

I drifted to the window to look at what we were nervous about. Far to the south, the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, where the marathon starts, was a thin strand of light. Turn around, and there was the dark rectangle of Central Park, where it ends. In between: everything. Brooklyn, Queens, a corner of the Bronx, the long canyon of First Avenue.

You can look at the route on a map forever to try to familiarize yourself with the course and come up with a race plan—don’t bomb up or down the Verrazzano because you’ll pay for it on the Queensboro Bridge, keep it steady in Brooklyn, give it everything on Central Park South. I’d run this course before. And still, from up there, no matter how much I’d planned, I had to ask myself: I signed up for what?

Six days later, there was no backing out. At 4 A.M. on Sunday I was on the F train. This being the morning after Halloween, I had company: a car full of people in costume, Darth Vader and Rosie the Riveter among them, ending their night as I was starting my day. It was also the morning the clocks fell back. The whole city got an extra hour of sleep. Nearly 60,000 of us didn’t get to sleep in, though.

From midtown, a bus to Staten Island. Traffic on the West Side Highway, a road I’ve run hundreds of times, the site of most of my training runs. (Prospect Park’s hills would have been the smarter choice more often, if I’m honest.) Out the window, the sky over Brooklyn went purple, then pink. Brooklyn, where nearly half this race is run, has been my home for most of my life now.

They say the best thing about Jersey City is its view of Manhattan. At 6 A.M. it’s the other way around: the sun rises behind you and lands gold on Jersey City’s glass towers, which throw it back across the old Hudson.

That’s how you measure 26.2 miles in New York. By subway, by bus, on foot, from the air. And, finally, by running it.

This one was going to be special no matter what. Fifty years ago, in 1976, the marathon broke out of Central Park, where it had been run in laps, and took to the streets of all five boroughs. About 2,000 people entered that first city-wide race, only 88 of them women. This year, more than 61,000 finished, nearly 29,000 of them women.

The New York City Marathon is a place where achievement comes in many sizes, and the stories it produces are unusually varied. Andreas Almgren of Sweden won the men’s race in 2:06:01—in the first marathon of his life. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui won the women’s race for the second time in three years. American Jess McClain caught two-time champion Hellen Obiri in the final strides to take second, the first American on the podium here since 2018. Marcel Hug won his eighth wheelchair title; Catherine Debrunner won hers by more than eight minutes.

The stories farther back are just as good. Rich Roll made it to the start and then to the finish. Now 60, he’d trained on just two five-mile run-walks a week, careful not to push his fused spine. And he didn’t run it for himself. He served as run support for former Army Master Sergeant Cedric King, a Purple Heart recipient who lost both legs above the knee to an IED. Afterward, Roll wrote on an Instagram post that the secret to a big life is to make it about “something much larger than yourself.”

William Goodge, a British ultrarunner, crossed the line in Central Park to finish his 50th marathon in 23 days, one in every state, a run that began in Honolulu on October 9. It earned him a Guinness World Record and money for Stand Up To Cancer, in honor of his late mother.

And then there’s Dave Obelkevich, 83, who has finished every five-borough New York City Marathon since that first one in 1976. On Sunday he lined up for number 49, his daughter beside him.

This is also the rare race where watching the last finishers come in is a highlight. This year the last one home was James Thomas, 78, known to his running friends as Marty. He crossed the line around 11:20 P.M., long after the winners had probably gone to bed. It was his 43rd New York City Marathon; he ran his first in 1980.

People call marathon Sunday one of the best days in New York. The reason is community: the bands along Fourth Avenue in Bay Ridge; the hush, then the noise, through Williamsburg as if they never stopped partying from the night before; the roaring crowds when you come off the silence of Queensboro Bridge onto First Avenue; gospel in Harlem; the strangers who yell your name when you need it the most.

This year, I’d need them more than I’d hoped.

My race did not go as planned. The wheels came off on the Queensboro Bridge, as they do for so many. Even people who have never run New York know its reputation for unraveling runners’ dreams. It’s quiet. No crowds, no boost of energy. People are cursing. They’re cramping. If you feel good here, you have a fighting chance. If you don’t, you might be cooked. It turns out I was cooked. I knew I would finish, but the bridge let me know it wasn’t going to be the PR I’d hoped for.

Still, my blowup at the London Marathon in April had taught me something: If you can’t lock into the pace you want, lock into joy. So I power-walked when I had to, to keep my legs from fully cramping. But whenever a kid stuck a hand out, I ran for the high five. And when someone shouted my name with enough conviction, I started running again, as if the words were magic. The signs helped keep me entertained. The best riffed on the Elizabeth Holmes meme: “There’s only two miles to go, why would I deceive you?” (Spotted at mile 18.) And, this being New York: “Run If You Hate Wemby.”

I don’t think I have ever enjoyed Sour Patch Kids as much as the ones a pint-size candy dealer with a giant sack of them pressed into my hand at mile 21, somewhere in Harlem, with five miles still to go. Sour, then sweet.

On the subway home, draped in the orange poncho, I talked with other finishers and unpacked the day. Some were elated simply to have finished. Others were crushed by times I’d have been thrilled with. It reminded me: it isn’t about times. Mostly.

At the dinner table that night, over take-out Kung Pao chicken, my kids and I unpacked it again. I told them I wasn’t happy with my result. That I have a lot to think about in how I train for the next one. But I got it done, and I got through it mostly injury-free. (Toenail count pending.)

My younger daughter was proud of something too. At her second cross-country meet, she ran a minute and a half faster than her first. She’s learning to push herself, gently.

Then we talked about what keeps you going when things get hard. My older daughter said she reminds herself that humans were built to run. That this is what our bodies were made to do.

I’ll take that into the next training block. And be more prepared for the Queensboro Bridge.

#8303. Red Bull’s Newest Ski Film Is Made By Pros—But Is Surprisingly For Everyone

(Photo: Courtesy of Hai Yen / Legs of Steel / Red Bull Content Pool)

Unless all of your friends are die-hard skiers, you’ve probably endured the unfortunate experience of trying to explain ski films. For those used to tidy narratives and strong plots, it can be hard to see why a film that relies mostly on epic drone photography and loose plot development is worth several hours of someone’s time.

Thankfully, now you don’t have to. Filmmaker and pro skier Paddy Graham and his motley crew have done it for you. In his newest film, “We Can’t Not,” Graham writes a love letter to his favorite format, the ski movie. It’s also a message to his family, who appear in the film. The premise: This is Graham’s last hoorah, and before he steps away from the wild (and dangerous) world of steep skiing, he wants to help his family understand what exactly making a ski film entails.

“Paddy has been asked a lot about what he actually does, and why,” Red Bull Media House executive producer Sarah Stow told SKI. The film is essentially a response to the question Graham is trying to answer: Why keep making ski films? Why keep skiing such big lines? Why do you even do this? He can’t not.

The film opens up as many others do: a montage of big mountain skiing set to rock music, a few yew soundbites, and close-up shots of freeride jackets with sponsor logos. Then it takes a turn. We meet our protagonist and start to see the film’s thesis unfurl.

That’s the first moment that I realized this film was going to be different.

The idea of answering a legitimate question is what separates “We Can’t Not” from other films: the journey that the audience follows as Graham sits around a dinner table trying to explain to his children and parents what he does when he says he makes ski films is not unlike conversations we’ve had with our ski-film newbie friends.

The issue with many ski films is they’re created for an audience that already loves to ski; in “We Can’t Not,” the audience can be anyone. One way in which Graham does this is by introducing his cast to the audience like we’re meeting for the first time. Each castmate has an intro that explains his distinct “why”: why he loves to ski and why Graham chose to feature him in the film.

“We really wanted to introduce the athletes so audiences connect with them,” Stow explained, “which is such a smart move in a sport where we often only see goggles and helmets.”

The four other skiers: Kye Peterson, Markus Eder, Tom Ritsch, and Finn Bilous, all complement Graham’s conceit: They’re all a little maverick themselves.

But really, the story isn’t about the group of irreverent skiers—it’s about what compels a group of irreverent skiers to do something as outrageous as shooting another ski film. And, for that matter, why ski films ought to keep existing into the next generation. After all, Instagram and TikTok are full of more short-form ski clips than one could ever get through.

The response, at least according to these diehards? A passion for the sport that runs several standard deviations deeper than your average weekend warrior.

A point made clear by the team’s decision to rent out Hyperbowl, a VR film studio outside Munich that, according to Stow, is “more used to Hollywood productions than a bunch of pro skiers turning up.”

At Hyperbowl, a studio outside Munich that Stow says is “more used to Hollywood productions than a bunch of pro skiers turning up,” the cast found that sometimes the most radical lines exist many miles away from the mountain. The Alaska backdrops had to be scanned on location in advance, and Stow says it was the studio’s first indoor mountain ski shoot. Her verdict: the team was “pushing innovation in this film, not just taking the classic safe route.”

The film’s other big swing is its narrator. Sean Bean, a voice that Game of Thrones and Lord of the Rings fans may recognize, narrates the film. Stow says Bean, despite not being a skier, got so into the project that he became a method voice actor. For one of the final scenes, where he tells the audience the film isn’t over yet, she says he ran in from another room to get the tone right.

Ultimately, the meta-filmmaking in “We Can’t Not” helps to underscore the point of not only their ski film, but all ski films: If you love something deeply enough, no lark seems crazy.

While the film could have used a few female voices—there are no female skiers in the film, though many women lined the production teams for Red Bull — the bigger lesson of “We Can’t Not” resonates in its pure obsession with the art form.

For those who’ve struggled to wrangle their non-skier friends to the theaters, there is a story worth seeing here. For you and for them.

You can watch “We Can’t Not” for free on Red Bull TV, and in select theaters across the world.
