#8281. Is Yellowstone National Park (Back) in Its Wild West Era?

A crowd waits for Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone (Photo: Grant Faint / Getty)

I was sitting on my tailgate, listening to the sounds of songbirds and car honks, when a scuffle broke out in a nearby picnic area. Shouts echoed from the woods as a crowd swarmed two dudes who were shoving and swinging at each other.

Welcome to a hot summer day in Yellowstone National Park. The tussling group seemed to be a motorcycle club, based on their headwear and matching T-shirts. Given their sweaty disposition, I’m not sure “staying hydrated” was listed in the bylaws.

“This place is nuts,” said my wife, returning from the restroom as the two dudes were separated. “What happened here?”

“Fist fight at the Old Faithful corral.” I shrugged.

Then we embarked on a long trek through the semi-apocalyptic parking lot. Frantic drivers whipped around corners, cutting each other off. Exasperated families double-parked and hurried away. Frustrated sightseers returned to their blocked vehicles and laid on the horn. Finally, my wife and I breathed a sigh of relief as we reached the safer confines of the world’s most active hydrothermal zone, the scalding Upper Geyser Basin.

Yellowstone seems to be having a moment as the poster child for rising threats facing the National Park Service (NPS), including bad visitor behavior. While the parks attract record-setting crowds, the Trump administration simultaneously gutted the workforce, cutting NPS staff by nearly 25 percent since 2025. Interpretive signs about important topics like Indigenous displacement and slavery were torn down and replaced by nationalistic propaganda. More trash than ever was recently pulled from Yellowstone geysers, including strange stuff like fidget spinners, fake nails, and a baseball cap displaying the words cowboy hat.

For outdoor enthusiasts watching these disturbing events, it can feel like there’s never been a worse time for national parks such as Yellowstone. My wife, who’d never been there before, was shocked by the wackier things we saw during one high-season day. I arrived better prepared, having come to Yellowstone a grand total of TWO times. My first visit happened 20 years before, when some young whitewater paddlers and I came through on a cross-country road trip. The park felt somewhat calmer back then, but by no means sane. There were about 3 million visitors that year, instead of about 4.5 million now.

Back then, occasional thrill seekers with camcorders chased wildlife, while today’s park paparazzi are influencers with smartphones. Then, like now, I saw a few tourists hopping off boardwalks and stepping across dangerous thermal crusts. I don’t think I’ve ever witnessed anyone stick their fingers in toxic waters, but I’ve definitely seen videos on Tourons of Yellowstone. Each time I’ve gone, we talked about the poor souls who fell and the impulsive daredevils who flung themselves into acidic hot springs, where they were fatally burned or entirely dissolved.

After my first visit, I mostly gave Yellowstone a wide berth. Later, I returned to the mountains and canyons of Wyoming, exploring real places and stories from the Wild West era for a book, Discovering the Outlaw Trail. That’s how I learned that Yellowstone National Park never saw any “good old days,” though some periods have been better or worse for various reasons.

In 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed the first national park into law, word had already spread in the East. Yellowstone was a landscape like no other, filled with abundant wildlife, erupting geysers, and plunging waterfalls. For ages, it was home to nomadic and resident Native peoples like the Mountain Shoshone. Now this volcanic plateau in the Rocky Mountains was threatened by westward expansion of the United States.

For a decade, no more than roughly a thousand visitors made the long and jolting stagecoach journey. Yet the bad behavior started immediately. Seeking souvenirs, vandals hammered away at mineral deposits. Poachers slaughtered countless bison, elk, and bears for their hides, leaving fields of carcasses. Squatters built illegal cabins within the boundaries, hoping the park law would be repealed. Tourists tossed trash, timber, and soap into geysers like Old Faithful. When the erupting fountains sent foaming debris sky high, onlookers cheered. The handful of park staffers watched on, horrified.

After the railroad arrived in 1883, things only got worse. With growing crowds came petty pickpockets, horse thieves, and gunslinging outlaws. Bandits hid behind bends in the road and robbed the passing tourist wagons one by one. The largest stagecoach robberies in U.S. history were said to have happened in Yellowstone. Not once, but three times.

The reason for the mayhem? During the lean federal budgets following the Civil War, Congress had been willing to establish the park, but they weren’t willing to fund it. With limited rules and near-zero enforcement, Yellowstone developed a reputation as a fun place to get away with things.

During our summer day in Yellowstone, my wife and I managed to break away from the crowds. To start, we took a six-mile hike through quieter parts of Upper Geyser Basin, which reminded us why this is a special place worth protecting.

We watched the angled eruption of Daisy Geyser with maybe a dozen fellow visitors. Then we walked past Punch Bowl Spring to a unique feature that few visit, Black Sand Pool. Under our feet, the ground tremored with loud thumps, the result of steam implosions happening beneath the pool’s surface.

During our hike, we met a friendly Oregon family that ranks Yellowstone among their favorite parks. To avoid the craziness, they devised a unique itinerary, staying a few nights each at several park lodges and hiking outward during the quieter mornings. In most ways, this family resembles the majority of parkgoers. Hikers who love the parks, follow the rules, and appreciate the rangers. While poor behavior may be increasing again, such offenders remain a highly visible minority of visitors.

That said, without a few key decisions made during the fading days of the Wild West, Yellowstone might have gone bad altogether.

Tucked away in the woods bordering Norris Geyser Basin, there’s a log building overlooking a small river. Today, this old Army post ironically holds the Museum of the National Park Ranger. Inside, a bronze bust depicts Harry Yount, a legendary figure from Yellowstone history. If the frontiersman’s face looks particularly tired, well, there’s a reason for that.

In 1880, as this nascent national park was being overrun by poachers and miscreants, the meager budget was enough to hire exactly one game warden. He was expected to single-handedly patrol over 3,300 square miles of parkland. Instead, Yount quit in protest after 14 months, reporting that one guy couldn’t do a job that required a well-funded ranger service.

And guess what, the government listened! It just took 35 years. In the meantime, they tried pretty much anything else. They invited some vigilante cowboys, offering them half the collected fines. Naturally, these volunteers avoided the gunslingers and targeted wealthier tourists. So, the U.S. Army was sent in. For decades, half-hearted soldiers chased outlaws beyond park boundaries. The soldiers went back to their posts and waited until the villains cartoonishly returned.

In 1916, the National Park Service was established. Finally, professional rangers assumed responsibility for management, interpretation, and enforcement within an improving park system. Disorder gradually decreased across the West and in Yellowstone, but not entirely. The national parks went on to become a beloved feature of the U.S.

The story of Yellowstone’s destructive early days, and its first park ranger, offers a cautionary lesson that’s easily forgotten: when crowds increase and park budgets and staffing decrease, lawbreakers rise again. We’re seemingly back where we started, with Yellowstone in its Wild West era again.

#8280. The Best Hiking Child Carriers for Travel, Day Hikes, and Long Trails

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Before our daughter AJ arrived, my wife and I braced for the end of an era. We figured our adventurous lifestyle would be long gone (or at least forever changed); our family trips would revolve around nap schedules instead of trails; and our days of spontaneity and exploration would grind to a halt. Turns out, we couldn’t have been more wrong.

At eighteen months, our daughter has probably logged more trail miles than the average adult. She’s joined us on ridgeline hikes in the Blue Ridge Mountains, alpine lake loops in the Rockies, coastal walks in New Brunswick, red-rock rambles in Arches and Zion national parks, and plenty of urban outings around Chicago.

And all the credit goes to the unsung hero of our gear closet: the hiking child carrier.

While she loves to explore the trail on foot in short stints under a mile (for now), we’ve found that she’s most content at longer distances taking in the view from above our shoulders. And when we’re lucky, she’ll even doze off for an afternoon nap mid-hike. We’ve tested several kid carriers on dozens of hikes, looking for the ones that balance comfort, fit, and storage. These are the ones we reach for again and again on our hiking adventures.

We take a lot of hiking-centric trips, and packing for them with a toddler is already a puzzle. Between a Pack ’n Play, a car seat, and a week’s worth of diapers, there’s not much bandwidth to lug along a bulky carrier. The Osprey Poco LT is the exception. At five pounds, nine ounces, and a whopping twenty-five liters of gear storage (nearly double what you’ll find in the Kelty and Deuter carriers below), its weight-to-capacity ratio stomps the competition.

Its internal aluminum frame keeps the pack light but provides enough structure and strength to carry a toddler up to forty pounds. There’s a massive lower zipper compartment that fits extra layers or a change of clothes, a soft cooler with snacks, and diapers with room to spare. And a built-in UPF 50 sunshade unfolds and clips to keep the sun off our kid’s sensitive skin.

But the real magic is in how it packs down. The Poco LT folds completely flat and can easily fit into an airplane’s overhead bin or other tight spaces like a jam-packed trunk on a road trip. I can’t say that about any other child carrier I’ve tested. Since getting this pack, we’ve completely ditched the stroller at the airport in favor of this pack as a lightweight transport option for our kiddo.

The tradeoffs? Thinner shoulder straps and a minimalist design mean it’s not the pack for very long days on the trail. Its shorter hip belt and slim profile also don’t fit larger bodies as well as some of the alternatives below. But for traveling to a place you expect to hike or walk five miles or less, it’s the ideal pick.

For smaller babies not big enough for a full-blown backpack carrier, Osprey also makes the Poco Soft Child Carrier. It cradles your young’un on the front of your body, and once they’re big enough, they can face outward to enjoy the view.

Gearing up for a day hike (especially with a kid) means bringing plenty of extras along for the ride: snacks, layers, sunscreen, bug spray, more snacks, and diapers—to name a few. Two pounds heavier than the Poco LT, this pack certainly feels bulkier. But what it lacks in packability it makes up for in convenient features. If you care less about cutting weight and more about pockets, comfort for your kiddo, and space, the Kelty Journey PerfectFIT Elite is your best bet.

Nine total pockets—including three front zippered pockets in different sizes, dual zippered hip pockets, and large mesh side pockets—offer ample storage for a day hike. We’re big fans of the zippered “dirty” compartment on the underside of the pack to stash soiled clothes, like when an unexpected diaper blowout strikes mid-hike. Six chunky grab handles make it easy to hoist the carrier (with some help from a partner or friend) onto your back or set it down gently. Once it’s down, an oversized kickstand keeps the pack sturdy and balanced, even when your kiddo’s kicking around inside. Kelty clearly cut no corners on the details with this pack.

A pack suitable for sleep is non-negotiable. Who wouldn’t want the serenity of their kid snoozing mid-hike? More miles, fewer meltdowns, as I like to say. AJ zonks out in the Journey PerfectFIT Elite more than in any other carrier. I suspect it’s the roomy seat and oversized chin pad (perfect for resting her head like a pillow), which seem to make settling in for a nap that much easier. We took her on numerous day hikes in the Blue Ridge Mountains around Asheville this fall, and she fell asleep on nearly all of them when we timed our outings around her usual naptime. Now, I’m not promising this pack will put your kid to sleep. But I’m confident its cozy, supportive setup will make a mid-hike nap that much more likely.

Backpacking families and peak-bagging parents who want to take on bigger mileage need a carrier that balances weight, capacity, and comfort. For longer hikes, I grab the Deuter Kid Comfort because it fits like a classic backpacking pack. Think of it as an overnight pack that happens to carry a kid instead of your tent, sleeping pad, and stove.

Fit is where the Kid Comfort shines. A sliding torso adjustment lets whoever’s wearing it (Mama, Momzie, Grandma, or Uncle Daniel, in AJ’s case) dial in a precise fit. And as a notoriously sweaty hiker, I appreciated that the back panel’s raised and ventilated mesh kept air moving without trapping heat on my back. The Kid Comfort’s height-adjustable seat has a cushion that widens as your kid grows. We started AJ in it at ten months old, and at eighteen months, she still rides comfortably with plenty of room for continued use over the next couple of years.

It’s eight ounces heavier than the Journey PerfectFIT Elite, but its greater adjustability and plusher padding make it that much more comfortable on longer, more technical routes. On a recent trip to Arches and Zion national parks, we spent long days exploring the trails. I noticed far less shoulder and hip fatigue with the Kid Comfort compared to the Osprey Poco LT and Kelty Journey PerfectFIT Elite packs, especially given all the scrambling over obstacles or on longer hikes. Ergonomic hip wings secure the weight of the load above your hips. Because the hip belt locks the load in place and the pack doesn’t shift or sway with every step, I felt confident scrambling up and down sandstone, squeezing through slot canyons, and crossing exposed slickrock with AJ on my back.

The tradeoff is its limited storage. At fourteen liters, it holds roughly half as much as the Kelty and Osprey packs. Two stretchy side pockets, hip belt pockets, a large stretch pocket on the back, and a zippered bottom compartment hold the essentials but not much more. It’s enough for a day-long outing, but one of us always also ends up carrying a daypack in addition to the Deuter so we can have everything we need. All to say: This pack is by far the most secure and comfortable on technical trails, especially over longer distances.

#8279. Space Mirrors Promise Daylight in the Dark, But Rescue Teams Aren’t Convinced

A floodlight operated by Reflect Orbital illuminates the night sky. (Photo: Kern County Sheriff’s Office)

In the middle of a dark night on the foothills of Mt. Whitney, onlookers were suddenly flooded by a cone of light 3 miles wide by 10 miles long.

The source was a high-powered floodlight, placed nearby as part of a test exercise by a startup called Reflect Orbital. The Los Angeles-based company’s mission is to “launch the future of sunlight” by placing a swarm of mirrored satellites in low Earth orbit built to redirect sunlight anywhere on Earth on demand. The ground-based floodlight was designed to mimic that effect.

Among a wide range of use cases including agriculture, entertainment, and defense, the company claims rescue as one potential use of its tech in the coming years.

On a country road outside Lone Pine, California, a handful of seasoned rescue volunteers and public safety officials would find out how much — if any — a light field roughly the size of Manhattan and twice as bright as a full moon would improve their chances.

Phillip Cash, operations leader for China Lake Mountain Rescue Group, said his team arrived at the site with optimism.

“My team is largely scientists, engineers, technicians,” he told DarkSky International. “We live for this sort of stuff.”

Group leaders reported to the San Francisco Chronicle and DarkSky International that they envisioned very limited uses for the technology in rescue. They struggled with glare, saw little promise of benefit for helicopter crews, and realized the light could also shut off unexpectedly.

In the test, China Lake MRG and Inyo County SAR rehearsed standard search-and-rescue tasks twice — once in the dark, once under the big light. Crews ran grid searches, stretcher carries, and rope rigging.

Cash first noticed the light made it easier to move around on the ground. His peripheral vision was improved, he told DarkSky, and he didn’t have to worry about stepping in a hole.

But from there, the efficacy mostly faded.

Glare was an issue. While that may or may not be the case with a satellite as the source, Cash noted most rescuers already wear hats at night for this very reason. Limiting any light from the sky or ambient sources preserves night vision.

Another limiting factor of the test was that the organizers placed white pylons in the field as rescue targets, instead of the usual manikins. This created artificial reflectivity that helped Cash’s team find their marks more easily. But, he told DarkSky, his team realized the light could have a problematic effect on actual human subjects — especially anyone lost.

“They’re more likely to go, ‘Oh, look at all this light. Maybe I can find my way back now,’” he said.

Cash was also doubtful it would help SAR helicopter crews locate or navigate at night, noting they already use night vision as standard practice.

His takeaway: For the most part, it’s better to leave the daylight in the daytime.

“It’s not going to make a huge difference to wilderness search and rescue except in a few cases,” Cash told the Chronicle. “We’re pretty good at working at night already.”

Officials’ minds remain open to the technology. A spokesperson for the Kern County Sheriff’s Office told Backpacker that they intend to let SAR groups lead the way on any future implementation. That’s particularly the case with a team like China Lake MRG, a nonprofit that supports its equipment bills mainly through fundraising.

“Given the circumstances, if we needed it, it would definitely be something we would utilize,” said Lori Meza, Kern County Public Information Officer. “But we have no idea what it would cost.”

That price tag could be a real issue. While Reflect Orbital has not officially published any pricing information for its prospective services, Sky & Telescope reported that the company plans to charge around $5,000 per hour for its services, with constellations of multiple satellites — necessary to recreate the kind of bright conditions the team experienced — costing far more. (By comparison, an Airbus H125 helicopter, like the Kern County Sheriff’s Office operates, costs about $2,500 an hour to run, according to charter operator Craft.)

“Most search and rescue teams, at least in California, will not be able to afford it,” Cash told DarkSky. “They won’t even think about affording it. We cannot pay for that sort of thing.”

Emphasizing that any cost was still unknown, Meza said Kern County officials only buy equipment for SAR teams in limited cases. She gave the example of a purchase of vehicles several years ago.

“We do provide certain resources, and there might be an isolated case here or there,” she said. “But a purchase like a contracted service would be a new thing.”

She added that the Sheriff’s Office isn’t taking a position on the technology itself, and that they were grateful to be part of the test.

Other observers are less neutral. DarkSky International has functioned as a sort of public watchdog on Reflect Orbital, lobbying for what it sees as responsible development. Its five principles of outdoor lighting have been widely adopted, and published by the U.S. Department of Energy.

DarkSky sees the same gap in the technology for rescue as China Lake MRG — usefulness, which is also principle one of five.

“The first question is ‘is it needed?’” said Drew Reagan, DarkSky senior marketing and communications manager. “And in this case, the rescue groups found the need was pretty minimal.”

Many of the potential impacts of Reflect’s plan are unknown, because the government has allowed it to move forward with no environmental review.

If its plans become reality, the change in the night environment could be massive. The Federal Communications Commission has given the green light for Reflect to launch its first functional satellite. Its launch plan would place 50,000 in orbit by 2035. Even if they weren’t de facto floodlights, Reagan pointed out, the reflectivity of that many satellites alone would noticeably brighten the night sky everywhere on Earth.

“This represents a fundamentally new technology that will have a direct impact. Not only for the dark sky community or astrotourists, but for migratory birds, for insects,” Reagan said. “It’s not DarkSky’s goal to plunge the world into medieval darkness. We want to be part of these conversations. We just want to make sure we look before we launch.”

#8278. This Climber Just Broke Dean Potter’s Half Dome Speed Record By Free Soloing ‘Snake Dike’

Michael Reese on the summit of Half Dome after breaking the trailhead-to-summit speed record (Photo: Courtesy of Michael Reese)

On October 28, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese set a new fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome, breaking an 11-year record set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour 12 minutes 58 seconds, following Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully and free soloing Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record from May 3, 2015, by about six minutes.

Potter, who famously competed with Hans Florine to set the speed record on the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft), saw the Grizzly Gully to Snake Dike line as a step toward blending trail running and climbing; he was aiming for a sub-two-hour time from trailhead to trailhead. He died 13 days after setting the record in a wingsuit accident at Taft Point.

Reese grew up in Boulder and came to climbing from running and triathlon. In September, he set a new speed record on the First Flatiron, at 7 minutes 51 seconds. After interviewing him last week in Boulder for a deep dive on the culture of free solo speed climbing, Reese told me he was headed for Yosemite the following day. I wished him luck. Having climbed both the First Flatiron and Snake Dike, I knew the latter would be a different game. The grippy, coarse sandstone of the Flatirons is a far cry from the slick, polished granite of Yosemite.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, I caught up with Reese to talk about his extensive training, the day itself, his safety margins on route, why he’s hoarded the same shoes as Potter since 2021, and why he thinks Potter’s record has stood for over a decade.

The following has been lightly edited for concision and clarity.

Michael Reese: Since I got into climbing in 2014, Dean Potter has been one of my idols, probably the one who I looked up to the most. The reason for that is he’s a hybrid athlete, you know? I come from a background in triathlon. I really like to mix cardio and strength. So Dean Potter was such an amazing individual because he had a professional-level aerobic and running fitness in addition to being one of the best free soloists, one of the best speed climbers, and one of the best BASE jumpers and highliners in the world. So I said, “Wow, how amazing is this individual to mix disciplines into territory no one’s ever seen?”

In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners. Of course, you know, this is 2021. Dean Potter had passed away years before. I went in 2021. I got totally destroyed because the approach was way too technical. I got lost, turned around in Grizzly Gully. It’s just such technical terrain. I went back on occasion, and started to learn the very complex approach of Grizzly Gully of alternating slabs, mazes, trees.

Bit by bit, I learned every year. I first went for a speed attempt in 2023. I went again in 2024, but I was really far off. I did 1 hour 37 [minutes] both times because it was really hard to figure out where to go. I wasn’t in as good of shape as I am in now, so I needed more fitness; I needed more practice.

Finally I came back this year, being in a lot better shape, spent two weeks practicing the route, then gave it a go.

Reese: Sixteen times before going for the record. Eight times free solo. Eight times with ropes and practicing the moves.  I practiced the crux 10 times in a row each lap, going back and forth across memorizing holds.  I didn’t really tick anything.  I jumped up and down until I purposefully would slip [while being clipped in]. I’d purposefully slip and find, “Okay, it took this amount of mistakes to actually cause a fall.”

Reese: Yes. The [complexity] of the Grizzly Gully approach, which is probably a low fifth-class approach with a lot of slabs. It has everything. It has running, it has steep, fourth-class dirt. That’s why I consider it the premier of technical mountain running, mixed running, and climbing, because you’re constantly switching gears.

Reese: We always did it a combination of simul-climbing and pitching it out. We would basically simul-climb to the crux section or sections. And then on those crux sections, I would be leading, and I would stop and [built a] traditional anchor and belay them up. That way they could give me a good belay for practicing the crux section.

Reese:  There was a lot of things that almost made it where I wouldn’t have been able to get the record. For example, I had gotten very sick just from being out in the cold. I had a cough. I had rolled my ankle two days before. So I was trying to nurse all these things, and I was just right on the fence of being like, “Am I healthy enough to go through this?”

Reese:  I’d scouted it out two days previously. Then I had a nice rest day where I just went for a picnic. I tried to ice my feet and I taped up my ankle.

My girlfriend started hiking a few hours before me to get in position because I wanted her to get some footage at the base. I hung out in Curry Village and rested. I did my typical routine where I drink a tablespoon of matcha powder to wake myself up and get amped up. I drank a ton of electrolytes because I knew that dehydration could be an issue. It was a very sunny day.

I went to the parking lot, I got on my shoes, and I put on gaiters to try to prevent a rock from going in[to my shoes in] the very dirty terrain. I had on just my watch, shoes, and shorts. No shirt because it was getting warmer. So then I did my typical warm up. I jogged for 15 minutes. I went up Grizzly Gully for a little bit to warm up my steep hiking muscles. I did some 30-second strides to get my heart rate elevated.

I  sipped some water, but tried not to overdo it, did some more strides, and then I meditated for a few minutes just to get in a good head space and say, “This is what I’ve been training for. This is my opportunity and it’s time to live in the moment.”

Reese: Not particularly. People looked at me like I was kind of crazy. Why am I sprinting back and forth at the trailhead? Why do I have no shirt when it’s 40 degrees out?

Reese:  Yeah. I connected my watch to GPS and began the effort from the Mist Trailhead on the pavement there. I had to swerve around some tourists for a minute and then I turned into Grizzly Gully. I didn’t see anyone [else] until I got to the base.

Reese:  Around noon. It was a pretty chill there, about 40 degrees. I wouldn’t mind it to warm up a little. And also because I needed to be very careful about other parties on route. Most places I could pass a party, but in a few places, like those first few pitches in the crux section, it could have been devastating to have a party on the way there.

Reese: I figured starting later would improve my chances of other parties at least being out of the crux section and a little bit further up, and, and that did luckily work out like that.

Reese:  Yeah, that’s a good question. A little bit of both. There’s a lot of places where the beta would vary so much I can’t rehearse everything. On the other hand, as you know, there’s a couple sections that the dike splits into two sections, and I do have each section rehearsed. So for the most part, I have options, and it would be okay besides that crux section. That would be pretty catastrophic.

Reese:  That’s a really good question. I do always prioritize safety. So if I came across a party and they were both in the anchor, or for example, if there was maybe just a just a follower that was securely on a tight top rope and it wouldn’t add any risk to them … and I was on record pace, I would be pretty keen to find a way to make it work, and maybe ask them just not to move, and I could tiptoe around. If there was a case where there was like a leader on the crux who was not looking solid, and I thought that going through would add risk to them or me … I would maybe bail on the attempt. Safety does come first. So yes, I would bail.

Reese:   I was going really hard, but I was saving just enough gas that I knew I wouldn’t, like, completely buckle on the crux. Then I hit the climb and felt really well. I instantly knew it was gonna be a good day on the rock. I was just kind of detecting every minuscule dish, kind of nailing the beta. And there were the people filming me at the crux section, cheering. I’d rehearsed it so much, it felt like a treat just to get across the crux and nail everything and feel really solid there. I still didn’t know if I would get it because I was gonna have to climb it faster than I ever had for the record still.

But it just flowed so well. So I did Snake Dike in 10 [minutes] 55 [seconds]. There was a special moment where I knew I would get the record because I knew I needed to finish them in, you know, 16 minutes or something. I knew I had done them in about 12 or 13 before. [That day] I did them in about 11 minutes. That Death March—that was the crux. As you know, that steep stuff after the Snake Dike, I was starting to kind of buckle, and I had a headache from dehydration. My knees and arms were starting to kind of buckle from lactic acid. But I knew I’d get the record, but I also just wanted to do the best I could and make a time that would last. So I pushed to the summit, sprinted across to the true summit, past the cables to the highest end on the north end. There was a party hanging out there.

I ran and tagged the summit, breathing hard. They were like, “Geez, dude,” like, “What did, what did you do?” I couldn’t even… My response was just dry heaving ’cause I’d gone so hard.

Reese:   The Five Ten Tennies. I bought a big stockpile of them before they went out in 2021 because I knew they were some of the best shoes and may not be made again. It’s the same ones that Dean Potter used on his attempt.

Reese:    I think the length of time honestly was kind of borderline. I think anything longer, it would be important to have something. Anything shorter, you don’t really need it. You do have a good point there. This actually was kind of a borderline scenario . Everyone’s different. For me, this one was right on the fence of bringing anything or not. And it depends on the day. If it’s a hot summer day, maybe I would change and bring something. Under the same conditions, I’m happy with not having anything.

Reese:    I think it’s because of how unique and special the line is. The magic is that most peaks, the fastest way is gonna be running around to the summit. On El Cap, the impressive nose record, you know, an hour 50… you can run around El Cap faster than that. You could run around the side and get up there in under two hours.

On Half Dome, it’s interesting, because from the Mist Trailhead to the summit, you summit up the cable. Most people go up the cables in the Subdome. So that requires running around everything, whereas Snake Dike allows a very direct line to the top.

One reason I think it’s lasted so long is Dean Potter was such an amazing athlete with his combined running and climbing. He had this high level of running combined with being able to solo Snake Dike, obviously a very easy free solo for him. So there are people that may be able to run a little bit faster, but they can’t solo Snake Dike. There are people that can solo Snake Dike, but they have nowhere near the fitness.

There have been some amazing athletes like Nick Elson from Canada.  He was able to tie Dean’s time by taking the shortcut through the forest and running around, splitting Liberty Cap and Broad Nick, shortcut through the forest to cut the switchbacks, and then up the cables.  Now everyone, including myself, starts at the Mist Trailhead. Which is an extra 60 seconds. [Editor’s note: Elson’s trailhead-to-summit time was 1 hour 20 minutes 57 seconds. He currently holds the round-trip speed record on Half Dome, with 2 hours 3 minutes 52 seconds].

When people said, “Oh, is Dean Potter’s vision really the best to go up Grizzly Gully and Snake Dike?” I think what I did proves that Dean Potter had the vision because Nick Elson, being one of the best trail runners… He’s extremely fit, one of the best athletes. I wouldn’t be able to beat his time by eight minutes to the summit off of pure fitness. So the eight-minute difference shows that Dean Potter’s line, the Grizzly Gully-Snake Dike, is just faster than the shortcut through the forest and going up cables.

Reese:    The honest answer is I don’t know. Maybe someone will get really motivated and beat it sooner rather than later. Maybe it’ll be another really long stretch. I tried to put enough of a difference where it’s gonna be a little bit hard.

Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day. I don’t know when that’ll be. The thing is, it’ll probably have to be beaten by Grizzly Gully-Snake Dike, because it’s already been shown that some of the best trail runners can’t go under 1 hour 20 minutes by any other means running around. I think and hope it’ll have to be done by someone comfortable soloing snakes, like a runner-climber hybrid. Which makes Half Dome so special. The fastest way to the top is by climbing. It’s gotta be done by a climber.

Just be sure to pick up something like this Caliart Acrylic Paint Set of 24 Colors with 12 Brushes, as some other paints will just slide right off.

A post shared by Zombie Pumpkins (@zombiepumpkins)

Born in June? Figured as much! You love a conversation starter, so why not turn your pumpkin into a tribute to your favourite film, TV show or character? From a recognisable character silhouette to an iconic symbol, there are endless ways to bring your fandom to life (although we're quite partial to the above tribute to Obsession!).

Whether you opt for a nostalgic favourite or the latest pop culture obsession, your birth month pumpkin is guaranteed to get people talking. it may be a little fiddly, though, so I recommend sketching it out properly before you get cracking.

Warm, sociable and full of personality, you need a birth month pumpkin that makes people smile. For you, then, the goal is a big cheerful grin, rounded eyes and perhaps a few quirky details (like the teeth seen above), all of which will give your creation a welcoming and playful feel.

Hey, it makes a lot of sense! You are, after all, all about bringing people together, so your pumpkin should be just as inviting as your Halloween gathering.

Hardworking, ambitious and never one to shy away from a challenge, August babies need a birth month pumpkin that makes a statement. Inspired by the colorful sugar skulls associated with Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead), this design features intricate floral patterns, decorative swirls and bold colours that transform an ordinary pumpkin into a work of art.

Take your time with the details, experimenting with vibrant paints, symmetrical patterns and marigold-inspired flowers. The more elaborate the design, the better – this is your chance to show off your creativity and create a pumpkin that's guaranteed to turn heads.

Intelligent, organized and with an eye for detail, you appreciate a design that requires a little patience. A pumpkin carved with the silhouette of a sleek black cat, complete with pointed ears, an elegant curled tail and carefully cut-out whiskers, is the perfect way to put your precision to the test (or, failing that, a cute cat face as per the above!).

Take your time mapping out the design before you start carving, making sure every line is just right. You could even add a crescent moon or tiny stars for an extra decorative touch.

Halloween falls in October, so it makes sense that your birth month pumpkin is a real doozy! Charming, sociable and naturally drawn to beautiful things, you need crescent moons, delicate stars and intricate celestial patterns, painted in gold and silver against a midnight-black background, or carefully carved to let the candlelight shine through.

The result? A sophisticated and eye-catching design that's guaranteed to be a conversation starter at any Halloween gathering.

A post shared by Chloe Ward | English Country Home & Seasonal Styling (@oaktreehome)

Empathetic, passionate and with a mysterious side, you love the idea of a little magic hiding just beneath the surface. Enter stage left, then, a birth month pumpkin pumpkin transformed into a tiny fairy cottage, complete with a carved doorway, glowing windows and a winding trail of vines.

Take your design a step further with miniature details, such as a tiny chimney, a moss-covered roof or little mushrooms (you could even copy your birth month mushroom!) nestled around the base. Add a flickering LED light inside to make the windows glow, creating an enchanting scene that looks as though a woodland fairy might appear at any moment.

Generous, optimistic and always up for an adventure, December babies are never afraid to try something a little different. Which means (obviously) that a cheeky ghost pumpkin, complete with a wavy silhouette, playful eyes and a mischievous grin, is the perfect way to bring some fun to your Halloween display.

Don't be afraid to experiment with an unusual shape or a more elaborate design. After all, you like to take risks, and Halloween is the perfect excuse to let your creative side run wild.

So, which birth month pumpkin design will you be trying? Whether you stick to a classic jack-o'-lantern or try something a little more adventurous this year, the honest truth of the matter is this: the very best Halloween pumpkin is the one that lets your personality shine through.

#8274. One Raised Bed, 7 Compact Crops – How to Start Growing Your Own Vegetables in October

Fall is a fab time to begin a productive veggie patch in a raised planter, and these small-space varieties will get your vegetable growing journey off to a great start.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is a great time to start a vegetable garden if you’ve never grown your own before, and these compact crops will bring an abundant harvest in a small space. Sow in October and growing vegetables is so easy as you don’t have to worry about pests or remembering to water your plants every day, and you can still raise plenty of tasty crops at this time of the year. You won’t have to wait long to enjoy your very first harvest, either, and just wait till you taste the difference between homegrown and shop-bought!

The secret to start growing your own vegetables in October is to use a raised bed or planter. Gardening in raised beds is so much more straightforward than growing veggies in the ground as it doesn’t matter a jot what your soil is like as you can instantly create perfect conditions with a tailored potting mix like Miracle-Gro Organic Raised Bed Soil, available from Lowe's.

Another big advantage to growing fall-sown veggies in a raised bed is that you can position the planter in a sheltered, sunny spot to help plants grow well in shorter days and cooler temperatures. You could even place it right up against a house wall to take advantage of your home's heat, and this also makes it simple to throw a layer of horticultural fleece over the top if you need to keep young seedlings cozy through a cold snap.

There are plenty of small-space veggies that thrive in a container, but here's my pick of the best vegetables to sow in October – all compact enough to flourish in a raised bed – if you want to grow your own this fall. So don’t keep dreaming about doing it done day – do it today!

All these vegetable varieties are cold-tolerant, but tailor your choice to your zone. Position your raised bed in a warm, sheltered area of your garden and you can absolutely cheat zone recommendations to successfully grow winter crops. I would happily grow all these varieties in Zone 7 and above, and if you live in a colder zone simply choose a covered raised bed (you'll find my recommendations below) or be ready with a duvet of horticultural fleece (ditto!) when temperatures plummet, and give it a go: for the price of a packet of seeds, it’s well worth the risk.

Think you can’t grow peas through winter? Think again! ‘Meteor’ is an exceptionally hardy variety that’s been bred to withstand freezing temperatures so is one of the best vegetables to sow in fall, with seeds that are smooth and round so resist rot in cool wet soil far better than traditional wrinkled types. What’s more, this variety only grows to a bushy 18 inches high (rather than the wild tangle of 6-feet-high stems of many pea cultivars) so it’s a great choice for a small space. Just push some twiggy sticks into the soil when you sow and the plants will look after themselves.

While you’ll have to wait until May to enjoy the fresh peapods, the plants will get busy through fall growing a strong root system, ready to burst into growth in early spring for an early harvest. And the big advantage of a fall sowing is that you won’t have to net your plants against the pea moth, a pest notorious for ruining summer pea crops. Meteor pea seeds are available from Mr Fothergills USA.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Carrot crops are normally sown in spring and summer but ‘Atomic Red’ is a cool-season specialist that flourishes in low temperatures. And just look at that color! Atomic Red is fully frost-tolerant and fast to grow so in milder zones you could be harvesting around 80 days after an October sowing. In colder climates, plants won’t crop until spring but the harvest will be well worth the wait: cool temperatures make the plant convert its starches into sugars to act as a protective antifreeze, so the carrots taste beautifully sweet.

As well as great flavor, Atomic Red carrots also keep their striking coral-scarlet color through cooking. With roots growing up to 11 inches long, this variety is the perfect size for a raised bed, where the loose soil will favour long, straight carrots. A fall sowing means there’s zero threat from pesky carrot flies, too. Atomic Red carrot seeds are available from Botanical Interests.

The name tells you everything you need to know about this small but hardy veggie! While standard kale varieties can reach up to 3 feet tall, Dwarf Siberian kale stays at a tidy 15 inches high so it’s a smart choice for a raised planter. It survives freezing temperatures and is super-tasty too, staying tender and mild (unlike some of its curly-kale cousins that can grow tough and bitter) and becoming sweetener when exposed to fall frosts.

Young leaves can be eaten raw in salads and smoothies and if you sow in October you'll be enjoying these by late November or December – or wait a few more weeks for mature leaves to sauté with a little garlic and oil. Just be sure to only harvest the outer leaves, leaving the central crown intact, so the plants keep producing as a cut-and-come-again crop. Dwarf Siberian kale seeds are available from Eden Brothers.

Homegrown garlic is a delight so you should definitely find room in your raised bed to plant some cloves. Softneck garlic is best in a small space and the incredibly reliable ‘California Early’ is a perfect choice if you're at the start of your veggie-growing journey. It's very easy to grow and has a highly compact, vertical habit so you can pack plenty into your bed. California Early matures around June, too, clearing your veggie bed in time for mid-summer sowings of other crops.

Because it’s a softneck variety, California Early garlic doesn’t need the long period of freezing weather that hardneck varieties do to form cloves, which means it’ll still form plump bulbs in the warmer conditions of a sheltered raised bed. A raised bed also means you can plant a little deeper than usual, which is the expert secret to growing garlic with the plumpest cloves, even if this your first time growing this crop. California Early garlic bulbs are available from Walmart.

Being able to pick fresh greens for a winter salad is such a joy, and the taste is a far cry from the disinfected leaves sold in many grocery stores. Also known as lambs lettuce and mache, corn salad is the easiest to grow through fall and winter and ‘Vit’ is my pick for glossy, tender leaves with a gourmet nutty flavor.

This French variety is so easy to grow as it’s vigorous and naturally resistant to mildew and, as it only grows to 6 inches high in upright rosettes, it’s a great crop to squeeze in between bigger plants. Vit is incredibly resilient in cold temperatures and quick to crop too, ready to eat in around 50 days. As well as eating mache raw, you can cook the leaves as you would spinach. Organic Vit corn salad seeds are available from Burpee.

Before you brush off the idea of growing radishes, hold up! Have you ever tasted a homegrown radish? Because it’s nothing short of amazing! ‘Purple Plum’ is my pick for an October sowing because this cool-season specialist crops incredibly quickly and, in a warm, sunny spot, you could be harvesting these little heirloom beauties within a month.

Purple Plum radishes are a super choice for a small space because their roots reach peak crunch when they’re just 1½ inches wide. As they’re so quick to crop, you can squeeze them in around slower-maturing crops, too. Another good reason to choose Purple Plum for an October sowing is that – unlike most other radish varieties – they don’t become woody or pithy in damp fall soil if you don’t get round to picking them at the perfect moment.

This is another vegetable that gets sweeter when touched by fall frosts, too, and you can also eat the radish tops, raw in salads or tossed into winter stir fries. Purple Plum radish seeds are available from Botanical Interests.

Another must for a fall sowing is arugula. One packet of seeds will provide a wealth of peppery leaves for salads and garnishes, or try making a zingy spring-is-coming pesto by swapping out basil for arugula. ‘Astro’ is the variety to reach for when sowing in October as it still germinates quickly in cool fall soil and, unlike many other arugula, keeps producing its flavorful green leaves once daylight hours drop below 10 hours a day. It tastes good, too, with a smooth, nutty flavor and a mild peppery bite.

While Astro arugula can tolerate light frosts, growth will slow and speed as temperatures lower and rise, or you can keep a steady supply coming by popping a clear plastic cloche or horticultural fleece over your crop. While you can leave foliage to grow up to 18 inches high, a big advantage to growing your own is that you can pick oh-so tender and tasty leaves when they’re around 4 inches high, and the plant will quickly grow more of this cut-and-come-again crop. Astro arugula seeds are available from Botanical Interests.

To successfully grow veggies in a raised bed, the planter needs to be at least 8 inches deep, and ideally a little deeper. However, few crops need more than an 18-inch depth of soil to grow well, and it's expensive to fill a very deep planter with potting soil. If you want to grow deep-rooting crops such as potatoes and heavy feeders like zucchini, it’s much more cost-effective to grow these separately in deep fabric planters, or choose an open-based planter that allows roots to grow into the ground.

Choose a raised planter with a built-in cover that makes it easy to keep fall-sown seeds warm for fast germination and shield plants from plummeting temperatures.

This mini greenhouse is separate to the 68” x 33” x 12.5” open-base planter, so is easily removed once weather improves in spring. It allows easy access to your crops and excellent airflow with huge roll-up windows, too.

With a planter box that’s just deep enough at 41” x 20.5” x 10.25”, this raised planter has a liner to prevent dirt from falling through the drainage holes and a tall mini-greenhouse cover with roll-up door.

This durable open-base 6’ x 3’ x 1” galvanised oval planter comes with a frame to hold the zippered screen. If you have hungry critters in your garden, this set-up will protect seedlings from becoming snacks, too.

Growing veggies on your patio means you can use the warmth and shelter of your house to keep plants cozy through winter. Dark-toned paving also absorbs the sun’s heat during the day then releases it later, so a patio often escapes frost, too. If you need to shelter plants during cold snaps, simply throw a lightweight plant cover or horticultural fleece over the planter. Choose one that allows sunlight and air to pass through, like this Harvest-Guard Cover from Walmart, and you can leave it on day and night.

If you’re serious about growing veggies long-term then the clever design of this durable planter means you can still grow deep-root crops without spending a fortune on soil. A smaller size is available.

A wheeled raised bed makes it easy to move your veggies to a sheltered spot over winter and this 37.4” x 15.7” 8.27” planter is just the job for dipping your toe into growing leafy greens and shallow root crops.

This smart wicker-look planter offers a good planting depth for a compact space, and a water reservoir and gauge make it easy to get irrigation right. A drainage tap makes this suitable for a balcony or indoors too.

Starting a veggie bed needn’t be expensive if you opt for an open-base raised metal planter that allows plants to grow down into the soil. There are all sorts of shapes and sizes available, of varying quality, so shop smart: only buy galvanised steel (and it’s a bonus if it’s powder-coated), check for central support strips that span the planter for added strength, and look for a protective strip running around the top edge for your own comfort.

You can buy drawstring frost covers to fit most sizes of these raised beds, such as this Raised Bed Frost Cover with Insulating Aluminium Liner from Walmart, that are quick and easy to pop on and off during cold snaps.

Measuring a generous 6’ x 3’ x 1’, this galvanized metal planter box gives you lots of growing space at a great price. It’s powder-coated for durability in a smart charcoal gray and features safety edging and anti-rust screws.

This well-priced 4’ x 2’ x 1’ galvanized raised bed kit is a great size for a starter veg patch and comes with all the tools and screws you need for assembly. It has a protective rubber edge and a central support strip.

You'll often find great deals on open-based planters with more unusual dimensions at the end of peak growing season, like this 8’ x 2’ x 17” rust-resistant bed in olive green, with support bars and a protective rim.

With soil temperatures still relatively warm and the risk of heat and drought extremes behind you, fall is the perfect time to transplant these key backyard favorites

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There’s something about fall that naturally inspires new beginnings and makes us want to head off in new directions. With the arrival of brisk breezes, shifting colors and falling leaves, we often feel the urge to rearrange living spaces, including those outdoors. While spring gets most of the glory for planting, autumn is a great season for dividing, moving and relocating key established ornamentals.

If you do transplant these perennials and shrubs now, you can take advantage of unique conditions. Fall brings cool air that reduces transpiration and moisture stress, while the soil remains warm from months of sun, and depending on where you live, you’ll be seeing more rainfall. This means relocated plants have time to establish strong roots before winter sets in, and it reduces transplant shock.

Rather than wasting energy recovering from a disruptive spring move, a fall-transplanted perennial can hit the ground running early next year. This doesn’t apply to every single plant, but if you have overcrowded perennials, let’s go! By giving key plants a fresh start this October, you boost their long-term health, enhance your curb appeal, and set your yard up for its finest season yet.

In my experience, it’s pretty rare to add a perennial or shrub and simply leave it in place untouched for the next decade. As landscapes mature, light patterns shift, beds crowd each other out, and soil nutrients may deplete. I plant perennials knowing that it’s very likely my hostas or peonies will, in time, need to be relocated. But that doesn’t bother me at all. It’s like kids outgrowing their shoes: relocating is a natural, normal part of growth and healthy backyard care.

Fall is considered the best season for transplanting. We have touched on changes in weather, and this generally means transplants won’t burn or dry out quickly. During spring, plants funnel energy into expanding leaves, shoots, and flower buds. If you dig up a plant in spring, you sever its feeder roots when energy demands are peak. In fall, though, top growth declines or enters dormancy, allowing the plant to redirect energy into root growth and cellular repair, which is exactly what transplants need.

While the air is cooler, the soil is still warm from summer sun. Depending on your USDA hardiness zone, this is ideal for the root growth. Plants transplanted in fall have a strong root network by spring. Also, it may not rain every day, but autumn brings more rain than summer. Plants prefer rainwater to tap water, and regular moisture favors root development. You can check ground levels before transplanting by using a diagnostic tool like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon.

Insect populations peak in summer and decline in fall, which means that your plants won’t have to be fighting aphids, mites or root-chewing grubs. This means newly moved plants won't have to battle active pest pressure while establishing in the vulnerable time after transplanting. Before moving these plants, just be sure to prepare the new site. Dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball and enrich the backfill with rich compost or worm castings to ensure smooth, stress-free root expansion of the following plants…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fall transplanting isn't ideal for every plant. Keep your garden gloves off tender perennials such as dahlias, gladioli, and tropical hibiscus. You should also avoid plants with deep taproots, like false indigo or butterfly weed, and broadleaf evergreens such as boxwoods, rhododendrons, and gardenias. Broadleaf evergreens retain leaves all winter and can dry out if their roots are disturbed now. However, these 6 stars are receptive to an October move. Many can be divided at the same time, giving you free extra plants to spread around borders or share with friends.

Hostas are amongst the easiest and most forgiving perennials to transplant or divide this month. Move them in fall, 4-6 weeks before your region's first hard ground freeze. This takes advantage of warm soil, while cool air prevents large leaves from scorching. A major benefit of an October move is visual. Top growth is often visible before heavy frosts flatten the leaves, helping you to position the plant exactly where you want it. Hostas work well in dappled shade, alongside ferns or coral bells.

Prepare the new site first by adding some organic leaf mold or compost into the soil. Use a sharp spade or fork to dig a ring around the outer drip line. Lift the root ball out gently. If the crown is overcrowded, slice it into smaller divisions using a sharp knife, ensuring each piece retains fleshy roots and a few eye buds. Replant at the original depth, water deeply, and apply a 2-inch (5cm) layer of organic mulch. If you need a good knife, try the versatile Fiskars Hori Hori Knife, available from Walmart. Its serrated edge is ideal for slicing through thick divisions with minimal damage.

Whether you are growing classic herbaceous peonies like Sarah Bernhardt or sturdy Itoh intersectional hybrids, this month is a great time for transplanting and division. Peonies (Paeonia spp.) dislike being moved during active spring growth, but in autumn they are entering dormancy. Moving them now gives roots time to anchor into the soil before it freezes, without the stress of supporting top foliage.

Once the foliage turns bronze or wilts after early frosts, cut the stems back to roughly 2 inches (5cm) above the ground. Carefully dig around the root mass, lifting the plant without snapping the thick roots. Rinse off any excess soil to expose the pink eyes (these are the dormant buds). If dividing, use a clean knife to create sections with at least 3-5 strong eyes and a generous root.

Replant in a sunny, well-draining spot, making sure the eyes sit no deeper than 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the surface. Give your peonies a gentle, slow-release phosphorus and calcium boost by adding a handful of Down To Earth Fish Bone Meal from Lowe’s.

If you live in a mild or moderate climate, then you can relocate crowded bearded iris (Iris germanica) this month, provided you get them settled at least 4 weeks before severe freezes so roots have time to establish. Transplanting allows you to relocate bearded iris plants to sunnier garden spots and eliminate iris borer eggs or leaf spot fungal spores that can hide in old foliage over winter.

Dig up the plant using a garden fork, shaking away loose soil. Slice or snap the healthy outer rhizomes from the central mass, throwing away the central rhizome. Inspect each piece for soft spots or borer holes, discarding damaged sections. Trim the leaves back into an inverted V shape 4-6 inches (10-15cm) tall to reduce wind rock and stress. Replant in full sun, settling the roots over a small soil mound in the planting hole. Make sure the tops of the rhizomes are slightly above the soil surface.

Add a light mulch, such as team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch from Amazon, to reduce the risk of frost-heave. However, it’s not a good idea to divide plants at this time. Wait until late summer, after the flowers fade.

Daylilies (Hemerocallis spp.) are legendary for their resilient nature, and in moderate climates (zones 4-9) you can transplant and divide them during October. Just make sure you do this 4 weeks before the first hard frost. Over time, daylily clumps get so densely packed that flower production can drop off. Moving and dividing every 3-5 years restores vigor, resulting in larger flower scapes and a longer bloom season.

Before digging up your daylily, trim the foliage back by half to make it easier to manage. Insert your spade beneath the root ball and lever the plant out. Pull the thick, fleshy roots apart by hand or use two back-to-back pitchforks to pry the clump into divisions. Prepare your new planting hole by adding a handful of earthworm castings, such as Earth Science Earthworm Castings from Amazon. Drape the roots over the mound. Position the plant so the crown sits an inch (2.5cm) below the surface. Backfill, press firmly, water well and mulch.

Moving a large hydrangea (Hydrangea spp.) in midsummer can lead to severe wilt and leaf scorching. However, moving one in late October is fine, as long as your shrub has stopped flowering or entered dormancy. Whether you are relocating a bigleaf (H. macrophylla), panicle (H. paniculata), or oakleaf hydrangea (H. quercifolia), transplanting your hydrangea this month gives the extensive root system time to settle into cool, moist soil before pushing out heavy spring leaves.

Select a new location that offers morning sun and afternoon shade, and water the hydrangea deeply 24 hours before moving. Hydrangeas have broad roots that grow wide rather than deep, so dig a wide trench around the outer branch perimeter. Lift the root ball with as much soil as possible. Transfer to the new hole at its original growing depth, backfill with native soil and organic compost, and tamp. Apply a gentle, diluted seaweed drench, such as GS Plant Foods Organic Liquid Kelp from Walmart, to minimize shock after transplanting your hydrangea. Insulate the base with 3 inches (8cm) of organic wood mulch to retain moisture through winter.

Roses (Rosa spp.) respond well to a late October move, provided the shrub has begun entering semi-dormancy following its final bloom flush. Relocating a rose in fall allows cut root ends to callus over and sprout fine feeder roots in warm soil, giving the plant a massive jumpstart over bare-root roses planted in spring.

Prepare the new planting hole in a bright, sunny spot that gets at least 6 hours of direct sunlight daily. Blend in some well-rotted compost, or optionally condition the soil with a little Wakefield Biochar Premium Soil Conditioner, available from Lowe’s. This enhances aeration and water retention around deep rose roots. Make sure you water your rose bush the day before digging. Prune top growth back by a third to a half. This makes canes easier to handle and balances top weight with root loss.

Using a spade, dig a deep circle around the root ball, angling the blade inward to preserve the main taproot and roots. Lift the rose and transfer to the new site. Make sure the graft union (the bump at the base of the stems) sits 2 inches (5cm) below the soil in colder regions for winter protection. Backfill, press firmly, and water deeply.

Inspired by Goldie Hawn’s fountain?Here’s how to layer moisture-loving plants around any water feature for a truly lush result.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whoever thought we’d be taking planting advice from Goldie Hawn? The talented actor is best known for her decades-long Hollywood career (and her enduring romance with Kurt Russell), but her garden is increasingly giving us plenty to talk about, too.

From the art of getting container planting just right (it's all down to Goldie's one-plant rule) to the beautiful floral displays of her daughter, Kate Hudson, there’s inspiration to be found in this family’s approach to outdoor spaces. And while you might not expect a Hollywood garden to offer much in the way of practical advice for the rest of us, sometimes the most effective design ideas are also the simplest.

That brings us to one particularly lovely detail in Goldie’s Pacific Palisades garden: the way plants and water work together.

Yes, Goldie Hawn’s Pacific Palisades home was featured in a People magazine shoot, and the outdoor space contained one of the best accidental lessons for garden design you’ll see this year.

Perched on a fountain that flows into a pool, she is surrounded by dense, lush planting on all sides, so much so that it looks like it might swallow her up. And, while the fountain is gorgeous, the lesson has very little to do with it and more with the plants themselves. Take away the plants, and you have a nice water feature, but leave them, and your garden feels like something straight out of Jurassic Park (in a good way, and without the dinosaurs).

Plants and water working together rather than separately is one of the most underused principles in garden design, and it applies to your tiny backyard in suburban North Carolina as it does in a Hollywood fountain at Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell’s house.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Kendahl Kreps, Director of Marketing at Oase North America, explains why water and plants work so well together. She says that“water has a naturally reflective, open quality, while plants introduce texture, colour, movement and enclosure. A fountain or waterfall gives the eye a focal point; planting softens the hard edges around it and makes the feature feel integrated into the landscape rather than simply placed in it.”

Aiza, sustainability writer at GreenerPulse, emphasizes this, saying, “a still surface doubles the planting in reflection, so the garden looks twice as full for free. Moving water brings sound and shimmer; plants bring stillness and texture. One without the other feels half finished.”

In the case of Goldie Hawn’s garden, the dense green plants around the fountain slow down your eye before it even reaches the water, and that’s not accidental.

As Goldie Hawn's garden has well and truly proven, placement is highly important, as not every plant is super happy with constant moisture around its roots. Jon Graham, CEO of Element Plumbing, Heating and Air, whose team installs outdoor water features professionally, notes that “the humidity around most water features runs roughly 15% higher than the surrounding yard; that’s why moisture-loving plants like elephant ears and Japanese iris thrive close to the source. Their broad leaves and fibrous root systems handle constant splash without rotting at the base.”

Aiza’s list for the wettest positions includes blue flag iris, pickerelweed, cardinal flower, marsh marigold, and dwarf cattail. Slightly further back, where the soil stays damp but not waterlogged: ligularia, astilbe, and hostas in shaded spots.

Kreps adds a practical favorite for smaller water features: “A common plant used near smaller water features is Creeping Jenny, which will actually use the excess splash to grow while walking itself into the feature.”

You’ll want to keep your plant design from becoming chaotic, as there is a fine line between that and lush, and the key is to make like Goldie Hawn and introduce layering. All three experts agree on the same basic formula, and Graham puts it clearly. He says, “Tall ornamental grasses at the back, mid-level sedges in the middle, and low ground covers like blue star creeper along the edge give the eye a clear path to follow.”

Kreps adds, “A lush planting scheme doesn’t mean putting dozens of different plants around the fountain. Instead, repeat a limited number of plants in groups and give each layer a clear job.”

Aiza recommends capping the palette at five to seven plants total, planting in drifts of three, five, or seven, and repeating each plant in at least three spots around the feature. The other essential: “Give the bed a crisp edge, stone or steel, so the planting reads as a designed shape even when it fills in.”

Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell live in California, where a jungle-like climate is highly achievable in their garden. However, even if you live in a cooler climate, you can still get the same thing; it just requires thinking about leaf scale rather than specific species.

“You do not need California weather, you need big leaves,” says Aiza. Hardy banana, gunnera, giant hostas like Empress Wu, canna lilies, and Fatsia japonica all create that broad-leaf drama in temperate gardens. “The trick is contrast: a few bold leaves rising out of fine ferns and grasses reads tropical even in zone 6.”

Graham adds that “in cooler climates, bold leaf texture does the heavy lifting — hostas, ligularia and hardy hibiscus all handle zone 4 winters and still produce that dense, tropical feel.”

Some plants seem like obvious choices near water, but actually they should be used with caution. Graham is direct on invasive spreaders: “The biggest mistake I see is planting invasive spreaders like mint directly near the water source. They overtake beds in a single growing season and can clog pump intakes within two to three seasons if planted less than 18 inches from the feature.”

Aiza flags purple loosestrife, yellow flag iris, and running bamboo as plants that look innocent near water and then cause serious problems. And lavender or rosemary, however beautiful elsewhere, will rot quickly in a consistently damp splash zone.

The lesson from Goldie Hawn’s Pacific Palisades garden is simple, then. Treat the water feature as an anchor, but remember the planting gives it the atmosphere you’re looking for. If you get the layers right and choose plants that actually want to be there, the result looks far more expensive than it actually is.

Planting compact flowering shrubs in fall gives roots time to establish before winter, rewarding gardeners with an explosion of color the following spring. What types of shrubs should you consider? You’ll want space-saving shrubs that punch well above their size.

Below is my shortlist of compact flowering shrubs to plant in fall for spring blooms. While you may want to add a few more bushes to fill up your space, these gems are a great way to get started.

The old saying goes that April showers bring May flowers, but in fact, the best spring flowers come from all that autumn rain. Fall is a wonderful time to plant shrubs, perhaps the very best time, if you want spring blooms.

First, the air grows cooler as October arrives while the soil is still warm. This combination supports root growth and, combined with shorter days, reduces heat stress and evaporation. Add the likelihood of fall rain, and you’ve got a wonderful window to plant shrubs.

These fall conditions help your plants establish root systems during the cooler months. That means the shrubs can invest their energy in foliage and flowers when spring arrives.

#8267. Baby Sign Language 101: Baby’s First Signs

Well before they utter their first words, infants as young as six months can learn to sign. Baby sign language is thought to reduce baby’s frustration levels, boost self-esteem, and bolster language development. And you don’t need to be an expert. Begin with three to five signs, saying the word as you sign it. Encourage other caregivers and siblings to join in. Then repeat, repeat, repeat. Your little one’s motor skills may not allow them to perfectly mimic the sign, so watch for hand gestures that indicate she’s trying, usually within two months of being introduced to it. Here are some great baby sign language starter signs.

Show your little one the sign for a person they know, like mommy, daddy, brother, grandma, or baby. It doesn’t matter if you plan to use mommy, mama, mother, or mom; the sign is the same — using an open palm with fingers spread, tap your thumb on your chin. For “daddy” and its variations, use the same hand position; only tap the forehead. Remember to point to the person as you sign.

Food is a great motivator. Teach your little eater the sign for their favorite food or the ones for eat, milk, or bottle. When Baby’s plate is empty, “more” and “all done” allow them to set the pace for the meal. To sign “more,” press the thumb and fingertips of each hand together, and then tap the fingertips of the two hands together several times. Look for baby to put their fists or palms together as they start to get the hang of this sign.

Animal signs are fun because they often mimic some aspect of the animal. Baby will love learning the signs for her beloved pet or for the animals around the neighborhood. Dog, cat, fish, and bird are all good candidates. You can even have a favorite stuffed animal act out the motions for its sign. The baby sign for “dog” is patting your hand to your hip, as if calling a dog. This is a slight modification from the American Sign Language version, which includes a snap that is too difficult for emerging motor skills.

It’s never too early to introduce your little bundle to being polite. “Please” is a great word to start with. Try this technique when it’s clear your baby desires something specific, like a toy or a drink, and he’s not upset or in any distress. Say that you will get it and ask if they can say “please,” demonstrating the sign as you do so. Then give them the item, regardless of whether they do the sign or not. Eventually the concept will begin to sink in, and they’ll be doing it on his own. With a flat hand and thumb extended, sign “please” by moving the palm of your hand in a circular motion in front of your chest.

Use the repetition of baby’s routine as an opportunity to teach her the signs of daily life. Learn “sleep” for naptime and bedtime. Let baby know it’s playtime by signing “play,” and then show her the sign for whatever you are playing with, be it a ball, blocks, or a book. The sign for “bath” mimics the act of washing. To do this sign, simply move both your fists up and down in front of your chest as if scrubbing it.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8264. 4 Quick Activities to Try If Your Kid Is Wired at Bedtime

As a parent, you probably know that bedtime can go two ways: one, your kid was so busy all day they’re exhausted and can’t wait to get that story and hit the pillow. Or two, they haven’t had a chance to expel the endless amounts of energy they store in their little bodies. The latter is where a normal nighttime routine can get tricky because that second wind is no joke. They’ll be jumping, singing, fidgeting, and doing everything they can to delay the inevitable “lights out” moment, meaning there’s even less time for you to binge a few episodes of your new favorite show.

If you’re dealing with a kid who’s wired at bedtime, there are a few things you can do to make the transition to dreamland easier. Mom and pediatric occupational therapist Courtney English recently shared a few of her favorite sensory activities that help kids calm down before bed, and they’re simple but effective. Her TikTok video shows what parents can do:

Dr. Megan Anna Neff writes for Neurodivergent Insights that “Proprioception plays a role in body awareness, self-regulation, coordination, posture, and the ability to focus.” Playing a short game of tag in their bedroom will allow kids to realize where they are at that very moment in time, helping them to center themselves and be present.

Massage is known to be a great way to receive proprioceptive input, and what English calls a sensory sandwich (putting your child between two pillows and pressing down) is a low-energy activity that’ll give their body what it needs to relax.

Vestibular input is another important factor for kids who are wired at bedtime. As Laura Petrix writes for the OT Butterfly, it’s “a network of parts in your inner ear that contribute to your sense of balance and coordination.” It allows our bodies to know when we’re falling, move in coordinated ways (like riding a bike), and know the right speed to walk around other people. The combination of singing and rocking helps to calm the vestibular system by providing auditory rhythm and linear movement.

This is another great type of massage or touch activity that provides proprioceptive input to the nervous system. Plus, it’s a great chance to get a few snuggles in there before they close their eyes.

These activities are no secret to occupational therapists, who use them often. In fact, English has offered other sensory activities that are appropriate for bedtime, including tossing around a weighted animal and doing the “clock move.” But they’re something we should all have in our back pockets next time we’ve got monkeys jumping on the bed.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.
